title: Man dies after two men stabbed at Ramsgate waterfront
author: Stuart Maisner
content:
![Aerial shot of Ramsgate harbour daytime](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/72ab/live/9886e930-9edf-11f1-8d55-75706e02ede8.jpg)
Police and the ambulance service were called to Ramsgate Harbour at 04:45 BST
- Published
A man who was stabbed in a Kent town overnight has now died from his injuries, with police confirming a murder investigation has begun.
Kent Police said officers were called to the Ramsgate Harbour area at about 04:45 BST to reports of a man with a knife. Two men had been stabbed, one in Harbour Street and one in Harbour Parade.
Both were taken to hospital, where the 52-year-old man who was found in Harbour Street later died, the force said.
A 21-year-old local man who was arrested shortly after the incident remains in custody, it added.
The second victim, a 48-year-old man found in Harbour Parade, has now been released from hospital.
Kent Police said it was not looking for anyone else in connection with the incident.
The force is appealing for anyone with information to come forward.
Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: Kent Police have launched a murder investigation after two men were stabbed near Ramsgate Harbour. A 52-year-old man found in Harbour Street later died in the hospital, while a 48-year-old man found in Harbour Parade has been discharged. A 21-year-old local man has been arrested and remains in police custody in connection with the attack.
key_points: A murder investigation has begun following a stabbing incident at the Ramsgate waterfront.
A 52-year-old victim died from his injuries after being found in Harbour Street.
A second victim, aged 48, was treated at the hospital and has since been released.
A 21-year-old local man was arrested shortly after the incident and remains in custody.
Police stated they are not looking for any other suspects in connection with the case.

title: Russia withdraws ambassador from Britain
author: Emily Smith
content:
![Mr Kelin being interviewed](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000337459341_17874683250060_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqnZlAO2SbRIMsCE2ccfSvVJgojZYlP8f0i9h2tPqCNsM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Mr Kelin being interviewed](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000337459341_17874683250060_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqnZlAO2SbRIMsCE2ccfSvVJgojZYlP8f0i9h2tPqCNsM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Russia has withdrawn its ambassador from the UK, declaring that Britain should “reconsider its policies”.
Andrei Kelin, who served as Moscow’s chief representative in London for more than seven years, left his diplomatic position on July 21.
A replacement has not been appointed, raising concerns of a breakdown in diplomatic relations between the two countries.
On Monday, Russia threatened Britain with “consequences” after British-made drones were used to strike Russian territory for the first time.
![The two men embrace. Mr Burnham is taller. Both wear black](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000496705723_17874684617850_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
A spokesman for the Russian embassy said Mr Kelin had made “considerable efforts to preserve contacts and channels of communication” with London and warned that the Government was choosing a “path of confrontation” with Russia.
“He left Britain in the hope that a more constructive and respectful dialogue could eventually be restored, should the UK reconsider its policies towards our country,” he said.
The spokesman added that the Kremlin had not submitted a replacement candidate to the Foreign Office, and said: “In the meantime, the embassy is headed by the chargé d’affaires.”
The ambassador’s departure was announced internally at the embassy during a party for Russia Day on June 11. No formal announcement or statement was made to the public.
Also that day, Nigel Casey, Britain’s ambassador to Moscow, held rare talks with Russia’s deputy foreign minister, and German and French representatives, to condemn Russia’s aggression in Ukraine.
![Mr Casey is surrounded by a press pack](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000451405836_17874683936180_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqEduPGWXTgvtbFyMaMlYatt5HfJMDGz2ut_fb3D_DyLc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
It is not clear why Mr Kelin left, after serving in the position since 2019, or whether Russia plans to leave a lower-ranking official in the post indefinitely.
Withdrawing an ambassador is a formal way of expressing displeasure with a country without completely severing diplomatic ties.
Later, a Russian embassy statement posted on Telegram said relations with the UK had waned, but there was nothing to suggest a wish to downgrade the level of diplomatic relations.
“The state of Russia-UK relations across all areas, they have deteriorated to an unprecedentedly low level entirely on London’s initiative,” it said.
The Foreign Office said it was “a matter for the Russian ministry of foreign affairs”.
“We have an ambassador and embassy in Moscow to engage and raise concerns with the Russian government,” it said in a statement.
“We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine, which has the right to defend itself against Russia’s illegal and unprovoked invasion.”
Britain will ‘pay’ for supporting Kyiv
The removal follows threats from the Russian embassy that Britain would pay a “higher price” should it continue to support Kyiv in its armed struggle against Vladimir Putin’s invasion.
“Reports that the Kyiv regime is using British drones to carry out strikes deep within Russian territory confirm that London is deliberately betting on an escalation of the Ukraine crisis, while hypocritically claiming to be striving for peace,” the embassy said, according to state media.
Mr Kelin criticised Britain in 2025, suggesting London had been involved in a Ukrainian drone attack on Putin’s warplanes in June that year.
The former ambassador said Ukraine must have had outside help with the strikes, which he described as a “very serious escalation” in the conflict.
The revelation also follows a Telegraph investigation that found Russia had built secret bases capable of firing high-powered drones deep into Nato territory.
Some 10 bases with newly built launch pads for Moscow’s most advanced long-range suicide drones have been installed.
Some of the bases are already being used to strike Ukraine, with their proximity to the border helping with mass aerial attacks, launched past Kyiv’s diminishing air defences.
Moscow has previously threatened to downgrade its relationship with the UK.
In 2024, Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said: “The issue of lowering the level of diplomatic relations is a standard practice for states that face unfriendly or hostile manifestations.”
summary: Russia has withdrawn its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, without appointing a replacement, raising concerns over a potential breakdown in diplomatic relations. The Russian embassy stated that Kelin left in the hope that the UK would reconsider its policies, accusing London of choosing a path of confrontation. This move follows recent Russian threats of consequences after British-made drones were used to strike Russian territory.
key_points: Andrei Kelin left his position as Russia's chief representative in London on July 21 after serving for more than seven years.
No replacement has been appointed by the Kremlin, and the embassy is currently headed by a chargé d'affaires.
The withdrawal follows Russian warnings and threats of consequences after British-made drones were used to strike inside Russian territory.
The Russian embassy stated that relations with the UK have deteriorated to an unprecedentedly low level due to London's initiative.

title: Stourbridge fire victims supported by community fundraising event
author: Bob Hockenhull; Elliot Ball
content:
![Chloe Fogg pictured at the event with long brown hair and wearing blue denim dungarees and a white top. Behind her are stalls and people gathered around them.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/8a1b/live/a475b050-9e4e-11f1-8871-ff7211da55c9.jpg)
Chloe Fogg said the community was in need of a boost after last week's fires
- Published
Musicians, traders, food and drink operators, and a "tight-knit community" have joined forces to raise funds for those affected by the Stourbridge fire last Thursday.
The event was held on Saturday at Old Halesonians Rugby Club in Hagley, with organiser, Chloe Fogg, saying the idea had come from "a place of just wanting to help".
"I also think the community needs a boost," she said, adding: "We need something positive to come out of the back of it."
It comes after 19 properties across five streets were destroyed in the blaze, which broke out in Stourbridge and multiple other areas across the West Midlands, on the hottest day of the year so far.
Another 18 houses in the town were damaged.
More than 100 firefighters fought to tackle the flames as they spread over more than 500 acres.
Fogg said Saturday's event had been a chance to "get everyone together for a positive cause" and to "raise some money for those people affected".
An online fundraising page for the event has already collected more than Â£1,000.
Hayley James and Lynne Bate were two of the people attending the fundraiser.
James said: "We've always been a close-knit community in Stourbridge.
"Everybody seems to know everybody, and I think in light of this, you've seen that amplified."
![Hayley James pictured with long brown hair and wearing a pale yellow top. She is stood in a large field with wooden benches and stalls behind her. Small groups of people are chatting and having a drink.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/4fe6/live/63d3d550-9e52-11f1-8871-ff7211da55c9.jpg)
James said Stourbridge had always been a "close-knit community"
Bate added: "It happened very close to where we live, it hasn't directly affected us but we know people it has done. It's just heartbreaking.
"It's not just the bricks and mortar, it's the memories, it's everything, isn't it?
"You just don't want to put yourself in that position - it's terrible."
![Lynne Bate has shoulder length curly grey hair and is wearing a blue top. She is also wearing oval-shaped sunglasses and is smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/6a70/live/61f079e0-9e53-11f1-8871-ff7211da55c9.png)
Bate described last week's scenes as "heartbreaking"
Fellow attendee, Joanne Benson, said: "It was just awful hearing the news, seeing so many homes destroyed by the fires.
"It's affected so many people and we just wanted to come and do our little part.
"Whatever we can do, every little counts."
![Joanne Benson has shoulder length blonde hair and is wearing a pair of brown sunglasses. Behind her is a large black and red bouncy castle.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/835e/live/4ccd4070-9e53-11f1-8871-ff7211da55c9.png)
Benson said she wanted to help and do her part for the community
summary: Musicians, traders, and local residents came together for a fundraising event at Old Halesonians Rugby Club in Hagley to support victims of the recent Stourbridge fire. The blaze destroyed 19 properties across five streets and damaged another 18 houses during the year's hottest day. An online fundraising page linked to the event has raised more than £1,000 to help those affected.
key_points: A community fundraising event was held at Old Halesonians Rugby Club following a major fire in Stourbridge.
The devastating blaze destroyed 19 properties and damaged 18 others across five streets.
More than 100 firefighters battled the flames as they spread across more than 500 acres.
An online fundraising page set up for the event has raised over £1,000.

title: Iran-linked hackers blamed for cyber-attack that shut down UK power plant
author: Ben Quinn
content:
Hackers linked to Iran have been blamed for a cyber-attack that caused a British power plant to be temporarily shut down.
The incident involved a small-scale energy generator, according to the UK government, which said that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system.
However, it marks an apparent escalation in the threat posed by Iran after the UK said it had given permission for the US to launch “defensive” operations against Tehran from British bases.
The power plant was shut down for four days as a result of the attack last month, according to the Sunday Telegraph, which first reported it.
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This story refers to an incident impacting a small-scale energy generator, and at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system. The UK has a highly resilient energy system. We work closely with the energy sector to protect infrastructure and ensure the highest security standards.”
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which deals with attacks on critical infrastructure, is understood not to have received any reported outages from regulated operators of power stations.
Hostile states such as Russia, China and Iran are increasingly targeting systems behind the UK’s key services, according to a warning this year from Richard Horne, the NCSC’s chief executive.
The government said last month the UK was “ready to defend itself” after Iran’s military warned any bases being used by the US were “legitimate targets”.
The UK has allowed the US to launch so-called defensive operations from British bases hosting American planes since the start of its war on Iran but has refused to help in offensive operations. That policy has not been altered by the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, who was notified last week that a decision had been made to extend the agreement with the US.
after newsletter promotion
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said last month that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.
Iran has been accused for years of carrying out cyber-attacks on various countries, including in relation to a massive power outage in Turkey in 2015 and several possible breaches of Israeli government websites in 2022.
US government security agencies issued a warning earlier this year of cyber-attacks on critical infrastructure by hackers linked to the IRGC.
The US has alleged that an Iran-affiliated group known as “CyberAv3ngers” carried out a campaign against it in 2023 that compromised at least 75 devices in multiple infrastructure sectors.
summary: Iran-linked hackers are being blamed for a cyber-attack that temporarily shut down a small-scale British power plant for four days last month. The UK government stated that there was no risk to the wider energy system and that the energy infrastructure remains resilient. This incident follows heightened tensions and warnings regarding hostile states targeting UK key services.
key_points: A small-scale UK power plant was shut down for four days due to a cyber-attack.
The UK government stated that the wider energy system was never at risk.
Hackers linked to Iran have been blamed for the incident.
The NCSC's chief executive warned earlier this year that hostile states are increasingly targeting UK key services.

title: CrossCountry cancels almost all trains after power cut
author: Gareth Corfield
content:
CrossCountry has cancelled almost all of its trains after a power cut at its Birmingham headquarters.
The long-distance rail operator warned of “significant disruption” on Sunday and said “services across almost all routes will be withdrawn until further notice”.
A power cut in Birmingham city centre has disrupted operations at CrossCountry’s main control centre, meaning systems used to manage its trains are unavailable.
The only CrossCountry route that is still running trains is between Peterborough and Stansted Airport, calling at March, Ely and Cambridge.
CrossCountry tickets are being accepted via any reasonable route on all other train companies’ services, according to National Rail Enquiries.
A spokesman for CrossCountry said: “A power cut in Birmingham city centre has affected the building where our control centre is located. As a result, many of the systems our control teams use to manage the railway are currently unavailable.”
The National Grid operates the electricity distribution network serving Birmingham city centre.
On Aug 7, a similar power cut in Manchester caused a power cut at a Network Rail signalling control centre, leading to chaos across north-western England as all trains came to a standstill as a safety precaution.
The incident was triggered by a fault at a transformer powering around 5,000 homes and businesses in Ardwick, Manchester. It also provided energy for Network Rail’s Manchester Rail Operating Centre, which is next to Ashburys station in Openshaw.
Services reduced and cancelled
Referring to Sunday’s rail disruption, a spokesman said: “Although colleagues are working hard to safely operate services using alternative processes, CrossCountry services will be significantly disrupted on Sunday Aug 23.
“While we will run as many trains as possible, passengers should expect significant reductions to services and cancellations across almost all routes throughout the day. We are sorry to passengers affected by this significant and unforeseen disruption.
“Ticket acceptance is in place with other train operators, and customers will be entitled to Delay Repay compensation. Customers who choose not to travel can claim a refund from their original point of purchase.”
Travellers delayed by more than half an hour are eligible to claim Delay Repay compensation from the train company via its website.
A further update is expected later this morning.
summary: CrossCountry cancelled almost all of its train services due to a power cut at its Birmingham headquarters that affected the main control centre systems. Only the route between Peterborough and Stansted Airport remains operational. Passengers facing delays of more than half an hour are eligible for Delay Repay compensation or ticket acceptance on other train operators.
key_points: A power cut in Birmingham city centre affected CrossCountry's main control centre.
Services across almost all routes were withdrawn until further notice, causing significant disruption.
The only route still running trains is between Peterborough and Stansted Airport.
CrossCountry tickets are being accepted on other train companies' services.
Affected passengers can claim refunds or Delay Repay compensation.

title: ‘These were brave officers’: tributes paid to police among seven killed in A66 crash
author: Mark Brown
content:
Tributes are being paid to two police officers who died on Teesside when a car travelling the wrong way along the A66 crashed head-on into their vehicle, also killing five young men.
PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were killed when the marked armed response vehicle they were in was struck by a Volkswagen Passat in the early hours of Saturday morning.
On Sunday, Anna Turley, the Home Office minister and local Redcar MP, said it was “devastating” to think about the grief of the families of everyone who lost their lives on Saturday morning. The whole community was “reeling”, she said.
“All of us in the community here are sending our heartfelt thoughts and sympathies to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives so tragically,” she told BBC Breakfast.
Turley said it was important to avoid speculation about what might have happened and allow families the privacy to grieve. “I do want to place on record my tribute to PC Blades and PC Clough. The bravery that we see from our police officers every day, every night is incredible. No one should not come home to their families at the end of their shift.”
She also said it was important to thank the emergency services who attended at the scene during “a really horrific incident”.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he was “devastated” to hear two police officers had lost their lives on duty, as well as five members of the public. “My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of everyone involved, and with everyone at Cleveland police. Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances. I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time.”
The Cleveland police chief constable, Victoria Fuller, said she and her deputy had on Saturday visited the families of the two officers to offer condolences and support.
![Victoria Fuller speaks to reporters outside Cleveland police central HQ](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ffdc8ea0a2e34a6c989e5415b31c12f9ed1159c5/0_0_4096_2728/master/4096.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“This is an incredibly sad day for Cleveland,” she said. “This loss is being felt across our communities, by our police family and by our partner agencies. These were brave officers, protecting our communities and serving our residents, who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift.”
Lauren Somerville, the chair of Cleveland police federation, said the grief among officers was “all-consuming, overwhelming”. She said: “Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland police family are feeling.”
The Tees Valley mayor, Ben Houchen, said in a statement on Facebook: “A horrible and tragic incident in South Bank this morning and my thoughts are with those affected, their families and the emergency services who attended the scene.
“Our police officers are heroes who put everything on the line to protect us, and I know all of Teesside will want to pay tribute to the officers and other emergency service workers involved for the bravery they have shown in responding to this incident.”
The five young men in the VW Passat have not been named by authorities, although they have been named on social media. The Independent Office for Police Conduct has opened an investigation into the circumstances leading to the crash at 3.39am in South Bank after a mandatory referral from Cleveland police.
Police vehicles had been pursuing the car before it joined the A66 although it is understood the pursuit had ended before the fatal crash. Ring doorbell footage published by several websites minutes before the crash shows a car being driven at speed down a residential road and being followed by police cars.
Ellie Westerman, who lives locally, told the Sun: “The noise woke me and I shot out of bed. You could feel the vibration in the house as the car went past and the police vehicles followed with their lights and sirens going. It was frightening that cars were being driven at that speed through a residential area.”
summary: Seven people, including two police officers and five young men, were killed in a head-on collision on the A66 when a Volkswagen Passat traveled the wrong way. The officers, PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough, were in a marked armed response vehicle struck during the early hours of Saturday morning. Leaders, including local officials and police chiefs, have paid tribute to the fallen officers and expressed condolences to all families affected. The Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating the incident following a mandatory referral, as police vehicles had pursued the Passat prior to the crash.
key_points: Two police officers and five young men died in a head-on crash on the A66 involving a car traveling the wrong way.
The victims included PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough of the Cleveland police.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating the circumstances of the crash following a mandatory referral.
Police vehicles had pursued the Volkswagen Passat prior to the collision, though the pursuit reportedly ended before the crash.
Community leaders, political figures, and police representatives expressed devastation and paid tribute to the bravery of the officers.

title: CrossCountry cancels 'almost all' UK services after power cut
author: Alice Cullinane
content:
![A red and white train is parked on railway tracks next to a train station.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/2055/live/eb901e80-9ec6-11f1-a815-1fffefa318e5.jpg)
Services across almost all CrossCountry routes have been cancelled
- Published
Trains across the UK have been cancelled after a power cut at train operator CrossCountry's control centre.
The power outage started in Birmingham on Saturday and as a result, many of the systems used to manage the railway are unavailable, the operator said.
Services across almost all its routes have been cancelled until further notice as it experiences "significant and unforeseen disruption".
Major routes cancelled include services between Manchester and Birmingham, which passes through Stoke-on-Trent, Coventry and Wolverhampton, along with routes from Leeds to York, Cheltenham to Cardiff and Glasgow to Edinburgh.
"We are working closely with relevant partners and will provide further updates as soon as possible," a CrossCountry spokesperson said.
While the operator usually calls at more than 100 stations, it said that the only route expecting a "near-normal" service was between Peterborough, Cambridge and Stansted Airport.
The company apologised to passengers affected by the "significant and unforeseen disruption" and said tickets were being accepted by other operators.
Customers are entitled to Delay Repay compensation if their train is delayed by 30 minutes or more, while those who choose not to travel can claim a refund for their journey.
summary: CrossCountry has cancelled almost all of its UK train services following a power cut at its control centre in Birmingham on Saturday. The outage has made many railway management systems unavailable, leading to significant disruption across major routes. The operator has apologised, accepted tickets on other services, and advised customers that they are entitled to refunds or Delay Repay compensation.
key_points: A power cut at CrossCountry's Birmingham control centre caused widespread train cancellations.
Major routes between Manchester and Birmingham, Leeds to York, Cheltenham to Cardiff, and Glasgow to Edinburgh were affected.
The Peterborough, Cambridge, and Stansted Airport route is expected to maintain a near-normal service.
Affected passengers can use their tickets on other operators, claim refunds, or apply for Delay Repay compensation.

title: Burnham expected to give mayors new powers over local planning decisions
author: Nadeem Badshah
content:
Andy Burnham is expected to give mayors new powers to take control of local planning decisions and greenlight large-scale developments in proposals to be presented next week.
The move would allow mayors to “call in” the decisions and direct councils to take them forward or refuse them.
They will also be able to grant upfront permission so developers can start building without having to apply.
It will apply to developments of more than 150 homes, commercial spaces of more than 15,000 sq m or any building 30 metres or taller – which is roughly 10 storeys.
Burnham told the Sunday Times that he understood the argument that devolving powers to mayors to push through such projects could disempower councillors, MPs and constituents.
He said: “Sometimes … challenge does need to be made to local decision-making, and actually it cuts both ways.
“It’s not all about nimbyism. Sometimes it’s the other way round.
“It’s a local authority putting forward something that’s unacceptable in terms of the impact on the community … so it’s a two-way street.”
Ten of the 14 devolved mayors from different parties have backed the move.
It will bring them into line with the mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, who was given the powers earlier this year in what was billed as an emergency measure aimed at unblocking dozens of stalled sites to get thousands more affordable homes built in the capital.
Burnham added: “In my view, it will prompt a much more joined-up discussion about planning and local authorities.
“I think knowing the mayor has that role, councils will come to the mayor and say: ‘How can we work this thing out so that it is acceptable?’”
The government is just over a quarter of the way to its target to build 1.5m homes in England in five years.
The decisions must be in line with planning rules, local plans set out for areas and the national policy, and ministers will retain a backstop power to intervene.
Mayors will also get more of a say on how national housing funding from Homes England will be spent in their areas, in addition to being able to charge a levy on development to fund large infrastructure.
A consultation will be published next week.
The Liberal Democrats said the move was a “direct attack” that would silence residents. Gideon Amos, the party’s housing and planning spokesperson, said: “Taking powers away from communities and local councillors is taking powers away from local people. This plan is a direct attack on communities across the country.
“Labour’s chaotic patchwork approach to devolution will simply not work to solve the housing crisis.
“Instead of silencing residents and handing mayors a blank cheque, the government should be empowering local councils with the resources to deliver genuinely affordable homes alongside the infrastructure to support them.”
summary: Andy Burnham is set to introduce proposals next week granting devolved mayors new powers to direct, approve, or block large-scale local planning developments. The measures apply to major residential, commercial, and high-rise projects, aligning regional mayors with London's leadership to help accelerate housing delivery. While backed by ten mayors and intended to encourage joined-up planning discussions, the proposals face criticism from the Liberal Democrats over concerns about silencing local residents.
key_points: Mayors will gain the ability to call in local planning decisions, direct councils, or grant upfront building permissions for large-scale developments.
The new powers apply to housing projects of over 150 homes, commercial spaces over 15,000 square metres, and buildings 30 metres or taller.
Ten of the 14 devolved mayors from various political parties support the proposed changes.
Mayors will also receive greater input on national housing funding allocation and the authority to levy development fees for infrastructure.
The Liberal Democrats criticized the plan as a direct attack that silences local communities and residents.

title: Police officers killed in wrong-way crash mourned in 'unimaginable loss'
author: Mallory Moench
content:
Watch: Cleveland Police names the two officers who died in crash near Middlesbrough
- Published
Two police officers killed in a wrong-way crash on the A66 near Middlesbrough have been remembered as "brave officers protecting our communities" in what has been described as an "unimaginable loss".
PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died when a car driving the wrong way struck a Cleveland Police vehicle at 03:39 BST on Saturday.
Five people in the Volkswagen Passat said to be in their late teens to early 20s were also killed. They have not been named.
The BBC understands a police pursuit of the car had ended before the crash, with the police vehicle just happening to be in the South Bank area.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is now investigating.
![An overturned car is seen under a tarp, surrounded by police vehicles on a road.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/3e0e/live/11b179c0-9ebc-11f1-94b5-69fe6cc868f9.jpg)
Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said on Saturday it was an "incredibly sad day for Cleveland", adding: "No one should leave their home and not return safely."
Fuller said she and her deputy chief constable visited the officers' families to "offer our condolences, support one another, and begin to come to terms with this unimaginable loss".
Politicians, including the prime minister and home secretary, have remembered the officers, with Andy Burnham saying he was "devastated" by the news.
![Brightly-coloured flowers are placed around the base of a green lamppost. They are on a patch of dry grass and in the background is a metal barrier and a road and behind that a brown wooden fence and houses](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/9f8e/live/5fc2c1d0-9ebe-11f1-bc1c-fb1a8090e7da.jpg)
Tributes have been left near the scene of the crash
Anna Turley, MP for the Redcar constituency where the crash happened, said the officers "went to work to keep people safe and they should have come home to their families".
She added: "Their loss will be felt deeply by their loved ones, fellow officers and right across the communities they served."
David Taylor and Stephen Martin, councillors for the Eston ward, said they were "deeply saddened" by the "unimaginable tragedy".
Tees Valley mayor Ben Houchen called the case "a horrible and tragic incident" in a statement on Facebook.
"Our police officers are heroes who put everything on the line to protect us, and I know all of Teesside will want to pay tribute to the officers and other emergency service workers involved for the bravery they have shown in responding to this incident."
Cleveland Police Federation chairwoman Lauren Somerville said the loss of the officers was "unfathomable", adding: "Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland Police family are feeling today."
Watch: Video appears to show police pursuit minutes before fatal crash
When someone dies following police contact, it is mandatory for the case to be referred to the IOPC, which is now investigating.
The watchdog said on Saturday that "at this early stage, we understand Cleveland Police sighted a suspicious vehicle and a pursuit began."
Security footage from a house on Lime Road in Middlesbrough appears to show a car being pursued by police vehicles three minutes before the crash.
The BBC understands the pursuit ended prior to the crash, and the police vehicle occupied by PC Blades and PC Clough just happened to be in the area at the time.
![A map showing where the crash occurred in relation to the wider Teesside area.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/0300/live/fd3844c0-9e33-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
The A66 is the major artery through Teesside
IOPC Director of Investigations Nicola Marfleet called it a "tragic incident" and said her "thoughts are with family and friends and all those affected, including the emergency services in attendance."
Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp also shared his condolences, adding the IOPC "must be given the time and space to complete their investigations without speculation".
The A66, which is the major artery through Teesside and the location of the crash is surrounded by industrial units and factories, remained closed on Sunday.
summary: Two Cleveland Police officers, PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough, were killed alongside five occupants of another vehicle in a wrong-way crash on the A66 near Middlesbrough. The collision occurred after a police pursuit of the Volkswagen Passat had reportedly ended, prompting a mandatory investigation by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC). Tributes and condolences have poured in from political figures, police leadership, and local representatives mourning the tragic loss.
key_points: PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died when a wrong-way car struck their Cleveland Police vehicle.
Five people in the Volkswagen Passat, aged in their late teens to early 20s, were also killed in the crash.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is investigating the incident following a prior police pursuit of the vehicle.
Tributes have been paid by politicians, local leaders, and police officials who mourned the officers as brave public servants.

title: Oxford colleges respond to death of professor Jason Arday
author: Matt Simpson
content:
Oxford University colleges have said they are "deeply saddened" about the death of a Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism.
Cambridge's Jason Arday, who resigned following a plagiarism row, was found dead at his Battersea home on August 14.
In a joint statement, Oxford's colleges said their thoughts are with Mr Arday's family, friends and colleagues at this "very difficult" time.
  Oxford University (Image: Contributed)
"We recognise that news of his death will have been difficult and distressing for members of our community," Oxford said.
"As a global university, Oxford values the diversity of our staff and students and the different perspectives and experiences they bring to our community.
"Equality, diversity and inclusion have long been a core part of our academic mission and that remains the case.
"It is guided by the importance we place on excellence, academic freedom and freedom of speech.
"Creating an environment in which our talented staff and students can belong, contribute and thrive is key to our enduring success. This won’t change."
The university said students affected can reach the welfare team, adding confidential support is available through counselling.
Mr Arday, a professor of sociology of education who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, quit following a series of media reports alleging he plagiarised his PhD thesis – completed at Liverpool John Moores University – and other research.
READ MORE: Delayed park and ride opening 'currently within budget' despite claims otherwise
Further questions were asked in the press about the truth of other claims he made, including saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5 million for charity.
An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Mr Arday of wrongdoing.
Fellow academic Nathan Cofnas, who initially made accusations of plagiarism, on Thursday was suspended by Ghent University.
Earlier this week, organisers said more than 30,000 people had attended a vigil for the 41-year-old in Trafalgar Square, central London.
Speakers at the vigil criticised the press coverage of Prof Arday, with MP Diane Abbott saying he was subject of a “vicious” and “bitter” campaign by people who did not believe a black man should be a Cambridge professor – and Lord Woolley describing the press coverage of Prof Arday as a “public execution” and a “lynching”.
The death of Prof Arday was referred to the Coroner for the Inner South District of Greater London on Saturday.
No medical cause of death was given, so the Coroner will be investigating, but the results may not be available “for several weeks”.
Only after this will a decision be made as to whether an inquest is to be opened.
Downing Street has declined to say “at this stage” whether Andy Burnham was considering an inquiry over the death of Prof Arday, arguing it was “right for us to let processes conclude”, such as an inquest.
summary: Oxford University colleges expressed deep sadness following the death of Cambridge professor Jason Arday, who was found dead at his Battersea home on August 14. Mr Arday had recently resigned following a plagiarism row and media scrutiny over various claims, though an investigation by Liverpool John Moores University had cleared him of wrongdoing. A coroner is investigating his death, with results expected in several weeks.
key_points: Cambridge professor Jason Arday was found dead at his Battersea home on August 14 following his resignation amid a plagiarism controversy.
Oxford University colleges issued a joint statement expressing sadness and offering support to affected staff and students.
An investigation by Liverpool John Moores University had previously cleared Mr Arday of wrongdoing regarding allegations about his PhD thesis.
Speakers at a recent Trafalgar Square vigil attended by over 30,000 people criticized the intense press coverage directed at Prof Arday.
The Inner South District of Greater London coroner is investigating the death, with medical cause results expected in several weeks.

title: Restriction zone scheme for offenders to start in October
author: Iain Watson; Ottilie Mitchell
content:
![A woman looks out of a window while sitting on a bed.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/4e93/live/e7605c80-9e8f-11f1-8854-6b09b84b2062.jpg)
- Published
A scheme that could see serious sexual and violent offenders confined to areas just a few miles wide after leaving prison will be launched in October, Justice Secretary Alex Norris has announced.
Government ministers say this is designed to give victims greater freedom and further reduce the possibility of unwanted contact
The intention to introduce "restriction zones" for violent offenders who leave prison and who are on probation was first announced by the government last year.
Probation officers will be able to limit where serious offenders can go for as long as it is deemed necessary. Those who breach their new boundaries could be recalled to prison.
This would go beyond the current practice of imposing "exclusion zones" which ban offenders from specific locations such as a victim's home or place of work.
Norris is expected to come up with proposals to further restrict the early release of some prisoners when Parliament resumes next month.
But the Conservatives say that the best thing Labour could do to protect victims is to bring forward emergency legislation which would stop the early release of thousands of criminals.
There is a risk that serious sexual and violent offenders and victims could encounter one another outside exclusion zones.
The new scheme will specify confined areas for offenders in plans tailored to them and developed in consultation with victims.
Norris said the scheme would use GPS technology monitored by probation officers so that "those who step outside the boundaries can be quickly identified and face being sent back to prison".
"Offenders should carry the consequences of their crimes, not their victims," he added.
Amy Glover, director of domestic abuse services at Advance, a charity supporting women and girls who have experienced domestic abuse, praised the "change in focus".
However, she also called for reform to the criminal justice system saying many survivors of abuse chose "not to pursue a criminal conviction, and for those that do only 5% reach conviction."
A domestic abuse survivor named only as Kristina called the restriction zones a "fantastic concept" but noted that a perpetrator had continuously breached her indefinite restraining order "without consequence".
"The biggest challenge would be to gain victims' confidence in authorities to follow through their promises of protection," she added.
The announcement of the restriction zone scheme's start date comes after a change to the government's early release scheme following a backlash.
Introduced to ease prison overcrowding, on 4 August the policy was updated so people sentenced for rape, serious child sex offences and grooming would not be eligible for early release.
The Prison Governors' association warned this change to plans at a "very late stage" put further pressure on prison staff.
The restriction zone scheme was criticised when it was announced last year for potentially putting pressure on probation staff, something the government says it hopes to alleviate with more staff and a greater use of technology.
If you are suffering from domestic abuse, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line
summary: Justice Secretary Alex Norris has announced that a new restriction zone scheme for serious sexual and violent offenders will launch in October. The initiative uses GPS technology monitored by probation officers to confine released prisoners to specific areas, aiming to prevent unwanted contact with victims. Breaching these boundaries can result in offenders being recalled to prison. Charities and survivors have welcomed the concept while highlighting challenges regarding enforcement and victim confidence.
key_points: The restriction zone scheme launches in October under Justice Secretary Alex Norris.
Probation officers will use GPS technology to monitor offenders and can recall them to prison if they breach boundaries.
The initiative goes beyond current exclusion zones by confining offenders to areas just a few miles wide.
Charities and survivors praised the focus on victim protection while emphasizing the need for reliable enforcement.

title: Iranian hackers shut down UK power plant
author: Tony Diver; Rozina Sabur; Matt Oliver
content:
The incident is understood to have been reported to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), a public-facing branch of the GCHQ spy agency that issues advice to companies on keeping national infrastructure safe from foreign threats.
British and American intelligence agencies have repeatedly warned of the risk posed by hackers from Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, which bombard critical national infrastructure and government agencies with attacks on a daily basis.
Major incidents have previously brought down NHS systems, schools and commercial manufacturing facilities, including production lines at Jaguar Land Rover.
Foreign hacking groups have also stolen customer information from retail businesses, including attacks last year, and voter records from the Electoral Commission.
However, no hacker is thought to have ever succeeded in bringing a British power plant to a standstill, despite warnings that attacks on national infrastructure are commonplace.
It is unlikely that the attack against the UK power plant was intended to inflict genuine harm on civilians, and is not thought to have been widely noticed by the public.
But it is possible that the incident was designed to prove that hackers linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps could gain access to systems in the UK and close down sensitive infrastructure sites.
‘Malicious cyber actors’
There are dozens of small-scale power plants across Britain connected to the grid. Many of them are gas-fired and only used for a few hours per week, for example when wind speeds are low and extra energy is needed.
A four-day outage at such a facility would not impact the wider grid. Some factories and other facilities such as hospitals also have their own separate power generators.
The US hacks affected dozens of wastewater treatment plants, causing flooding and a loss of pressure from taps, and forcing some authorities to advise customers to boil their water before drinking it.
The first reports of an incident emerged in Minnesota on July 26, followed by a series of similar security breaches in Michigan, Georgia, South Dakota and New Jersey.
The FBI attributed the incidents to “malicious cyber actors”, but US government sources later confirmed to media outlets that the threat was likely to have originated in Tehran.
Iran has dramatically stepped up its cyber attacks on Western countries in the wake of the conflict in the Middle East, and especially since the US and Israel began air strikes in February.
summary: Iranian-linked hackers successfully shut down a small UK power plant in an incident reported to the National Cyber Security Centre. Intelligence agencies from Britain and the US have repeatedly warned about daily cyber attacks on critical infrastructure by foreign threat actors. While the UK outage did not impact the wider grid or cause civilian harm, similar recent attacks by actors likely originating in Tehran have affected US wastewater treatment plants.
key_points: An incident involving hackers shutting down a UK power plant was reported to the National Cyber Security Centre.
The attack is believed to have been designed to prove that hackers linked to Iran could access and close sensitive UK infrastructure sites.
The targeted UK facility was a small-scale power plant, meaning a four-day outage did not impact the wider grid.
US intelligence and government sources confirmed that recent cyber attacks on US wastewater treatment plants likely originated in Tehran.

title: Mayors to get powers to overrule local councils on planning decisions
author: Kate Whannel
content:
![Housing development](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/7205/live/1fb3cdf0-9d83-11f1-adf5-2dc21c9cc109.jpg)
- Published
Mayors across England will be given new powers to overrule local councils on some planning decisions.
The change would apply to proposals with more than 150 homes, more than 15,000 square metres of commercial space or buildings over 30 metres.
Mayors in 13 areas including Manchester, Liverpool, the West of England and the West Midlands will gain similar powers to Sir Sadiq Khan in London, who is already able to "call in" planning decisions.
Housing minister Matthew Pennycook said the powers were an "essential part of the toolkit that mayors need to effectively deliver new homes and regeneration".
The Conservatives questioned whether it was right for councils to lose the "ability to make planning decisions in their own communities".
The powers will also be available to mayors in the Combined Authorities in North East England, South Yorkshire, West Yorkshire, York and North Yorkshire, Hull and East Yorkshire, Greater Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, East Midlands, and Tees Valley.
Housebuilding has fallen in London in recent years, but Pennycook insisted the "call in" powers had helped the mayor "unblock strategic growth sites" in the capital.
In the 2024 general election, the Labour government promised to build 1.5 million homes in England by the end of the decade but housebuilders have warned the target could be missed.
Pennycook said the government was "absolutely determined to stick with that ambition".
He acknowledged the target was "really stretching" but said nearly 180,000 children were in temporary accommodation and "any smaller target wouldn't be commensurate with the scale of the challenge".
In addition to gaining the new "call-in" powers, mayors are set to be able to grant "up-front permission", which the government says will allow building to begin "without a developer having to apply".
A consultation on how the powers will work is due to be published next week.
The government has sought to stress that local councils will continue to decide the majority of applications and that all decisions must still follow planning rules.
It has also said mayors will get a "bigger say" over how housing funding is spent in their area, with the government directing national agency Homes England to focus on local mayors' priorities.
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who served as mayor for Greater Manchester for nearly a decade, has repeatedly expressed his desire to transfer more powers to local mayors.
"Challenge does need to be made to local decision-making and actually it cuts both ways," he told the Sunday Times.
"Sometimes it's the other way round. It's the local authority putting forward something that's unacceptable in terms of the impact on the community. It's a two-way street."
Last month, Burnham promised to give all mayors a share of income tax revenue, saying he wanted to "bring power home" to "every postcode".
Earlier this week, he announced a secondment programme to send high-performing civil servants to work in mayoral offices.
The approach has faced criticism from some in his own party and the Liberal Democrats, who fear it could create a "two-tier system" that discriminates against those areas that do not have an elected mayor.
Responding to the new powers for mayors, Sir James Cleverly, the shadow housing secretary, said the government was "simultaneously stripping councils across the country of their ability to make planning decisions in their own communities, while making it easier to build traveller sites against local wishes".
Sir James also suggested Labour mayors had failed to meet housing targets, adding: "The Conservatives are the only party with a plan to get Britain building and moving again with our plan to scrap stamp duty on the family home."
Gideon Amos, the Liberal Democrat housing and planning spokesperson, said "taking powers away from communities and local councillors is taking powers away from local people".
"Instead of silencing residents and handing mayors a blank cheque, the government should be empowering local councils with the resources to deliver genuinely affordable homes alongside the infrastructure to support them," he added.
Mothin Ali, deputy leader of the Greens, said "more powers for mayors to direct local councils" was "more tinkering from the Labour government when local authorities continue to be forced by government into austerity budgets".
Reform UK accused Labour of "centralisation in disguise", saying: "Westminster is stretching its tentacles outward instead of giving real power, resources and decision-making capabilities to devolved authorities."
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âTop political analysis in your inbox every dayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6133/live/2bce6ee0-0b00-11f0-97d3-37df2b293ed1.png)
summary: Mayors across England are set to receive new powers allowing them to overrule local councils on major planning decisions involving large housing developments, commercial spaces, and tall buildings. The government argues these "call-in" powers and up-front permissions are essential to help meet its target of building 1.5 million homes by the end of the decade. However, the policy has drawn criticism from opposition parties who warn that stripping local communities of their decision-making abilities creates a centralized system.
key_points: Mayors in 13 areas across England will gain powers to "call in" and overrule local council planning decisions for large-scale projects.
The new rules apply to proposals with over 150 homes, more than 15,000 square metres of commercial space, or buildings taller than 30 metres.
Mayors will also be able to grant up-front permissions allowing construction to begin without a developer having to apply.
The Labour government defends the policy as necessary to reach its target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the end of the decade.
Opposition parties, including Conservatives, Liberal Democrats, and Greens, criticized the policy for stripping local communities and councils of their decision-making power.

title: Securing return to EU single market ‘would win Burnham the next election’
author: Kate Devlin
content:
Taking Britain back into the EU single market would win Andy Burnham the next general election and help him achieve a legacy to rival Tony Blair’s, a former Tory minister turned Labour adviser has claimed.
Nick Boles, who served as a minister in David Cameron’s government before quitting the Conservatives in 2019 over the party’s Brexit stance, has urged the new prime minister to seize the opportunity created by “pretty scary” world events since 2016 to strike a deal with European Union leaders that would protect the continent and offer the UK a much-needed economic boost.
Mr Boles is calling for the creation of a “European Confederation”, which he says would provide some of the benefits of European integration such as single market access and youth mobility, but without having to accept free movement or being forced to join the Eurozone.
Under his proposal, which has reportedly been put to the prime minister, the UK would be invited to join the confederation in return for a commitment to spend 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence and to extend the protection of its nuclear umbrella across the continent.
He believes the move to access the single market again would also deal a “devastating” blow to the Tories and Nigel Farage’s Reform, securing victory in the next general election and writing Mr Burnham into the history books.
Polling has repeatedly shown Britons favour closer ties with the European Union, with research carried out by YouGov in June to mark 10 years since the EU referendum revealing that 59 per cent of voters support a closer UK-Europe relationship, compared with just 20 per cent who do not.
When it comes to the single market, half of Britons support rejoining compared with 26 per cent who do not.
Mr Boles, who helped to prepare Labour for office before it entered government, told The Independent: “If [Mr Burnham] sorts out social care and takes us into the single market and [a new] European Confederation, that is a more substantial legacy than anyone in the last few years. It would certainly rival Blair's.”
He said a new post-Brexit deal could provide a “devastating” dividing line with other parties that would win the Labour leader the next general election, by putting the party “in a commanding position” on an “abundantly popular side” of the argument.
It would allow him to say “vote Labour to get back into the European single market…or vote Tory or Reform to stay out in impecunious isolation,” he said.
“It’s a pretty devastating divide. Particularly with public opinion where it currently seems to be with regard to the success or otherwise of Brexit.”
Former Labour leader Neil Kinnock is among those who have argued that Mr Boles’ plan is a “practical approach”.
Mr Boles urged Mr Burnham, whose optimism he likened to that of the very popular former US President Ronald Reagan, to grasp the nettle.
As a new PM, he was not held to Sir Keir Starmer's “reset” of relations with Europe, which faced criticism for its lack of ambition, he said.
![Nick Boles, the former Tory MP who quit the party over Brexit and went on to help Labour prepare for government, said the move could deal a ‘devastating’ blow to the Conservatives and Reform](https://static.independent.co.uk/2022/05/05/15/PA-42102999.jpg)
Of Mr Burnham he said: “He refuses to be sort of bowed by... how terrible everything is, how difficult it all is, how everybody before has failed.
“You sense that he's a bit of a gambler ... he likes to roll the dice.”
“There’s a moment in Europe, whether we take advantage of it or not – they’re all talking about how they’re going to deal with this changed world.”
Mr Boles said “feelers” had been put out from within the Burnham government about his essay, published earlier this month by the think tank Demos. “People are interested. People have asked to have conversations,” he said.
He said the new proposal could show the UK was “humbler” and that “it’s no longer ‘oh those selfish British, you know, trying to have their cake and eat it’” while also offering a solution which would be of benefit to both sides.
Mr Boles also said the political circumstances had changed drastically since the 2016 referendum.
He said it was “highly unlikely” the UK would have voted to leave the EU if the world had been as dangerous then as it is now.
“I think it is one of those sad accidents of history that the pressure to have the referendum... came to a head just at the time when it was most likely to win, and indeed, perhaps the only time when it was ever likely to win,” he said.
A government spokesperson said: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy and create more opportunities for working people and communities across Britain.”
![Join the Independent’s new campaign](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/06/04/16/17/europe-way-back-banner.jpeg)
What you will get by joining:

- Free weekly newsletter: Every Wednesday, political editor David Maddox and political correspondent Millie Cooke will be in your inbox with exclusive reporting, analysis and insight on the biggest developments shaping relations between Britain and Europe. Each week, they will explain what’s happened, what it means, and what the key political figures, experts and decision-makers are saying about it.

summary: Former Tory minister and Labour adviser Nick Boles has claimed that taking Britain back into the EU single market through a proposed "European Confederation" would help secure a general election victory. Under his proposal, the UK would gain single market access and youth mobility in exchange for committing 3.5 per cent of GDP to defence and extending its nuclear umbrella. Polling indicates that a majority of Britons favour closer ties with the European Union and support rejoining the single market.
key_points: Nick Boles urged the government to strike a deal with the EU to join a proposed "European Confederation" providing single market access and youth mobility without free movement or the Eurozone.
The UK would offer to spend 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence and extend its nuclear umbrella across the continent under the proposal.
Recent YouGov polling shows that 59 per cent of voters support a closer UK-Europe relationship and half of Britons support rejoining the single market.
Boles argues this policy would provide a winning political dividing line against the Conservatives and Reform in the next general election.

title: Vigil held to honour family who lost their lives in sea off Shoreham
author: Cash Murphy; Stuart Maisner; Ewan Murrie
content:
![A vicar with lots of people with heads bowed in a town square daytime](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a7ed/live/5d906f30-9e13-11f1-95e0-53a570c83624.jpg)
Prayers and a one-minute silence were held in Shoreham town centre on Saturday
- Published
The community in Shoreham, West Sussex, has paid its respects to a family who died after getting into difficulty in the sea on Tuesday.
Hassan El-Khawas, 55, Zeina Alayn, 37, and their 14-year-old daughter Sara, died despite the efforts of paramedics at the scene. It was confirmed on Friday that six-year-old Saja El-Khawas had died in hospital.
A vigil took place earlier at Kingston Beach, where the incident took place, alongside a one-minute silence in Shoreham town centre.
Reverend Pat Alden said: "When something happens, whether it's something we celebrate... or tragic circumstances like this, the community comes together."
'Heartbroken'
Alden added: "Shoreham is the sort of place where the community comes together at times like this. We are a very close-knit community."
Tom Rutland, East Worthing and Shoreham MP, who attended the vigil, said the whole town was "heartbroken, particularly by the development that Saja has lost her life sadly too".
![a composition of photos of three family members - a man who is smiling, a woman looking gently at the camera, and a young teenage girl, who is smiling](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1040/cpsprodpb/8c71/live/8992d010-9da9-11f1-95ab-d3b679e2384a.jpg)
Saja's parents and elder sister died on Tuesday despite attempts to save them
Alden added: "The way everybody has come together and marked today with this minute's silence, and there were people who met with paddleboards and kayaks over at Kingston Beach as well this morning, it's been a really lovely way to pay to the very sad loss of these lives."
Wesley Horscroft attended on behalf of paddlers in the Kingston beach community.
He said he had originally planned to go out alone and "put some flowers on the water" to honour the family, before he decided to invite others.
"It's kind of grown and a lot of people wanted to turn up to do the same," he said.
He said Saja's death had added an "another layer" to the grief felt in the town.
![Wesley Horscroft pictured on Kingston Beach, Shoreham. He has blondish hair and a ginger beard. He is wearing a black t-shirt. Paddleboarders can be seen in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/2ff0/live/27a1e520-9e36-11f1-8a71-eb9ef5df2469.jpg)
Wesley Horscroft was among those to meet with paddleboards at Kingston Beach
According to Sussex Police, the family had travelled down from their home in London on Tuesday to visit Shoreham, which is about 6.3 miles (10.1km) from Brighton.
The force said the family had entered the water from the beach at Shoreham Fort at about 14:00 BST before getting into trouble.
A Sussex Police spokesperson said the investigation remained open, and the "current hypothesis" was that it was "a tragic accident, with no third-party involvement".
Addressing Saja's death on Friday evening, Ch Supt James Collis said: "This heartbreaking update is one we all feared in the aftermath of Tuesday's tragic events.
"The impact of this tragedy has been felt across the country and I know the Shoreham community, emergency responders and all involved will continue to be affected for a long time to come."
![Reverend Pat Alden during the community vigil in Shoreham-by-Sea on 22 August. She is dressed in typical vicar attire and is holding a piece of paper.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/9c0b/live/38520bd0-9e1c-11f1-9834-b7317ffa53cf.jpg)
Reverend Pat Alden addressed those who had gathered for the vigil
The family lived in London and were British citizens of Palestinian origin, with roots in the Rashidieh refugee camp in Lebanon.
Their extended family had lived in the UK for many years, the Palestinian Forum said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the incident a "terrible family tragedy".
Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: The community in Shoreham, West Sussex, held a vigil and a one-minute silence to pay respects to a family of four who tragically died after getting into difficulty in the sea. Hassan El-Khawas, Zeina Alayn, and their 14-year-old daughter Sara died on Tuesday, while their six-year-old daughter Saja passed away in the hospital on Friday. Sussex Police stated that the current hypothesis is that the incident was a tragic accident with no third-party involvement.
key_points: A vigil and one-minute silence were held in Shoreham town centre and at Kingston Beach to honor the family.
Hassan El-Khawas, Zeina Alayn, and their daughter Sara died at the scene, and six-year-old Saja died later in the hospital.
The family lived in London and had traveled to visit Shoreham on Tuesday when they entered the water and got into trouble.
Sussex Police are treating the incident as a tragic accident with no third-party involvement.

title: Thousands of sex offenders in England and Wales could get libido-suppressing drugs
author: Rajeev Syal; Faisa Mohamed
content:
Drugs that help control the libidos of people who have committed sexual offences could be rolled out for thousands of male prisoners in England and Wales from December 2028, an expert has said.
Prof Belinda Winder, who has evaluated the use of sex drive-suppressing medication in prisons, said about one in four sex offenders – equating to 3,750 current prisoners – would be considered for the treatment.
Government sources have told the Guardian that Andy Burnham’s administration is keen to expand the voluntary use of sex drive-suppressing drugs amid a scramble to ease the prison overcrowding crisis.
However, ministers are re-evaluating whether to press ahead with Shabana Mahmood’s pledge to explore mandatory chemical castration of serious sex offenders, such as paedophiles and rapists.
About 15,000 prisoners in England and Wales are serving a sentence for a sexual offence, and more than 850 men a month are arrested on suspicion of online child sexual abuse offences.
A pilot programme, the medication to manage problematic sexual arousal treatment pathway (MMPSA), will be expanded from 10 to 20 prisons in November. The next phase will extend from south-west England into two additional NHS regions, the north-west and north-east.
It is meant to target sex offenders who experience intrusive, persistent and intense sexual thoughts, persistent arousal, and unhealthy sexual urges and sexual behaviours. Prisoners on the trial can be offered drugs including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as sertraline, which helps to limit invasive sexual thoughts, and anti-androgens, which reduce the production of testosterone and limit libido. In some cases, it reduces testosterone to pre-pubescent levels.
Winder said officials could be ready to launch the drugs in prisons and probation services across England and Wales within 28 months if the pilot continued to progress.
“They [the Ministry of Justice] could be ready in December 2028 to roll the programme out if the interim findings look useful,” she said.
Those on the scheme would have to receive clinical support if they were to commit to taking the drugs and not reoffend, Winder said. “I am optimistic that a properly resourced, voluntary national MMPSA pathway could ultimately be developed … A good national service needs appropriately trained clinicians, clear referral routes, appropriate psychological support alongside medication,” she said.
Last year Mahmood, the then justice secretary, told MPs she was exploring a national rollout of voluntary chemical castration for sex offenders and whether it could be made mandatory.
Two experts have told the Guardian that the plan will not work. Winder, a co-chief investigator of a Prozac clinical trial with sex offenders, said she had significant concerns.
“A mandatory approach would require screening a very large prison population to identify the much smaller group for whom treatment might actually be appropriate,” she said. “It would have substantial clinical and resource implications.”
There were also concerns that if it was mandatory, there could be a breakdown of trust with offenders and it could be open to abuse, she said.
“Trying to impose and monitor daily medication among people who do not necessarily want to take it could be extremely inefficient. It could also introduce a range of consequences that we simply do not yet understand, including effects on trust, disclosure, engagement and the therapeutic relationship.”
She rejected characterising the drugs as a form of “chemical castration”. “People say that because some people like the idea of castrating people who commit sexual offences,” she said. “But these drugs are not permanent, unlike castration, and must be taken consistently to work.”
Burnham announced earlier this month that prisoners convicted of rape, grooming and serious child sexual offences would be excluded from the early release scheme that is due to begin in October. Other sex offenders serving sentences of less than four years will still be eligible to leave prison early.
There are comparatively low reoffending rates among sexual offenders compared with other cohorts. According to government data, 11.7% of sex offenders reoffended in 2023, compared with 53.9% of those with an index offence for theft.
Prison campaigners have urged caution before going ahead with a national programme. Critics have previously pointed out that long-term testosterone suppression can cause osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease. There is limited data because randomised controlled trials remain scarce.
Andrew Neilson, the director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, said: “The history of prison-based treatment programmes in this area has proven troubled, which is both a reason for exploring alternatives but also a reason to exercise caution before expanding new approaches more widely. It’s also important that nobody is forced into these chemical interventions and that participation is truly voluntary.”
Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the prison officers’ union the POA, said: “Anything that potentially protects the public is welcome but I would be cautious about the rollout until we are in receipt of evidence that proves success.”
A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “This government is determined to tackle the root causes of sex offending, which is why we’re working at pace to extend the existing pilot to a further two regions.”
Additional reporting by Faisa Mohamed
summary: Libido-suppressing drugs could be rolled out voluntarily to thousands of male sex offenders in prisons across England and Wales by December 2028, pending pilot results. A pilot program testing medications such as SSRIs and anti-androgens is expanding to more prisons and NHS regions. Meanwhile, ministers are re-evaluating whether to pursue mandatory chemical castration, a concept that experts warn could damage trust and clinical relationships.
key_points: Around 3,750 male prisoners in England and Wales could be considered for voluntary sex drive-suppressing treatment by December 2028.
A pilot program providing medications like SSRIs and anti-androgens is expanding from 10 to 20 prisons across additional NHS regions.
Experts have raised concerns that making chemical castration mandatory would damage trust, strain resources, and prove difficult to monitor.
About 15,000 prisoners are currently serving sentences for sexual offences in England and Wales.
Critics and prison campaigners have urged caution, noting potential long-term health risks like osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease from testosterone suppression.

title: Two men die in multi-vehicle crash in Surrey
author: Stuart Maisner
content:
![A two-lane road in the countryside daytime with cars in the distance](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/941/cpsprodpb/b4a9/live/64c96770-9e27-11f1-8c7d-f12be985a317.png)
The crash happened on the A246 at East Clandon on Friday evening
- Published
Two men have died in a multi-vehicle crash in Surrey, police have said.
The collision took place on the A246 Epsom Road at East Clandon just after 23:00 BST on Friday, and involved three Seat Leons, one black, one white, and one grey, Surrey Police said.
The driver of the white vehicle, a man in his late teens, and the passenger, a man in his early 20s, died at the scene. Their next of kin have been informed.
A 22-year-old man from Woking, a 21-year-old woman from Guildford and a 19-year-old man from Guildford have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and remain in police custody.
Epsom Road was closed to allow officers to carry out enquiries at the scene.
Surrey Police is appealing for witnesses or anyone with dashcam footage to come forward.

Three people have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and remain in police custody as officers appeal for witnesses.
key_points: A multi-vehicle crash occurred on the A246 at East Clandon just after 23:00 BST on Friday.
The collision involved three Seat Leons: one black, one white, and one grey.
A teenage driver and a man in his early 20s died at the scene.
