title: Seven killed, including two police officers, in UK ‘wrong-side’ car crash
author: Anadolu; AP; Reuters; The Associated Press
content:
![Ambulances lined up in London, United Kingdom. \[File: Alberto Pezzali/AP Photo\]](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/ap_6a89cfae15d0b-1787416494.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Seven people, including two police officers, have died in a head-on collision during a pursuit, after a vehicle driving down the wrong side of a major road hit a police car in the United Kingdom.
All occupants of both vehicles were pronounced dead at the scene near Middlesbrough in northeast England on Saturday, according to the Cleveland Police.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Landmark trial on Meta’s impact on children’s mental health begins in US
- list 2 of 3Four killed in helicopter crash in Brazil’s Rio de Janeiro
- list 3 of 3Singapore-flagged container ship crashes into riverbank in India
A total of 12 people have been killed in less than a week in separate accidents involving cars driving on the wrong side of the road in the UK and Ireland, as a similar collision occurred in Dublin on Sunday.
The Cleveland Police said five members of the public were travelling along the wrong side of the road in a Volkswagen Passat when it collided with a marked police vehicle heading in the correct direction at around 3:39am (02:39 GMT).
Authorities are investigating the exact circumstances of the crash but said they understood that officers had begun a pursuit when they sighted a “suspicious vehicle”.
“This is an incredibly sad day for Cleveland,” Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said.
The police force said it had formally identified the passengers in the Volkswagen Passat and was contacting their families.
Fuller named the two dead officers as police constables Matthew Blades, 37, and Tom Clough, 38, describing them as “brave officers … who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift”.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on X that he was “devastated” to hear about the loss of life and urged people “to avoid speculation at this time”.
The incident follows two similar recent head-on crashes near Dublin, with authorities there highlighting a social media-driven trend for “wrong-side” driving among young people.
After the collision in Dublin on Sunday, Ireland’s prime minister, or taoiseach, Michael Martin, said it was the latest in a series of similar incidents. “There can be no tolerance for this reckless behaviour that we have seen on our roads recently. It must stop,” Martin said.
Irish police chief Justin Kelly added that it came after another head-on crash on a motorway and warned that “what makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media”.
An Irish parliament committee has asked short-form video platform TikTok to explain how it removes content “that appears to glorify dangerous and illegal behaviour on our roads”. On Tuesday, Ireland’s media regulator made a similar request.
summary: Seven people, including two police officers, were killed in a head-on collision near Middlesbrough in northeast England after a car driving on the wrong side of the road hit a police vehicle during a pursuit. The victims included five members of the public in a Volkswagen Passat and Cleveland Police Constables Matthew Blades and Tom Clough. The incident is part of a broader concern over recent wrong-way driving incidents in the UK and Ireland, with authorities noting that some cases are driven by reckless social media trends.
key_points: A head-on crash near Middlesbrough resulted in seven deaths, including two police officers.
The collision occurred when a Volkswagen Passat traveling on the wrong side of the road hit a marked police car during a pursuit.
The two deceased officers were identified as Police Constables Matthew Blades and Tom Clough.
Authorities in the UK and Ireland have raised alarms over a dangerous social media trend involving wrong-side driving.

title: Constance Marten can appeal against sentence for killing her baby
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![Constance Marten](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000499162522_17874096468420_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqISd2Q5fDp-tXRkcRUZhKaOTIg_UJUfaXZgg_L3G-w1c.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Constance Marten](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000499162522_17874096468420_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqISd2Q5fDp-tXRkcRUZhKaOTIg_UJUfaXZgg_L3G-w1c.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Constance Marten has been granted permission to appeal against her 14-year prison sentence for the manslaughter of her baby daughter while on the run with her partner.
Marten, 39, and Mark Gordon, 52, a convicted rapist, were in hiding from the authorities when their baby daughter, Victoria, died in a tent on the South Downs in East Sussex in January 2023.
The couple had fled to prevent Victoria from being taken into care, as their four other children had been, their Old Bailey trial was told.
Marten, whose Eton-educated father was a page of honour to Elizabeth II, and Gordon were found guilty of Victoria’s manslaughter, child cruelty, concealing the birth of a child and perverting the course of justice following two trials spanning six months each.
Judge Mark Lucraft KC jailed them both for 14 years and imposed a further four years on extended licence for Gordon.
Marten has now been granted permission to appeal against the sentence, and has renewed her application for permission to appeal against her gross negligence manslaughter conviction. A court date is yet to be set.
![Constance Marten holding Victoria under her coat](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000440135871_17874098520831_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq75uHg2sRmEqDvgdOkWoQYJXiz3kMxWeckdbQy1i3tFo.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Judge Lucraft accepted the prosecution’s case that Victoria died from hypothermia after being exposed to “significant cold stress”. He rejected the defendants’ claims that Victoria was smothered in a “terrible accident” as they slept in the tent.
Their offence was made worse because the baby was vulnerable and the defendants failed to listen to past warnings, he said.
In a televised sentencing, Judge Lucraft told the defendants: “It is clear throughout the period neither of you gave much or any thought for the care or love for your baby.”
The judge said they had displayed “arrogance” and treated Victoria with “neglect of the most serious type”.
Police had launched a nationwide hunt after the couple’s car burst into flames on a motorway near Bolton, Greater Manchester, on Jan 5 2023.
The defendants travelled across England and went off-grid, sleeping in a tent on the South Downs where Victoria died days later. After seven weeks on the run, they were arrested in Brighton.
Police subsequently found baby Victoria, lying dead inside a Lidl bag and surrounded by rubbish in a disused shed near the campsite in which they had been staying.
summary: Constance Marten has been granted permission to appeal against her 14-year prison sentence for the manslaughter of her baby daughter, Victoria. Marten and her partner, Mark Gordon, went on the run to prevent the child from being taken into care, leading to the baby's death from hypothermia in a tent in January 2023. Marten is also renewing her application for permission to appeal against her gross negligence manslaughter conviction.
key_points: Constance Marten was previously sentenced to 14 years in prison alongside Mark Gordon for the manslaughter of their baby daughter.
The couple went into hiding on the South Downs in January 2023 to avoid having their child taken into care.
Judge Mark Lucraft concluded that baby Victoria died from hypothermia after being exposed to significant cold stress.
Marten has now been granted permission to appeal her sentence and is renewing her appeal against her conviction.
The pair were arrested in Brighton after a seven-week nationwide police manhunt.

title: 'Three pedestrians injured' in crash, including two teenagers, sparking appeal
author: Joe Regent
content:
Police are appealing for witnesses after three pedestrians were injured in a collision involving a Range Rover and a caravan in Skelmersdale.
The incident happened on Beechtrees at around 8.30pm on Wednesday, August 19, when a dark blue Range Rover Vogue towing a caravan was involved in a collision.
The caravan reportedly became detached from the vehicle, mounted the pavement, and struck two 18-year-old women.
Both women were taken to hospital with serious injuries.
One remains in hospital, while the other has since been discharged.
The driver of the Range Rover left the scene in the vehicle, colliding with a woman in her 30s who was believed to be trying to stop him from leaving.
She suffered minor injuries.
The Range Rover was later traced to the West Yorkshire area.
A 44-year-old man from Rotherham was arrested on suspicion of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and assault.
He has been released on bail pending further enquiries.
Police are urging anyone who witnessed the collision or has dashcam, doorbell, or CCTV footage of the Range Rover before or after the incident to come forward.
Inquiries remain ongoing.
summary: Police are appealing for witnesses after a collision in Skelmersdale where a detached caravan struck two 18-year-old pedestrians, causing serious injuries. The driver of the Range Rover then fled the scene, hitting another woman who suffered minor injuries. A 44-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and assault, and subsequently released on bail.
key_points: Three pedestrians were injured in the incident on Beechtrees on August 19.
A caravan detached from a dark blue Range Rover Vogue and mounted the pavement, hitting two 18-year-old women.
The driver struck another woman in her 30s while leaving the scene before driving away.
A 44-year-old man from Rotherham was arrested and later released on bail.
Police are currently seeking witnesses and relevant video footage as inquiries continue.

title: Teenage girl killed in tragedy which closed motorway

content:
UK regional news website of the year

“Motorists with dashcam are also asked to check for footage that may assist the investigation.
“Anyone with relevant information should call 01622 798538 or email sciu.td@kent.police.uk quoting reference, 46/138541/26. Dashcam footage can be uploaded here.”
Investigators remain at the scene.
summary: A teenage girl died after being struck by vehicles on the M20 motorway in Kent early in the morning. The incident occurred on the eastbound carriageway near Teapot Lane, Aylesford, at around 3.20am.

title: Herts driver who killed girl, 13, sentenced to 12 years in jail
author: Dan Mountney
content:
A man who killed a 13-year-old girl in a car crash in Hertfordshire has been jailed for more than 12 years.
Dwane Moody, 40, of Rowney Lane, Dane End, was sentenced at St Albans Crown Court today (August 21), after admitting causing death by dangerous driving and a string of related offences.
Moody also pleaded guilty to causing death while uninsured, causing death while not in accordance with a licence, two counts of perverting the course of justice, and aggravated vehicle taking.
He was jailed for 12 years and eight months and banned from driving for 17 years and four months.
The crash, which happened at around 7.30pm on Saturday, January 31, claimed the life of 13-year-old Evelyn Haylock, who was sitting in the front passenger seat of the vehicle.
Two other teenage passengers suffered minor injuries.
  Dwane Moody. (Image: Herts police)
Detective Constable Lewis Stanley of the Serious Collision Investigation Unit said: "This is a tragic case in which a young girl lost her life unnecessarily.
"Evelyn's family have shown immense strength throughout this investigation and our thoughts remain with them as they continue to come to terms with their devastating loss.
"Dwane Moody made a series of reckless and selfish decisions that evening.
"Not only did he drive dangerously, resulting in a fatal collision, but he then attempted to evade responsibility by pressuring others to provide a false account of what had happened.
"It speaks volumes of his character that he, a grown man, was trying to persuade the other passengers, both teenagers, to lie for him whilst they were trying to save Evelyn.
"They suffered a hugely traumatic ordeal and I would like to commend them for their brave actions.
"No sentence can undo the pain caused by Evelyn’s death."
Moody and the three teenagers had been at a party in Dane End before the collision.
He had consumed alcohol before taking another guest's vehicle and driving away with the group of teenagers.
Witnesses reported the car being driven erratically at high speed, and as Moody drove up Whitehill, he failed to navigate a corner and crashed through a fence, seriously injuring Evelyn.
The two surviving teenagers called 999 and began administering first aid.
Moody then urged them to lie and say another vehicle forced them off the road.
  Evelyn Haylock was killed in the crash. (Image: Herts police)
He left the scene but later returned with the vehicle’s rightful owner. Moody then threatened one of the teenagers, insisting that they should tell the police the false account of what had happened.
Emergency services arrived and arrested Moody, who was taken to hospital as a precaution but discharged with no injuries before being placed in custody.
Evelyn and the other teenagers were taken to hospital, but she died on February 4.
In a statement read out in court, Evelyn’s mother said: "She was a child who absolutely loved life.
"She brought an infectious energy into our home, and her presence was pure light.
"One of her absolute favourite places to be was on her trampoline. I can still close my eyes and see her jumping, laughing, and defying gravity, just bursting with youth and happiness.
"She had so much life left to live, so many more days to jump, play, and grow. Evelyn’s feet will never touch that trampoline again. Her laughter has been permanently silenced.
"The defendant didn't just cause a crash; he shattered my entire universe."
Evelyn’s father also paid tribute to his daughter, saying: "Evelyn was the light of all our worlds, there wasn't a day that would go by without her making us laugh or smile.
"She would pop up throughout the day and say the most random things that would make us all burst out laughing.
"Our family is a chain, and she was the strongest link keeping us all together and now that link is no longer there but we are still holding on strong, never losing her name and keeping her in our hearts."
summary: Dwane Moody has been sentenced to 12 years and eight months in prison for causing the death of 13-year-old Evelyn Haylock in a Hertfordshire car crash. Moody, who had been drinking and driving without a licence or insurance, crashed the stolen vehicle while driving erratically at high speed. He also pleaded guilty to perverting the course of justice after attempting to pressure surviving teenage passengers into lying to the police.
key_points: Dwane Moody was sentenced to 12 years and eight months in jail and banned from driving for over 17 years.
Moody pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving, driving without a licence or insurance, aggravated vehicle taking, and perverting the course of justice.
Thirteen-year-old passenger Evelyn Haylock died from injuries sustained in the crash, which occurred on January 31.
Moody drove erratically at high speed after consuming alcohol and failed to navigate a corner on Whitehill.
Following the crash, Moody attempted to cover up his actions by coercing the teenage passengers to lie to the police about what happened.

title: Third arrest in Leicester murder probe after cyclist punched
author: Samantha Noble
content:
![A man in glasses wearing a suit](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/458/cpsprodpb/2792/live/7d2f2b10-9e0e-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
George Glover's family said they were "so proud of the young man he'd become"
- Published
A third person has been arrested as part of a murder investigation following the death of a "loving and loyal" man in Leicester.
George Glover, 27, was punched as he cycled along Narborough Road, close to the junction with Noel Street, at about 06:30 BST on Monday, Leicestershire Police said. He died in hospital on Thursday.
A 24-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder on Friday and remains in custody.
A 31-year-old man and 39-year-old woman, who were previously arrested on suspicion of robbery and conspiracy to commit murder, also remain in custody, the force said.
In a tribute released by police on Friday, Glover's family said they were "so proud of the young man he'd become".
They said: "George was a much-loved son and big brother to his three siblings. His loss is already felt so deeply."
Officers from the East Midlands Special Operations Unit are continuing to appeal for anyone who may be able to assist with their inquiries to get in touch.
Det Insp Kevin Hames said: "If you can help but haven't yet contacted us, please be assured it's not too late and anything you're able to provide â including any footage â could be vital to our investigation."
Listen to BBC Radio Leicester on Sounds and follow BBC Leicester on Facebook, external, on X, external, or on Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to eastmidsnews@bbc.co.uk, external or via WhatsApp, external on 0808 100 2210.
summary: A third person has been arrested in connection with the murder investigation of George Glover, a 27-year-old cyclist who was punched in Leicester. Glover was attacked on Narborough Road and died in hospital days later. Police and his family have released tributes and are continuing to appeal for witnesses and footage to assist the investigation.
key_points: George Glover, 27, died in hospital after being punched while cycling on Narborough Road in Leicester.
A 24-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder, joining two other suspects in custody.
Glover's family paid tribute to him as a much-loved son and brother.
Leicestershire Police and the East Midlands Special Operations Unit are appealing for public assistance and footage.

title: WATCH: CCTV captures jealous killer as he stalked ex-wife before murdering her
author: Simon Parkin
content:
The movements of a jealous killer who stalked his ex-wife and lay in wait before brutally murdering her are revealed in CCTV.
Raymond Williams, 61, slashed the throat of Tania Williams outside her home after seeing her with another man during a night out in Norwich.
The 49-year-old mother-of-four was found with severe injuries and significant blood loss close to her home at Catherine Gardens in Thorpe St Andrew and died despite the efforts of neighbours and paramedics to save her life.
  Raymond Williams was found guilty of the murder of his estranged wife Tania Williams (Image: Norfolk Constabulary)
  Raymond Williams leaving his accommodation in Dereham Road before heading into Norwich city centre to seek out Tania (Image: Norfolk Constabulary)
Williams, who previously served as a Norfolk police community support officer, was found guilty of her murder following a trial at Norwich Crown Court, which heard he had been “consumed with jealousy”.
CCTV and video footage shown to the jury included the last moments of Tania’s life and captured her former husband “going from bar to bar” to track her down before driving to her home to confront her.
Footage shows him leaving his flat in shared accommodation in Dereham Road before heading into the city centre.
  Tania Williams (Image: Norfolk Constabulary)
  Raymond Williams was a well known figure on the Norwich nightlife scene (Image: Facebook)
The trial heard he had approached a man she was with, telling him they were still married and pointing to his wedding ring.
Williams is then seen on CCTV searching for Tania before eventually locating her in Revolucion de Cuba, on Queen Street.
READ MORE: Raymond Williams guilty of the Thorpe murder of his ex-wife
Further footage captures both Williams and Tania walking out of the venue and down Queen Street, with Tania appearing to be trying to distance herself from him.
As Tania heads in one direction to catch a bus home, Williams is seen jogging down Wensum Street towards where his white Vauxhall Corsa was parked on Fishergate.
  Raymond Williams jogging down Wensum Street towards his car, before driving to Thorpe (Image: Norfolk Constabulary)
  The white Vauxhall Corsa parked on Yarmouth Road as Raymond Williams 'laid in wait' for Tania to arrive home (Image: Norfolk Constabulary)
Security footage then shows this car parked on Yarmouth Road as he “laid in wait” for Tania, who is then seen on CCTV getting off her bus and walking towards her home in Catherine Gardens.
At 11.30pm, neighbours heard petrified screams, including a female voice saying: “What are you going to do? Kill me?”, before Tania was discovered lying on the ground in a “pool of blood”.
Two hours later, armed police arrested Williams at his accommodation.
By now, he was dressed completely differently after disposing of everything he was wearing earlier in the evening in a bid to avoid forensic detection.
  Raymond Williams being arrested outside his home on Dereham Road two hours after the killing (Image: Norfolk Constabulary)
  Armed police officers force Raymond Williams to the ground during his arrest (Image: Norfolk Constabulary)
CCTV had captured him acting suspiciously around bins in nearby alleyways. Footage showed him taking off his watch and dropping it down a drain.
The watch had been given to him by Tania.
Williams will be sentenced on September 21.
Senior Investigating Officer Detective Inspector Sam Pontin said: "This was a thorough and complex investigation involving officers and staff from across the force.
"Thanks to the strength of the evidence presented, the jury was able to reach its verdict and hold Williams accountable for his actions.
"While no verdict can undo the pain caused by Tania's death, I hope today's outcome provides her family with some measure of justice."
summary: Raymond Williams, a 61-year-old former police community support officer, was found guilty of murdering his 49-year-old ex-wife, Tania Williams, outside her Norwich home. CCTV footage tracked Williams as he stalked her through city centre bars after seeing her with another man before lying in wait to slash her throat. Following the attack, he attempted to evade forensic detection by changing his clothes and disposing of items in bins and a drain before being arrested by armed police. He is scheduled to be sentenced on September 21.
key_points: Raymond Williams was convicted of murdering his estranged wife, Tania Williams, after a trial at Norwich Crown Court.
CCTV footage captured Williams tracking Tania from bar to bar in Norwich city centre out of jealousy.
Williams waited near her home in Catherine Gardens before launching the fatal attack.
He attempted to avoid forensic detection by changing his clothes and disposing of his belongings and watch.
Williams is scheduled to be sentenced on September 21.

title: ‘Multiple’ people die in crash involving police vehicle and car in North Yorkshire
author: Geneva Abdul
content:
‘Multiple people’ have died in a collision involving a police vehicle near Middlesbrough.
A number of people were killed in the crash on the A66 in South Bank, North Yorkshire, in the early hours of Saturday morning, according to local authorities.
“Around 3.39am this morning, a collision took place involving a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 in South Bank,” a Cleveland police spokesperson said.
“Sadly, the collision has resulted in multiple fatalities. There are significant emergency vehicles on the scene and the road will remain closed for some time.”
North East ambulance service said it had been called to a two-vehicle crash and sent 14 units to the scene including ambulance crews, a specialist paramedic, a hazardous area response team and a doctor from Great North air ambulance service.
Police have yet to confirm the number of fatalities.
Anna Turley, the MP for the Redcar constituency where the crash happened, said: “I am deeply saddened to hear of the fatal collision on the A66 this morning. My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of those who have lost their lives, and with everyone affected by this terrible incident.”
Police said they were working to identify the victims and contact their families, and that the incident was “quickly evolving”. The A66 remains closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane in Eston.
summary: Multiple people have died in a collision involving a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 in South Bank, North Yorkshire. The crash occurred in the early hours of Saturday morning, prompting a major response from emergency services. The road remains closed in both directions as authorities work to identify the victims and contact their families.
key_points: A collision involving a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat occurred on the A66 in South Bank.
The incident resulted in multiple fatalities, though the exact number has not yet been confirmed by police.
The North East ambulance service dispatched 14 units to the scene, including paramedics and a hazardous area response team.
The A66 remains closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane.

title: Multiple deaths after Teesside crash between police vehicle and car
author: Tom MacDougall; Tom Mullen
content:
![Generic shot of two Cleveland Police vehicles](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/524/cpsprodpb/6780/live/3eddc630-9e06-11f1-afde-61b39e745f81.png)
Police said they were working to identify the victims and contact their families (generic image)
- Published
Multiple people have died in a crash involving a police vehicle and a car, police have said.
The collision involved a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough in Teesside, at about 03:39 BST, Cleveland Police said.
North East Ambulance Service said three vehicles were involved in total and "a number of patients died at the scene".
A police spokesman said: "Sadly, the collision has resulted in multiple fatalities. We are working to identify the victims and contact their families."
The road remains closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane and the force said it would do so "for some time".
'Quickly evolving'
The public are asked to use alternative routes.
The force said there were still "significant emergency service vehicles" on the scene.
It added: "This is a quickly evolving incident and we ask that members of the public respectfully avoid speculation."
The North East Ambulance Service said 14 "ambulance resources" were called to the scene.
"Sadly, despite the best efforts of everyone attending, a number of patients died at the scene," the service said.
"We send condolences to all of those affected by such a tragic event and thank everyone for all they did to help."
summary: Multiple people died in a collision involving a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough. Cleveland Police and the North East Ambulance Service responded to the scene, deploying significant emergency resources. The A66 remains closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane while authorities work to identify the victims and contact their families.
key_points: A crash involving a police vehicle and a car occurred on the A66 in South Bank near Middlesbrough.
Multiple fatalities were confirmed at the scene by both police and the ambulance service.
The North East Ambulance Service dispatched 14 ambulance resources to the incident.
The A66 remains closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane.
Police are working to identify the victims and notify their families while asking the public to avoid speculation.

title: Palestinian-British girl, 6, dies days after family drowned off UK coast
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![Dozens of people have drowned across Europe this year amid record heatwaves. \[File:Charlotte Coney/Getty Images.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty_6a88e88850-1787357320.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
A six-year-old Palestinian-British girl whose parents and sister drowned earlier this week has also died in hospital, according to local police.
Saja el-Khawas was taken to hospital in critical condition on Tuesday but has since died, Sussex police said Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Why extreme heat is much more dangerous for the elderly than we realised
- list 2 of 3Heatwaves and energy crunch: Can Europe withstand a double shock?
- list 3 of 3Palestinian refugee and two relatives drown off English coast
Saja’s father Hassan El-Khawas, 55, her mother Zeina Alayn, 37, and her 14-year-old sister Sara El-Khawas all died at the scene after getting into difficulty in the water at Shoreham, Sussex, on Tuesday.
The family lived in London but travelled to Shoreham to visit the beach as the United Kingdom sweltered under its latest heatwave of the year.
An investigation into what happened remains open, but the current theory is that it was a “tragic accident, with no third-party involvement”, the police said.
British newspaper the Daily Telegraph reported on Tuesday, citing the Palestinian embassy, that the family was originally from the Rashidieh refugee camp in southern Lebanon.
Hassan reportedly came to the UK as a refugee, and previously lived in the Rashidieh camp, one of the most populous Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham previously described what happened to the el-Khawas family as a “terrible family tragedy”.
The Palestinian Forum in Britain held a gathering to commemorate the family on Thursday.
Drownings have surged across Europe as people seek relief from the heatwave on the continent, with incidents reported in France, Germany and the UK.
summary: A six-year-old Palestinian-British girl has died in the hospital days after her parents and sister drowned off the coast of Shoreham, Sussex. The family, originally from Lebanon and living in London, had visited the beach during a UK heatwave. Sussex police are treating the incident as a tragic accident with no third-party involvement.
key_points: Saja el-Khawas, 6, died in the hospital following a drowning incident off the Sussex coast.
Her father Hassan, 55, mother Zeina, 37, and sister Sara, 14, died at the scene.
The family traveled from London to Shoreham to visit the beach during a heatwave.
Police state the current theory is a tragic accident with no third-party involvement.
The family was originally from the Rashidieh Palestinian refugee camp in southern Lebanon.

title: No closure for terror victims, says Burnham, as survivors tell ceremony about life after attacks
author: Live Reporting Edited by Kieran Kelly; Alex Smith
content:
![](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/128/cpsprodpb//vivo/live/images/2025/10/22/fd38c218-8299-43dd-a813-87b46b60630d.jpg.webp) Katie Williams
Live reporter
![Thelma Stober speaking during the inaugural National Day for Victims and Survivors of Terrorism](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/8/21/40f64116-3d13-49cd-8b15-ff65b611361b.jpg.webp) Image source, PA Media
7/7 survivor Thelma Stober speaking during the ceremony today
Today, the UK marked its first national day for the victims and survivors of terrorism, with a two-minute silence and a ceremony in London.
We heard from survivors, bereaved family members and a representative for the emergency services, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham also addressing the congregation.
Survivor of the 7/7 bombings Thelma Stober told those gathered: "Your pain is real, your loss matters, your voices matter."
Meanwhile, Paul Price, who lost his partner and sustained life-changing injuries in the 2017 Manchester Arena attack, told those gathered he had to "climb mountains" every single day following the attack - but discovered that "hope and resilience can be rebuilt brick by careful brick".
Closing the event, Burnham expressed his "deep admiration" for those in the room, but said "too often" people had not had "the support they deserved".
He vowed to consult on a permanent national memorial to victims and survivors, and said the government would look at reforming compensation and access to legal assistance.
We're now bringing our live coverage to a close. Watch more from today's event here.
summary: The UK marked its first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism with a ceremony in London featuring a two-minute silence and speeches from survivors and officials. Prime Minister Andy Burnham acknowledged that victims have often lacked proper support and vowed to consult on a permanent national memorial, as well as review compensation and legal assistance. Survivors, including a 7/7 bombings survivor and a Manchester Arena attack survivor, shared their ongoing struggles and messages of resilience.
key_points: The UK marked its inaugural national day for victims and survivors of terrorism with a ceremony and two-minute silence in London.
Survivors such as Thelma Stober and Paul Price shared their personal experiences of trauma and resilience following terror attacks.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated that victims have often not received the support they deserved.
Burnham vowed to consult on a permanent national memorial and reform compensation and legal assistance access.

title: Burnham axes Whitehall jobs as civil servants moved to regional mayors' offices
author: Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Burnham vows to 'rewire Britain' with devolution push and 'No. 10 North' in Manchester](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/06/490787f28e7a1e58d92e4476226fa3aeY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MzQzMzIz-2.85612233.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Around 90 civil servants will take up posts in the regions under the scheme for secondments of six to nine months.
The Government billed the move as the “largest transfer of Whitehall capacity to local leaders yet”.
But the union representing senior civil servants swiftly warned of possible compulsory job changes and large number of posts going in London as part of the proposed major reforms.
![Then mayor of Greater Manchester Andy Burnham (left) and Mayor of Liverpool City Region Steve Rotheram (Danny Lawso/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/02/10/a71b6dd9eb14e8274b31f925d0eaed09Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg1NzQ3Mzky-2.63923811.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Speaking afterwards, he said: “No10 North is putting more power into every postcode across the country so communities can unleash and unlock their own potential.
“I'm bringing together Mayors from different political parties to work on these challenges, because people deserve problem-solving rather than point-scoring.”
From the autumn, high-performing civil servants will be seconded into mayoral authorities around the country.
Read More
The move aims to build capability and capacity and accelerate the transfer of power to local areas, No10 said.
In an initial pilot, every mayoral authority will receive between five and ten civil servants on a 6–9-month secondment.
But Dave Penman, General Secretary of the FDA union of senior civil servants, raised concerns over the way the Government is handling the reforms.
He posted on X: “Quotes from senior No.10 figures and anonymous briefings about ‘uncomfortable’ headcount cuts raises significant questions not only over the number of civil servants involved, but the location and potentially compulsory change of employer.“
He added: “The Government is entitled to change the way the country is governed, but it also has a duty to be a good employer.
“Not just because that’s what any government should aspire to, but because effective management of the workforce delivering that change will result in better outcomes for the public they serve.”
![Figures show the UK Civil Service workforce is close to a 20-year high (Mark Phillips/Alamy)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/12/16/12/16120341-9c3195ad-174c-4204-be0f-bb018f7e1871.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
As part of the announcement on Friday:
* A new Civil Service Fast Stream pilot will be set up in Yorkshire and the Humber, providing more opportunities to build successful careers in regions outside London
* The Future Leaders Scheme, a civil service programme to develop high potential individuals, will be expanded to include mayoral and local authority officials
* A digital devolution programme will be launched to unlock government data and build AI, digital and data capability in mayoral authorities
* Ministers will work with mayors to fast-track major sports-led regeneration projects and bring forward jobs, investment and housing in the regions
Communities Secretary Angela Rayner said: “We want to see more power and resource shifted away from Westminster and back into the hands of our communities where it belongs.
“We’re also giving our mayors the tools they need to push on and deliver on what matters for their community, whether that’s new transport links, more safe and secure homes, regeneration projects, or everything in between.”
But it has been criticised as running counter to the PM’s devolution pledge by taking decision-making away from local councils.
It has also led to warnings that more homes could be built on greenbelt in commuter areas around the capital.
summary: Around 90 civil servants will be seconded to regional mayoral authorities for six to nine months in what the Government describes as the largest transfer of Whitehall capacity to local leaders. While ministers say the move will build capability and shift power away from Westminster, the FDA union of senior civil servants has raised concerns regarding potential compulsory job changes and headcount cuts in London. Additional measures include a new Fast Stream pilot in Yorkshire and the Humber, an expanded Future Leaders Scheme, and a digital devolution programme.
key_points: Approximately 90 civil servants will take part in six to nine-month secondments to regional mayoral authorities, with each authority receiving between five and ten staff in an initial pilot.
The FDA union representing senior civil servants warned of possible compulsory job changes, headcount cuts in London, and concerns over how the Government is handling reforms.
A new Civil Service Fast Stream pilot will be established in Yorkshire and the Humber to provide regional career opportunities.
The Future Leaders Scheme will be expanded to include mayoral and local authority officials.
Communities Secretary Angela Rayner stated the initiative aims to shift power and resources away from Westminster and back to communities.

title: 'High-performing' civil servants to be seconded into mayoral authorities
author: Tevye Markson
content:
"High-performing" civil servants will be seconded into mayoral authorities from this autumn, the prime minister has announced.
Civil servants will be seconded into mayoral authorities to “build capability and capacity and accelerate the transfer of power to local areas” as part of the PM Andy Burnham’s plan to “shift power, funding and accountability from Whitehall to local leaders”.
The initial pilot will see every mayoral authority receive between five and ten civil servants on a six–to-nine-month secondment.
“The teams will provide the skills and expertise needed to support a once-in-a-generation devolution settlement,” No.10 said.
Mayors will be given the freedom to request the type of skills they need.
Eighteen mayoral strategic authorities are expected to be included in the initial secondment programme, with two further strategic authorities currently forming that could benefit in future.
The announcement comes after Burnham last month announced a new wave of devolution that will give greater powers for housing, transport and skills to regional mayors.  
No.10 has also today announced an expansion of the Future Leaders Scheme, the civil service programme to develop high potential individuals, to mayoral and local authority officials.
The cross-government development scheme, until now only for high-potential grade 6 and 7 civil servants, provides a leadership development curriculum which supports officials in accelerating their development as well as learning more about their personal leadership effectiveness.
The plans were announced after the PM today convened mayors from across England for the first No.10 North “virtual situation room”.
No.10 also announced that a new Civil Service Fast Stream pilot will be launched in Yorkshire and Humber, “providing more opportunities to build successful careers in regions outside London and creating a new pipeline of future leaders with experience working in local and central government”.
Applications will launch alongside the next intake in October, with successful candidates starting in September 2027.
In a further announcement, No.10 said a digital devolution programme will be launched to “unlock government data and build AI, digital and data capability in mayoral authorities”.
It said this will “improve access to government data, create a common data-sharing model between Whitehall and mayoral authorities, expand AI and data skills training, and help local leaders use technology to improve public services and support economic growth”.
No.10 said the package of reforms follows direct requests from mayors at the first meeting of the National Economic Council, held at the end of July, where local leaders called for “stronger local capability, faster decision-making and closer partnership with government”.
Announcing the plans, Burnham said: “No10 North is putting more power into every postcode across the country so communities can unleash and unlock their own potential.
“I’m bringing together mayors from different political parties to work on these challenges, because people deserve problem-solving rather than point-scoring.”
First secretary of state Louise Haigh added: “The days of Westminster hoarding power are over. This government has kickstarted the biggest transition of power and resources in a generation, taking it from Whitehall and putting it back in the hands of local communities.”
Government 'has duty to be a good employer' – union boss raises concerns in response to announcement
FDA general secretary Dave Penman has raised concerns about the manner of today's announcements.
Commenting on X, Penman said: "Quotes from senior No.10 figures and anonymous briefings about ‘uncomfortable’ headcount cuts raises significant questions not only over the number of civil servants involved, but the location and potentially compulsory change of employer. Without the forthcoming white paper, the lack of detail and language used will only cause uncertainty.
"The government is entitled to change the way the country is governed, but it also has a duty to be a good employer. Not just because that’s what any government should aspire to, but because effective management of the workforce delivering that change will result in better outcomes for the public they serve."
summary: The prime minister has announced that high-performing civil servants will be seconded into mayoral authorities starting this autumn to support local devolution. The package of reforms also includes expanding the Future Leaders Scheme to local officials, a new Civil Service Fast Stream pilot in Yorkshire and Humber, and a digital devolution programme. While the government aims to shift power and resources from Whitehall to local leaders, union boss Dave Penman has raised concerns regarding a lack of detail and potential workforce uncertainty.
key_points: High-performing civil servants will be seconded to mayoral authorities for six to nine months, with each authority receiving between five and ten personnel.
The Future Leaders Scheme is expanding to include mayoral and local authority officials.
A new Civil Service Fast Stream pilot will launch in Yorkshire and Humber, with applications opening in October and candidates starting in September 2027.
A digital devolution programme will unlock government data and build AI, digital, and data capability in mayoral authorities.
FDA general secretary Dave Penman raised concerns that the announcements and language used could cause workforce uncertainty.

title: Four questions Andy Burnham answered during Bradford visit
author: Victoria Scheer; Gemma Dillon
content:
![A close-up view of Burnham seated indoors, captured from the chest up. Burnham has short, neatly styled hair and is facing slightly toward the camera.
He is wearing dark rectangular glasses, a dark blazer, and a dark shirt. One hand is raised in front of the body, with the fingers held horizontally as if emphasizing a point while speaking. A ring is visible on one finger.
The photograph is sharply focused on the person in the foreground, while the background is heavily blurred. Several other people appear to be present in the background, but they are out of focus and their features are not clearly visible.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/84c8/live/c7ed5a60-9cb9-11f1-84cf-fd4cfd9d6c84.jpg)
Prime Minister Andy Burnham during a visit to the Grange Interlink Community Centre in Bradford on Thursday
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has set out a number of priorities during his visit to West Yorkshire on Thursday.
Speaking at a waste dump in Bradford, he said he would crack down on fly-tipping and look into equipping fire and rescue services with more resources to tackle wildfires and flooding.
He also spoke about plans to boost infrastructure and support British farming.
Below are the four questions he answered from BBC Yorkshire.
How will you tackle fly-tipping?
During his visit to Bradford, he said West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester would be the first areas with new region-led approaches to waste crime.
This would include giving mayors and council leaders the lead in co-ordinating councils, police, regulators, and other enforcement agencies.
"It's a new approach, it's needed because this issue has grown and grown but we're confident now that we've got the right resources in place," he said.
"If you look at the clean-up costs of the huge (illegal) sites, well, they are double-figure millions and you can't leave a situation growing and then the costs over there are huge when actually you should be spending the money upfront, and that's the change that we're making."
He said fines for fly-tipping would increase from Â£300 to Â£5,000 and offenders could be given up to nine points on their driving licence.
"What we're doing here is making sure that those who do this, and blight communities, all of a sudden will be in a position where it's no longer easy to do," he said.
Do you support West Yorkshire's tram plans?
"I supported her [Tracy Brabin] in my former role, I won't be changing my tune now," he said.
"West Yorkshire needs a mass transit system like Greater Manchester, like the West Midlands and and that is what it will get."
He said the proposed scheme would involve extending the tram south of Leeds, connecting areas where a lot of new housing is planned, particularly around South Bank, and potentially continuing towards a redeveloped Elland Road.
"When you've got those big regeneration schemes around the infrastructure you can capture some of the value that is created to pay for the infrastructure in the first place, so we'll look at all of that to make this stack up," he said.
Is there a north-south divide in how wildfires are treated?
Burnham was asked the question following an article about Alison Hume, the MP for Scarborough and Whitby, who claimed a devastating wildfire in the North York Moors last year was "overlooked" by the government and national media because it was in the north of England.
Burnham said he understood her point but said from his own experience wildfires always received a national response.
He accepted wildfires were a growing problem and pledged to look into the resources available to fire and rescue services in autumn, which he believes are currently insufficient.
"We don't have that aerial support that other countries have that can make dealing with those fires much quicker.
"We're looking towards the end of the year now and yes a bit of rain and we think there may be a wetter end of year coming and that's when the fire service has to turn to flooding.
"Flooding still isn't a statutory responsibility of the fire and rescue service, so I'm going to hold a summit to say it's a changing world out there, our fire and rescue services are on the front line of that changing world, sometimes I think they feel they're out there without the resources but I'm going to make sure that we change that and adequately equip them to face all of this."
Will wildfires and hot summer impact cost of food?
Burnham did not directly answer the question but acknowledged farmers have had a difficult summer.
He said during a visit to a farm in Cornwall last week, he was shown potatoes much smaller than usual, with some not good enough to sell.
"It's been a really, really tough time. I'm here today in Bradford with the Environment Secretary Angela Eagle and I was very pleased that Defra moved quickly to provide extra flexibility to farmers in this difficult time so more ability to graze cattle in areas that have been set aside for environmental improvement, more funding to build reservoirs on the farm so in years to come we can manage these issues better.
"No one's going to say that this is a whole solution but at least I can say in my first month and a difficult summer I have had it brought over to me the challenges that British farming is facing."
He hopes in the futures changes can also be brought to government food procurement policies when it comes to food in schools, hospitals and prisons.
He said: "I think British farming should work with the government to make sure we change procurement to secure British farming through that going forward."
summary: During a visit to West Yorkshire, Andy Burnham addressed four key questions from BBC Yorkshire regarding regional priorities. He outlined plans to tackle waste crime through increased fines and region-led enforcement, confirmed support for West Yorkshire's proposed tram system, and pledged to review resources for fire and rescue services to handle wildfires and flooding. Additionally, he acknowledged the severe challenges faced by British farmers this summer and highlighted government support measures.
key_points: Fly-tipping fines will increase to £5,000, and offenders may receive up to nine points on their driving licence under a new region-led waste crime approach.
Burnham confirmed support for West Yorkshire's mass transit system, including proposed tram extensions south of Leeds.
He pledged to hold a summit and review resources for fire and rescue services to better equip them for handling wildfires and flooding.
Defra has provided extra flexibility and funding for farmers to help manage the difficulties caused by a tough summer.

title: More students planning to live at home for uni over 'insane' living costs
author: Vanessa Clarke
content:
![Beatrice and Amelia stand side by side outdoors, looking towards the camera. Amelia is wearing a dark sleeveless top with sunglasses resting on their head, while Beatrice is wearing a white top with patterned ruffled sleeves. The background is softly blurred and shows a modern building entrance.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/c94d/live/f132db30-97db-11f1-bb4c-d758974ed97b.jpg)
Friends Amelia (left) and Beatrice (right) are living at home when they start university this September
- Published
More new students are choosing to live at home for university this year than at any point in the last nine years, new data shows.
Over 81,000 UK 18-year-olds said in their accepted university application that they intended to live at home this year, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) - just over one in three students in that category.
In 2017, it was closer to one in five.
The figures vary across the UK - with 48% of applicants in Scotland intending to live at home, compared with 20% in Wales - but the trend is rising across the board.
Students told the BBC the rising cost of living was a major influence in deciding what to do after school or college.
For friends Beatrice and Amelia, who are from St Helens, Merseyside, the cost of accommodation was a big factor in their decision to live at home while studying.
Both are heading to university in September, but neither will be moving into student accommodation.
Beatrice is going to the University of Manchester to study maths and plans to commute by train, a journey which can take about 50 minutes in total.
"My first choice was Manchester and then my second was Liverpool, so I knew I could commute," she says, adding that the price of accommodation would have been "a few grand a year".
Amelia, who is going to study at Liverpool John Moores University - approximately 20 minutes away by train - says the accommodation she found was between Â£300 and Â£400 a week.
Although neither is looking forward to the commute, both are still hoping they can get the full experience of university while living at home.
However, fellow student Jessica, who is also going to study at Liverpool John Moores University, feels she will miss out.
She says she would have loved to live on campus and enjoy student life, but the price of renting is "ridiculous" and "insane".
"I have a part-time job as everything is so expensive, and then commuting is going to kill a lot of my free time as well," she says.
"It is a bit sad really when you think about it."
But she is pleased that staying at home means she will still be able to have her mum and dad's cooked dinners.
Earlier this year, BBC News followed the daily journey of one first-year student who said she was saving over Â£7,000 on accommodation by commuting 90 minutes into Manchester each day from home.
A record number of UK 18-year-olds have been accepted into university this year.
But student rents have risen sharply in recent years, alongside other living costs.
The Higher Education Policy Institute (Hepi) said last year that students needed Â£61,000 over the course of a three-year degree in order to have a "minimum socially acceptable standard of living" - and that's excluding tuition fees.
Its report found that in 2024 the cost of renting in university-owned accommodation ranged from Â£108 per week, for 40 to 44-week contracts in Northern Ireland, to Â£338 a week for the shortest contracts in London, where rent makes up nearly half (46%) of students' costs.
In most areas it was between Â£140 and Â£180 a week, with private halls usually being more expensive.
Many students are eligible for a maintenance loan, which can help with the cost of accommodation, but the average annual price of a room on campus is increasing much faster, according to some student unions.
Hepi says most young full-time students now work in paid employment during term time to make up the difference between their maintenance loan income and the cost of living.
For some students, it means a rethink about what university looks like.
The Open University, which offers distance learning and online courses, says more teenagers than ever are starting courses with it.
Almost 3,400 18-and 19-year-olds joined the university last year â making up 9.5% of new starters, compared with 5.7% six years ago.
Traditionally, it has been popular with mature students wanting to continue working while studying from home.
Its vice-chancellor, Prof Dave Phoenix, says it points to a shift in how younger people are thinking about university, adding that studying online "means they can avoid moving costs and high accommodation bills and, for others, it means keeping a job".
But a recent report, external by Prof William Whyte, from the University of Oxford, argues that the value of on-campus life extends far beyond the price of accommodation, and plays an important role in personal development and the wider university experience.
"The question isn't simply where students live. It's what they gain from living and learning together as part of a university community," he says.
"Currently, we have no real policy on accommodation for the overwhelming majority of students who want to leave home for study. It's time for a serious debate about the role accommodation plays in the university â and how we will pay for it."
A spokesperson for the Department for Education says the government recognises that too many students are facing financial hardship.
They say they are increasing maximum maintenance loans and reintroducing maintenance grants to help with living costs, as well as working with universities and councils to improve access to student housing.
Data analysis by Isobel Cottam & Phil Leake. Additional reporting by Emily Doughty
summary: Data from Ucas shows that over 81,000 UK 18-year-olds plan to live at home while attending university this year, representing the highest proportion in nine years. Driven by the rising cost of living and expensive student accommodation, students are increasingly choosing to commute or pursue distance learning. While this helps avoid high rental bills, some students feel they are missing out on the traditional on-campus university experience.
key_points: Over 81,000 UK 18-year-olds (just over one in three) intend to live at home for university this year, compared to about one in five in 2017.
The rising cost of living and expensive accommodation, with rents continuing to surge, are the primary reasons cited by students for staying at home.
The Open University is seeing a record number of younger teenagers (18 and 19-year-olds) starting distance learning courses to avoid moving and high accommodation costs.
Experts and student unions note that while living at home saves money, on-campus life plays an important role in personal development and the wider university experience.

title: Girl, 6, dies three days after Shoreham sea incident that killed parents and sister
author: Harry Cockburn
content:
A six-year-old girl has died in hospital three days after being pulled from the sea off Shoreham in West Sussex, in an incident that also killed her mother, father and sister.
Saja El-Khawas died on Friday after the deaths of her sister Sara El-Khawas, 14, and her parents Hassan El-Khawas, 55, and Zeina Alayn, 37, on Tuesday.
Saja had been in hospital in a critical condition since the incident.
Police, paramedics, coastguard crews and a lifeboat attended the scene at Shoreham Fort early on Tuesday afternoon after a report of four people in difficulty in the water.
In a statement, Sussex police said: “It is understood the family travelled down from their home in London to visit Shoreham, and entered the water from the beach at Shoreham Fort around 2pm on Tuesday afternoon, before getting into trouble.
“The investigation into the incident remains open, but following review of CCTV footage and initial witness accounts, the current hypothesis is that this was a tragic accident, with no third-party involvement.”
Her identity and death were confirmed in a legal notice from solicitors acting on behalf of Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS foundation trust, as well as the Palestinian Forum in Britain. The Palestinian embassy previously confirmed her father was a British citizen of Palestinian descent.
Sussex police said the family’s next of kin “are aware and continue to receive the full support of our officers during this unimaginably difficult time”.
Ch Supt James Collis said: “This heartbreaking update is one we all feared in the aftermath of Tuesday’s tragic events.
“I cannot imagine the devastation felt by the wider family of Hassan, Zeina, Sara and Saja after this loss. On behalf of everyone at Sussex police, I extend our thoughts and heartfelt condolences.
“The impact of this tragedy has been felt across the country, and I know the Shoreham community, emergency responders and all involved will continue to be affected for a long time to come.”
“I would like to thank all of the public who have shared their sympathies and kind words, and once again ask for the victims’ family and loved ones to be left to grieve in privacy.”
summary: A six-year-old girl has died in hospital three days after being pulled from the sea off Shoreham in West Sussex. Her death follows the tragic drowning of her mother, father, and fourteen-year-old sister in the same incident on Tuesday. Police have stated that the current hypothesis is that the incident was a tragic accident with no third-party involvement.
key_points: Six-year-old Saja El-Khawas died in hospital three days after the Shoreham sea incident.
Her parents, Hassan El-Khawas and Zeina Alayn, and her sister Sara El-Khawas, died following the incident on Tuesday.
The family had traveled from London to visit Shoreham and entered the water from the beach at Shoreham Fort.
Police investigations indicate the event was a tragic accident with no third-party involvement.

title: Meghan reportedly in talks to join Guy Ritchie’s TV series The Gentlemen
author: Benjamin Lee
content:
The Duchess of Sussex is in talks to make her acting return in Netflix’s hit series The Gentlemen.
According to Variety, Meghan is in discussions to join the third season, which has yet to receive an official greenlight. The Gentlemen is a spin-off from the 2019 crime comedy of the same name with Guy Ritchie acting as creator of both.
Meghan’s role in the show is as-yet-unknown, with a contract reportedly still not in place and no official announcement.
Reports have emerged quickly after news that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex would relocate to the UK from the US, where they have lived for six years. It is believed that they will return in September, with early rumours suggesting it was related to Meghan’s return to acting.
Meghan’s best-known acting role was in the legal drama Suits, in which she played the character Rachel Zane for seven seasons. Her other small-screen appearances include CSI: NY and 90210, while film roles have included a small part in the comedy Horrible Bosses and 2015’s crime thriller Anti-Social. She also led two Hallmark movies: When Sparks Fly and Dater’s Handbook.
She recently filmed a cameo playing herself in the Amazon comedy Close Personal Friends alongside Brie Larson and Jack Quaid.
Harry and Meghan had previously signed a deal with Netflix in 2020 worth a reported $100m. It was renewed last year.
Meghan’s main release with the streamer was lifestyle series With Love, Meghan. The show received negative reviews from many critics, with the Guardian’s Chitra Ramaswamy calling it “toe-curling stuff” in a one-star review.
In a 2022 interview, Meghan claimed a return to acting was unlikely. “I’m done,” she said. “I guess never say never, but my intention is to absolutely not.”
The first season of The Gentlemen proved to be a hit with both critics and audiences for Netflix. The second season will premiere in September with returning cast members Theo James and Kaya Scodelario joined by Love Island host Maya Jama.
summary: The Duchess of Sussex is reportedly in discussions to join the third season of Netflix's hit series The Gentlemen, created by Guy Ritchie. Her potential role remains unknown, and a contract is not yet in place as the upcoming season has not received an official greenlight. This news follows reports that the Duke and Duchess are planning to relocate back to the UK from the US.
key_points: Meghan is in talks to appear in the third season of Netflix's The Gentlemen.
The third season has not yet received an official greenlight and no contract is in place.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are reportedly planning to relocate to the UK from the US.
Meghan's best-known acting role was playing Rachel Zane in the legal drama Suits.

title: Migrant jailed after raping woman in locked Bournemouth Beach Portaloo
author: Richard McLaughlin
content:
A MIGRANT who raped a woman after locking her in a Portaloo on Bournemouth beach has been jailed for nearly seven years.
Mohammed Abdullah, 19, raped a woman on Bournemouth beach in the early hours of July 6, 2025, and was jailed for six years and nine months.
Abdullah travelled from London with a group of men before crossing paths with the victim.
The victim’s credit card was not working and her phone had run out of battery when Abdullah gave her a lift on his bike, took her to a Portaloo and raped her.
The court heard Abdullah knew the area would be quiet because he had cycled past it before taking her to the Portaloo and raping her.
Speaking at Bournemouth Crown Court on Friday, August 21, the victim said the attack had “taken a massive toll” on her life.
“Before this my beach was my favourite place to go,” she said, adding that she now suffers from “flashbacks.”
“I can feel him breathing on me and putting his hands up my skirt.”
The victim said she “did not trust men anymore” after the rape and no longer felt comfortable being touched by family or friends.
“I believed I was safe, but I was wrong.
“Since the attack my life has changed significantly.
“I rarely go out and instead spend most of my time with my pets who provide me with the security and comfort I need.”
“I’m constantly torturing myself with what I should have done that night.”
The victim said the attack happened shortly before a significant moment in her life and affected her relationship with a terminally ill family member who died in the following months.
Mr Tutt further said Abdullah came from a “difficult and deprived” background and had no previous convictions at the time of the offence.
A jury convicted Abdullah on May 15 of rape and assault by penetration after a trial at Bournemouth Crown Court.
Abdullah, whose address is in West Drayton, Middlesex, arrived in the UK from Syria in 2023 and was given permanent leave to remain under a family reunion scheme.
Judge Robert Pawson condemned Abdullah’s not-guilty plea as “absolute nonsense”, saying he raped the woman as she protested.
“She was weeping and she was crying like a child,” he said.
“People, women in particular, should not have to face that risk. They are entitled to feel that they can go out when they want, they can dress how they want, drink or sober without the risk of anyone.”
Abdullah was jailed for six years and nine months for rape and four years for assault by penetration, to be served concurrently.
He must also remain on the sex offenders’ register for life and pay the required victim surcharge.
summary: Mohammed Abdullah, a 19-year-old migrant, has been sentenced to six years and nine months in prison for raping a woman in a locked Portaloo on Bournemouth beach on July 6, 2025. A jury convicted Abdullah of rape and assault by penetration following a trial at Bournemouth Crown Court. The victim stated that the attack has severely impacted her life, causing ongoing trauma, flashbacks, and a profound loss of a sense of safety.
key_points: Mohammed Abdullah was sentenced to six years and nine months in prison for rape and assault by penetration.
The attack took place in a locked Portaloo on Bournemouth beach in the early hours of July 6, 2025.
Abdullah arrived in the UK from Syria in 2023 and was given permanent leave to remain.
The victim reported suffering from severe emotional trauma, flashbacks, and significant lifestyle changes since the attack.
Judge Robert Pawson placed Abdullah on the sex offenders' register for life.

title: Meghan in talks for role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, BBC understands
author: Daniela Relph; Paul Gribben
content:
![Duchess of Sussex, head and shoulders pic](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/9235/live/6a8b1d10-7bcd-11f1-b543-9988255dfa81.jpg)
- Published
The Duchess of Sussex is in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, the BBC has learned.
Discussions are in their early stages but this would be Meghan's first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.
Much of the two previous series of The Gentlemen, which was created by Guy Ritchie, have been filmed in the Cotswolds - the area it is rumoured Harry and Meghan will set up home when they return to the UK later this month.
The Gentlemen, starring the actor Theo James, is a comedy series about a duke who becomes a drug baron.
The details of the discussions and any role Meghan might be offered have not yet been revealed.
Actors Hugh Bonneville and Vinnie Jones have appeared in previous series of the show.
Meghan was best known in acting for her part in the US legal drama, Suits, in which she played lawyer, Rachel Zane, for seven seasons. Her last episode aired in 2018.
The duchess put her career on hold after her marriage to Prince Harry in May 2018. At the time, she told the BBC she did not view quitting acting as giving anything up, but rather as "a new chapter".
She recently returned to acting for the first time in nearly a decade, with a cameo as herself in forthcoming comedy Close Personal Friends, which stars Lily Collins and Brie Larson.
A return to acting could be lucrative for Meghan. The BBC understands that while based in the UK she also hopes to expand the global reach of her US-based lifestyle and cooking brand, As Ever.
News of her possible return to acting comes after it was announced that Prince Harry and Meghan are to move back to the UK.
The BBC understands Prince Harry and Meghan intend to relocate from the US later this month to a private, non-royal residence outside London, as first reported by the Daily Telegraph and the Sun.
The couple's children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are enrolled to start at a British school in September.
There are no current plans for either Prince Harry or Meghan to resume their roles as working royals.
Their plan to move to the UK follows a visit in July by Prince Harry, Meghan and their children to see King Charles III at his Highgrove home in Gloucestershire.
It was the first time the King had seen his grandchildren in person in more than four years, and the couple's first visit to the UK together since 2022.
Returning on a longer term basis has reignited questions over the level of the couple's publicly funded security in Britain.
Their UK security was downgraded after they stopped being working royals in 2020 and moved to the US, where they have paid for their own protection.
The Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec), an independent body overseen by the Home Office, will now have to make a new decision about security as previous arrangements were based on the Sussexes not living in the UK permanently.
summary: The Duchess of Sussex is reportedly in early discussions for a role in the Netflix series The Gentlemen, marking her first significant acting role since her marriage. This news coincides with plans for Prince Harry, Meghan, and their children to relocate from the US to the UK later this month. The move back to the UK follows a visit to King Charles III in July and has raised questions regarding the couple's publicly funded security arrangements.
key_points: Meghan is in early talks for a role in the Netflix comedy series The Gentlemen.
Prince Harry and Meghan plan to relocate from the US to a private residence in the UK later this month.
The couple's children are enrolled to start at a British school in September.
There are no current plans for the couple to resume their roles as working royals.
The move back to the UK prompts a new review of the couple's publicly funded security by Ravec.

title: Arran ferry evacuated over 'bomb threat' as passenger rescued from sea
author: Paul Hastie
content:
![A crowd of people stands on a grassy area beside Clyde Marina, with yachts and sailboat masts visible behind a fence in the background. A large blue building marked âCLYDE MARINAâ stands to the left, while people gather along the roadside and waterfront under bright sunshine. A speed limit sign and several parked vehicles are visible near the marina entrance.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/19ee/live/942278c0-9d8e-11f1-adf5-2dc21c9cc109.jpg)
Passengers were removed from the ferry on foot at Ardrossan harbour
- Published
A ferry service on Scotland's west coast has been evacuated over a bomb threat after a passenger was rescued from the water.
CalMac said a person was reported overboard on the MV Caledonian Isles 16:40 sailing from Brodick on the Isle of Arran.
The vessel's fast rescue craft was launched to recover the passenger. The BBC understands that they then claimed there was a bomb on board.
The ferry operator said emergency protocols were put in place. The vessel was searched and 329 people were removed on foot when it berthed at Ardrossan.
Passengers from the ferry and others waiting at the port were taken to a nearby Asda car park by police while the search was carried out.
When this was complete, police declared that the situation had been resolved and allowed people back on board to collect their vehicles.
![A large passenger ferry docked in a harbour. Parked vehicles can be seen in the foreground](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/2da9/live/f1197a30-9d96-11f1-9233-8716b68cda7b.jpg)
The MV Caledonian Isles berthed at Ardrossan after the alarm was raised
Remaining scheduled sailings from Ardrossan were cancelled on Friday evening to allow crew to be debriefed and emergency equipment to be replenished
An extra service to the island was added at 19:50 on the MV Alfred from Troon.
CalMac CEO Duncan Mackison said: "This was a fast-moving situation that was handled professionally by our crew, Ardrossan port staff and emergency services and I would like to extend my thanks and gratitude to them."
The operator said affected passengers who had bookings would be contacted by customer services.
CalMac is the UK's largest ferry operator, running 29 routes across 200 miles of Scotland's west coast.
summary: An Arran ferry was evacuated and searched following a bomb threat made by a passenger who had earlier been rescued from the sea. A total of 329 people were safely removed from the MV Caledonian Isles at Ardrossan harbour while emergency services handled the situation. Police later declared the incident resolved, allowing passengers to return for their vehicles, though remaining Friday evening sailings were cancelled.
key_points: A passenger on the MV Caledonian Isles was reported overboard and recovered by the vessel's rescue craft.
The rescued passenger allegedly claimed there was a bomb on board the ferry.
Emergency protocols were enacted, and 329 people were evacuated on foot at Ardrossan harbour.
Police searched the vessel, resolved the incident, and allowed passengers back to collect their vehicles.
Remaining scheduled sailings from Ardrossan for Friday evening were cancelled.

title: Meghan set to star in Guy Ritchie Netflix series
author: India McTaggart; Lily Shanagher; Victoria Ward
content:
![The Duchess of Sussex](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499062882_17873347733090_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqrnykcIhNBTQGIhNzmTaT-Sh_XV7FumfGnw8MWlaE_-Y.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![The Duchess of Sussex](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499062882_17873347733090_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqrnykcIhNBTQGIhNzmTaT-Sh_XV7FumfGnw8MWlaE_-Y.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The Duchess of Sussex is set to star in a Guy Ritchie Netflix series when she moves to the UK.
The Telegraph understands that the Duchess is in advanced discussions to join the cast for the third series of The Gentlemen. It is unclear how many episodes she will be appearing in.
Theo James stars in the action series as a British aristocrat who inherits his family’s estate and discovers it is home to an underground cannabis empire.
News of the Netflix role comes after entertainment sources told news.com.au on Thursday that the former Suits actress had been offered a part in an upcoming project based in Britain, which sources close to the Sussexes have not denied.
![The Gentlemen](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000368360968_17873347878350_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The Telegraph revealed on Wednesday that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were returning to the UK later this month, with their children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, already enrolled at a British school before September.
It is understood the offer of the role, which was only made recently, formed part of the decision-making process in the family relocating to the UK but was not the sole reason.
The Duchess worked as an actress before meeting Prince Harry, and was best known for her role as lawyer Rachel Zane in seven seasons of the US legal drama Suits.
In 2017, she went on an acting hiatus and told the BBC that she viewed her career break as “a new chapter”.
She returned to acting for the first time in nearly 10 years, playing herself in the upcoming comedy Close Personal Friends, starring Lily Collins and Brie Larson.
![The Duchess was best known for her role as lawyer Rachel Zane in seven seasons of the US legal drama Suits](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000375681453_17872960270720_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqfURdS4UbDpUGnz5FIlFfrRYAJJa2yLtNxwGHGzIYZhI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The family intends to relocate from the US to a private, non-royal residence thought to be outside London later this month.
The Duke and Duchess’s status as non-working royals and private individuals will remain unchanged.
It is understood that the King was not aware of the move until last Sunday, but he is said to be pleased his younger son is coming home and is looking forward to spending more time with him and his family.
The Telegraph understands Harry – who misses the UK and wants to be closer to his wider family – hopes to regain the King’s trust by no longer discussing private family matters in public or giving television interviews.
Prince Harry has spent years revealing details about the monarchy and his personal life. However, the couple plan not to expose their children to the public eye and British media organisations have been urged by the regulator not to disclose the location of the new family home or the children’s school.
![The Telegraph revealed that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were returning to the UK later this month](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000478812322_17872959772770_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRo0U4xU-30oDveS4pXV-Vv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The Duke, whose own private security team claimed he was the focus of six terrorist plots, has long fought to be guaranteed police protection, but this has so far been rejected by the courts and the Home Office committee responsible for such decisions.
But the family’s return is set to prompt a review of taxpayer-funded security.
