Two senior government sources told The Telegraph that the Royal and VIP Executive Committee, the body that determines the security arrangements of high-profile figures, was likely to review the couple’s security arrangements in light of their plan to return to Britain, and that it might be easier to arrange protection when they are in the UK full-time.
Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said on Thursday that the Duke and Duchess’s security was a “private matter”, despite the potential cost for taxpayers if their security were reinstated.
No 10 sources said Mr Burnham’s comments reflected the fact that the Sussexes were private citizens, not working royals, and that their security in California was privately funded.
![The Sussexes' partnership with Netflix led to the production of a cookery show named With Love, Meghan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000491106383_17872960970470_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRo0U4xU-30oDveS4pXV-Vv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The couple will retain their homes in Montecito, California, and Portugal, while the Duchess will continue to run her US-based lifestyle brand As Ever – which sources insist is thriving – from their new base.
Despite her hiatus from acting, the Duchess has worked on a number of commercial projects with Netflix under her and her husband’s company Archewell Productions.
The Sussexes had a five-year $100m deal with the streaming service, which imploded last year amid reports published in Variety that the relationship between key executives in the company and the couple had soured.
During that time, the couple produced a six-part documentary on their life, a polo documentary and a lifestyle show named With Love, Meghan, that failed to make the top 1,000 most-watched programmes on the streaming platform.
In 2021, Andrew Morton, a royal biographer, said the late Queen had told the Duchess she was not obliged to become a full-time member of the Royal family when she married Prince Harry, and could continue with her acting career should she wish.
“[The Sussexes] were given a degree of latitude,” Morton told the Royally Obsessed podcast.
“They did say to Meghan: ‘If you don’t want to embrace royal duties full time, please be our guest and continue your acting career.’ Those opportunities were open to her.”
summary: The Duchess of Sussex is in advanced discussions to star in the third series of Guy Ritchie's Netflix show, The Gentlemen, as she and Prince Harry prepare to relocate back to the UK from the US. The family plans to move into a private residence outside London this month, with their children already enrolled in a British school. The relocation decision, which forms part of a move to be closer to family, comes alongside potential reviews of the couple's taxpayer-funded security arrangements.
key_points: The Duchess of Sussex is in advanced discussions to join the cast for the third series of Netflix's The Gentlemen.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex and their two children are relocating from the US to a private residence outside London later this month.
The acting offer formed part of the family's decision-making process to return to the UK, though it was not the sole reason.
The family's return is expected to prompt a review of taxpayer-funded security arrangements by the Royal and VIP Executive Committee.

title: The Troubles: Families welcome day marking victims of terrorist attacks
author: Lili Busby
content:
![Claire has brown hair and brown eyes. She is wearing a cream coat with a white top. She is standing on a silver bridge, behind her there are buildings and a river.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/6609/live/a905a6c0-de29-11ef-bf7d-c305fe575a19.jpg)
Claire Hayes' brother was killed in the Omagh bombing
- Published
The UK's first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism has been held in London where those affected by the violence of the Troubles were in attendance.
The day aimed to recognise people impacted by terrorism including victims and their families, witnesses and the emergency services, as well as raising awareness about specialist support.
For the rest of the UK, these could be terror attacks such as the London Bridge terror attack, the Manchester Arena attack in 2017 or the 7/7 bombings.
But in Northern Ireland, many will be remembering the atrocities of the Troubles, which lasted 30 years and cost the lives of more than 3,500 people.
The government said it introduced the national day for victims and survivors of terrorism following campaigning from victims and survivors for better recognition of their lived experiences.
Claire Hayes is part of a delegation from victims group the South East Fermanagh Foundation who travelled from Northern Ireland to England on Friday.
Her brother Alan Radford was just 16 years old when he was killed in the Omagh bombing.
Twenty-nine people, including a woman who was pregnant with twins, were murdered in the Real IRA attack on 15 August 1998.
![An image of emergency services including police officers, fire men and ambulance staff searching rubble along the main street of Omagh.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/f328/live/4acd8640-9d4a-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
The Real IRA Omagh bomb attack killed 29 people in 1998
'My brother no longer a statistic'
Hayes called for Stormont to do more to mark the remembrance of those killed in terrorist attacks in Northern Ireland, but said the UK-wide event is a "monumental day".
"It's been very welcomed that Alan is no longer just a statistic, that he is being recognised, that he was a human being, who was here, who was murdered and his life mattered," she told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster.
However, Hayes said has been campaigning for the commemoration to happen for years.
She said there are questions as to why Stormont and its own ministers have not provided them with a day to mark victims locally.
"They like to try and cleanse what has happened in Northern Ireland and I think this is going to be another pushing point for them that they really don't want to," Hayes said.
Hayes also called for more education in Northern Ireland schools about the impact terrorism has on victims.
'Victims are the most important'
Tanya Williams-Powell, whose grandfather was abducted and murdered by the IRA more than 50 years ago, said victims are the "most important" when it comes to remembering terrorist attacks.
Thomas Niedermayer was kidnapped from his home in west Belfast two days after Christmas in December 1973.
Powell told the Nolan Show that she felt there is often more interest into why the perpetrator commits a terrorist attack.
"It can almost be glorified. I think it's really important that we teach history honestly," said Williams-Powell.
"The victims are the most important and we need to make sure as much as we can that young people don't glorify it and continue the violence."
![A man with short fair haired wears a black suit and blue shirt. He stands in front of a blue screen.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/992/cpsprodpb/26ef/live/04423d70-84d0-11f1-bc1a-3f050829cba4.jpg)
Sir Chris Bryant said he has been "amazed and inspired" by victims and survivors of the Troubles
Speaking ahead of the first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism Secretary of State Chris Bryant said "few places have borne more pain than in Northern Ireland".
"I'm amazed and inspired by the fortitude and grace so many victims, survivors, and bereaved families have shown over the years, often suffering in silence," he said.
"As we stand with the victims and survivors of terrorism we commit ourselves anew to keep people safe and remember the past with honesty."
The chosen date for the national day of 21 August coincides with the UN International Day of Remembrance and Tribute to the Victims of Terrorism, which began in 2017.
While the UK event took place in London for its debut year, the Home Office has said people across the country could mark it at home by observing a moment of reflection and sharing posts about the day on social media.
  - Published18 hours ago
 ![A man in a black jacket and with glasses, ginger hair and a beard stands on the riverside by the River Thames with Westminster Bridge and the London Eye in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a399/live/36ece130-9c95-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
summary: The UK's first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism was held in London, bringing together those affected by violence including the Troubles in Northern Ireland. The event aimed to recognize impacted individuals, families, witnesses, and emergency services, while raising awareness of specialist support. Families of victims welcomed the national recognition but called for more local remembrance and education in Northern Ireland.
key_points: The UK held its first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism in London on 21 August, coinciding with the UN International Day of Remembrance.
The government introduced the day following campaigning from victims and survivors for better recognition of their lived experiences.
Claire Hayes, whose brother was killed in the 1998 Omagh bombing, welcomed the UK-wide event but criticized Stormont for not providing a local day of remembrance.
Tanya Williams-Powell, whose grandfather was murdered by the IRA, emphasized the importance of focusing on victims rather than glorifying perpetrators in history education.

title: Prince Harry and six others face privacy case legal bill of up to Â£34.5m
author: Dominic Casciani; Henry Moore
content:
![Prince Harry, Liz Hurley and Elton John attend court.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/b9d1/live/0b65a550-9d63-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
- Published
Prince Harry and six other public figures face paying up to Â£34.5m to the publisher of the Daily Mail after a High Court judge imposed an exceptional order for legal costs over their failed privacy case.
The seven claimants, also including Sir Elton John and Liz Hurley, must pay an initial Â£9.54m by Friday of next week to Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL).
The judge ruled that the case was a rare one in which the claimants should have to pay far in excess of the costs that had been agreed before trial, criticising how they presented their claims as "unreasonable to a high degree".
On 7 July, Judge Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed the claims of unlawful information-gathering, which ANL denied.
The Duke of Sussex and the other six claimants have until 2 October to attempt to launch an appeal.
Those other claimants are Sir Elton John and his husband David Furnish, former Liberal Democrat deputy leader Sir Simon Hughes, racial justice campaigner Baroness Lawrence, and actresses Sadie Frost and Liz Hurley,
They had insurance to cover up to Â£16.2m of Association Newspapers' costs in the event of losing the case - but Friday's ruling means the newspaper group could now try to recover up to the Â£34.5m that it said it had to spend to defend itself. This means the duke and others could face a bill of some Â£18m.
Justice Nicklin said: "I regard a claim for costs in excess of Â£34 million as, on its face, excessive and as giving rise to real concerns as to whether all of the costs now claimed by Associated were reasonably incurred and are reasonable in amount."
But he added he had "decided not to impose a ceiling on Associated's recoverable costs", as it would "be too broad-brushed, would risk unfairness, and would be vulnerable to the charge that it was arbitrary".
The judge also ruled that ANL's costs should be determined on an indemnity basis, which is more favourable to the publisher in terms of the amount it can recover, aside from where orders had already been made.
He added it was "striking" that "not a single allegation of serious wrongdoing was voluntarily withdrawn" by the group of seven claimants.
He said: "That matters. Serious allegations of criminality or grave impropriety cannot properly be left hanging over individuals in that way.
"If a party no longer advances such an allegation, or no longer has a proper evidential basis for advancing it, the allegation should be withdrawn clearly and in terms.
![Doreen Lawrence, David Furnish, Sir Simon Hughes and Sadie Frost attended court.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/03e7/live/35b48730-9d64-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Baroness Lawrence, Sir Simon Hughes, Sadie Frost and David Furnish were among the seven claimants
"The claimants' failure to do so was not ordinary forensic judgment. It was not a proper or disciplined way to deal with serious allegations. It was unreasonable to a high degree."
In a statement released on Friday, the publisher called the ruling "a devastating critique of an attempt to destroy a newspaper and the reputations of its journalists, editors and executives".
Friday's decision comes just days after Prince Harry and Meghan duke announced their plan to return to the UK, with their children Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, enrolled to start school in September.
During the trial, dozens of people gave evidence including Prince Harry and the other claimants. The Duke of Sussex flew in from the US to attend court in person.
Many current and former Associated Newspapers journalists and executives gave evidence denying illegal activity.
Sir Simon Hughes told the BBC he was "disappointed" by the judgement.
"I am now taking the time necessary to consider both the substantive and the costs judgment and whether to pursue appeals against decisions in either judgment or both," he added.
In a joint statement following the judge's ruling last month, Prince Harry and Baroness Lawrence, who beccame a public figure after her son Stephen was murdered in 1993, said: "We came to court seeking justice and accountability. But we have received neither."
"It is a complete and obvious whitewash, but sadly not altogether unexpected", the pair added.
In a civil case such as this, the legal convention is that the losing party must reimburse "reasonable" legal fees incurred by the other side. They also have to settle their own legal costs.
ANL had asked for more than Â£9.9m as an interim payment ahead of future hearings to decide its legal costs in depth.
However, lawyers for the claimants had argued the interim payment should be limited to about Â£7.9m.
summary: Prince Harry and six other public figures face legal bills of up to Â£34.5m after a High Court judge ordered them to pay costs to Associated Newspapers Limited following their failed privacy case. The claimants must pay an initial Â£9.54m by next Friday and have until October 2 to attempt an appeal. The judge criticized the claimants for how they presented their case, describing their failure to withdraw serious allegations as unreasonable to a high degree.
key_points: Prince Harry, Sir Elton John, Liz Hurley, and four others lost their unlawful information-gathering privacy case against Associated Newspapers Limited.
The claimants must pay an initial Â£9.54m by Friday of next week, with total costs potentially reaching Â£34.5m.
The judge ruled that ANL's costs should be determined on an indemnity basis and criticized the claimants for maintaining serious allegations without proper withdrawal.
The claimants have until October 2 to attempt to launch an appeal against the decision.

title: More than half of terror attack victims denied compensation
author: Rob White
content:
![Memorial in London for Manchester Arena terror attack victims](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/money/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498933054_17872303476370_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Memorial in London for Manchester Arena terror attack victims](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/money/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498933054_17872303476370_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Have you struggled to secure compensation from the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority? We want to hear from you. Email rob.white@telegraph.co.uk*.
More than half of terror attack victims are denied government compensation, The Telegraph can reveal.
Figures obtained through a Freedom of Information request found that up to 177 applications were submitted by survivors during the past two years, but as many as 92 were rejected.
The Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority (Cica), which oversees claims, approved less than 8pc of cases, with £62,000 paid out in total, the figures confirmed.
The majority of successful applications were from people injured in the 2017 Manchester Arena bombing.
Brendan Cox, whose late wife, Jo Cox MP, was murdered in 2016, said the figures were “another indicator of a broken system”.
Cica operates Britain’s state-funded compensation scheme for people affected by violent crime, including acts of terrorism.
Victims can claim for injuries they sustained, mental health support and bereavement if a close relative was killed.
Cica has paid out £345m in redress over the past two years, but survivors of terrorism received just £62,150 between August 2024 and August 2026.
During that period, between 165 and 177 applications were made by people stating they were injured by acts of terrorism, but up to 92 were rejected. Between 2 and 12 were approved and 75 to 87 remained unresolved.
Cica confirmed that the majority of successful claims resulted from the 2017 Manchester Arena bombing, in which 22 people were killed and more than a thousand were injured at an Ariana Grande concert.
The figures come on Britain’s first memorial day for those affected by terrorism, with events and tributes expected across the country.
Mr Cox, who founded Survivors Against Terror, a campaign group, said: “This looks like another indicator of the broken system at Cica.
“It’s not just that people are often turned down even when claims are strong, it’s that even when claims are agreed, the process is so dehumanising that many claimants wish they had never started the process.
“The most galling thing is the Government knows the system is broken and knows that survivors are being failed. They have promised many times to fix the broken system, but nothing has changed and no progress has been delivered. It’s completely unacceptable.”
Johanna Parks, of the charity Victim Support, said: “The high proportion of rejected claims raises serious questions about whether the current process is working effectively for victims, and we urge Cica to look into the reasons behind these figures.
“Survivors need and deserve better. That means a process which is trauma-informed, fair, and timely, which supports survivors rather than causing them further distress.”
![Brendan Cox](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000491906107_17872287204470_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqgsaO8O78rhmZrDxTlQBjdLdu0TL-Cg_AMOUqySXmFgU.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
In a Telegraph investigation earlier this year, Cica’s compensation process was severely criticised by survivors, who said they had been “dehumanised, retraumatised and completely let down”.
Claimants can only claim for up to three injuries and compensation levels are fixed by Parliament. However, payouts are reduced for each injury, with 100pc paid for the worst, 30pc for the second and just 15pc for the third.
Cindy Butts, the independent public advocate, whose office is funded by the Ministry of Justice to provide victim support after major incidents, said the current system was “outdated and restrictive”.
She said: “When half of applications for criminal injuries compensation are being rejected, we have to ask whether the system is genuinely working for the people it was created to support.
“As we mark the first national day of remembrance for victims and survivors of terrorism, we must honour people not only by remembering what happened to them, but by changing the systems that too often let them down.”
Campaigners have spent years fighting for reform and in 2019, Baroness Newlove, then the victims’ commissioner, said the compensation process was “extremely traumatic, highly complex and retraumatising”.
However, the Johnson government did not respond to the findings and in 2025, Alex Davies-Jones, Labour’s victims minister, also decided not to make changes.
A government spokesman said: “These brave victims should be able to access the financial compensation and support they deserve. This taxpayer-funded scheme paid out more than £180m last year to victims of violent crime, including terrorism, on top of a record £550m investment in wider victim support services.
“That’s alongside the recent launch of a dedicated support service for survivors of terror attacks, which provides specialist assistance throughout their recovery and helps them navigate the compensation process.”
summary: Data obtained through a Freedom of Information request reveals that more than half of terror attack victims applying for government compensation through the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority (Cica) have had their applications rejected over the past two years. Out of nearly 180 applications submitted by survivors, up to 92 were denied while only a small fraction were approved, totaling just £62,150 in payouts. Campaigners, charities, and victims have heavily criticized the process as outdated, dehumanizing, and broken, noting that the government has failed to deliver promised reforms.
key_points: Over half of terror attack compensation applications submitted to Cica over the past two years have been rejected.
Cica paid out a total of £62,150 to terror survivors between August 2024 and August 2026, with most successful claims coming from the 2017 Manchester Arena bombing.
Campaigners and advocacy groups like Survivors Against Terror and Victim Support have criticized the compensation process as dehumanizing and broken.
Despite previous calls for reform by commissioners and campaigners, governments under both past and current administrations have not implemented requested changes.

title: Prince Harry and others ordered to pay interim £9.5m to Daily Mail publisher
author: Caroline Davies
content:
The Duke of Sussex and six other high-profile claimants must make a £9.54m interim payment by 4pm on 28 August towards the Daily Mail publisher’s legal costs after losing their high court case over allegations of unlawful information gathering, a judge has ruled.
Associated Newspapers Ltd strongly denied the claims made by Prince Harry and co-claimants including Doreen Lawrence and Elton John.
Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed all the claims last month after an 11-week trial in London earlier this year.
The court has been told that ANL’s total costs were more than £34m.
More details soon …
summary: Prince Harry and six other high-profile claimants have been ordered to make an interim payment of £9.54m towards the legal costs of Associated Newspapers Ltd by August 28. The ruling follows the dismissal of their high court case alleging unlawful information gathering after an 11-week trial. Associated Newspapers Ltd had denied the allegations, and the publisher's total costs were reported to be over £34m.
key_points: Prince Harry and six co-claimants must pay £9.54m in interim legal costs.
The payment is due by 4pm on August 28 to Daily Mail publisher Associated Newspapers Ltd.
Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed the unlawful information gathering claims after an 11-week trial.
Associated Newspapers Ltd's total legal costs exceeded £34m.

title: Meghan could return to acting once back in UK
author: Daniela Relph; James Chater
content:
Watch: Is Meghan returning to acting?
- Published
The Duchess of Sussex could make a return to acting after she moves back to the UK, according to reports.
Sources close to the Sussexes have not denied reports that Meghan has been offered an acting role in the country.
Australian outlet news.com.au, external first reported that one of the reasons behind Harry and Meghan's decision to return to Britain was that the duchess had been offered a job in an upcoming project.
No details of any role or project have been confirmed. The Sussexes are expected to arrive back in Britain before the end of August, with their children enrolled to start school in September.
'Key part of the puzzle'
Senior entertainment reporter Bronte Coy, who broke the story on news.com.au, reported that Meghan being offered a part in a "top secret" UK production had played a "significant" role in the family's return.
"This is such a key part of the puzzle," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.
"I think when we all heard that news that Harry and Meghan were moving here, and within a matter of days, and the kids were enrolled in school, everyone was asking, what is Meghan going to be doing?"
"I'm told it's significant, and she's very excited about it," Coy said about Meghan's latest project.
Coy also suggested she thinks "we will find out relatively soon".
As an actress, Meghan was best known for her part in the US legal drama, Suits, in which she played lawyer, Rachel Zane, for seven seasons. Her last episode of Suits aired in 2018.
The duchess put her acting career on hold after her marriage to Prince Harry. At the time, she told the BBC that she did not view quitting acting as giving anything up, but rather as "a new chapter".
She recently returned to acting for the first time in nearly a decade, with a cameo as herself in the upcoming comedy Close Personal Friends, which stars Lily Collins and Brie Larson.
A return to acting could be lucrative for Meghan. The BBC understands that while based in the UK she also hopes to expand the global reach of her US-based lifestyle and cooking brand, As Ever.
Prince Harry and Meghan plan to relocate from the US to a private, non-royal residence outside London, with their children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, enrolled to start at school in September.
The decision follows a visit in July by Prince Harry, Meghan and their children to see King Charles III at his Highgrove home in Gloucestershire.
It was the first time the King had seen his grandchildren in person in more than four years, and the couple's first visit to the UK together since 2022.
The BBC understands the King was unaware of the move before last weekend, but he welcomes the opportunity to see more of the Sussex family in a private and personal capacity.
There are no current plans for either Prince Harry or Meghan to resume their roles as working royals.
Questions have also been raised over whether the Sussexes will receive publicly funded security in Britain. Their UK protection was downgraded after they stopped being working royals in 2020 and moved to the US, where they have paid for their own protection.
Ailsa Anderson, the late Queen's press secretary, said she does not think there will be any plans to give the Duke and Duchess of Sussex official security, adding: "It's a very costly business and they are not working members of the Royal Family."
She told BBC Breakfast that Prince Harry and Meghan's return to the UK was "totally unexpected and fairly astonishing".
But Dai Davies, a former head of royal protection and divisional commander in the Metropolitan Police, said the system for deciding whether someone should receive such protection is "carefully measured".
Davies told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he suspects a review into the Sussexes' security may take place if Prince Harry is to bring his family to the UK and "plans to remain here".
He said that official security is "enormously expensive, especially if you're moving into a premises which is not security prepared".
On Friday, the duke is expected to find out more about how much he, and other high-profile complainants, will have to pay the Daily Mail publisher in costs over a failed legal battle.
The group - which includes Sir Elton John, Baroness Doreen Lawrence and Elizabeth Hurley - sued Associated Newspapers Limited over claims of unlawful information gathering, but last month all their claims were dismissed.
summary: Reports suggest that the Duchess of Sussex could return to acting following her family's planned relocation from the US to the UK. Sources indicate she has been offered a role in a top-secret UK production, which played a significant part in the decision to move. The couple and their children are expected to arrive in Britain before the end of August, with no plans to resume working royal roles.
key_points: Meghan has reportedly been offered an acting role in a top-secret UK production, prompting the family's return.
The Sussex family plans to relocate to a private residence outside London before the end of August.
King Charles III was unaware of the move beforehand but welcomes the opportunity to see more of the family.
There are currently no plans for Prince Harry or Meghan to resume their duties as working royals.
Questions remain regarding whether the family will receive publicly funded security upon their return.

title: Leaderless Oldham Council faces government takeover
author: Ed Barnes; Angela Ferguson
content:
![A historic brick building with a red door stands to the left of a public square on an overcast day.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1152/cpsprodpb/029c/live/45e319b0-6974-11f1-a610-610c6ec6d3a5.jpg)
Parties in Oldham have failed to form an administration to take control of the council
- Published
Government commissioners could be brought in to run a leaderless council, after councillors once again failed to form an administration.
Members of Oldham Council held an extraordinary meeting on Thursday evening to resolve the stalemate of no political party having an overall majority.
The authority's chief executive is now advising the government of the situation, which came about after Labour lost eight seats and Reform UK took seven in the elections in May, leaving no party with an overall majority.
An Oldham Council spokesperson said: "As a result, the council's monitoring officer will write to the Secretary of State to formally advise of the situation."
The spokesperson said council services continued to operate as normal, and arrangements remained in place to ensure the council could fulfil its statutory responsibilities and continue delivering for residents, communities and partners across the borough.
"We will now await further correspondence from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government," they said.
'Passing the buck'
The latest meeting was called following a report by the council's top legal officer, Alex Bougatef, who said it was his legal duty to declare the local authority is breaking the law.
Presenting the report, Bougatef said the lack of anyone in charge raised serious concerns about decision-making, accountability, and effective governance.
He said: "The appointment of a leader is not optional. It's a statutory requirement."
On Thursday evening, seven proposals were put forward and all of them failed to pass, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.
Labour and Reform put forward bids to form a minority administration, as well as an alliance made up of smaller parties and an independent councillor.
Reform also put forward proposals that would see councillors elected at the ballot box in May 2027, arguing it should be up to the people to decide.
However, other parties argued this was not a "quick fix" and described the proposal of further elections as "passing the buck", warning the council would still require a leader over the coming nine months before any election.
![Oldham Council's chamber: a wood-panelled room with red seats and wooden desks in a u-shape around a central podium. There are people sitting in most of the seats. At the back is a screen with the Oldham Council logo.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/f41b/live/32d2c900-9d2d-11f1-ba3e-c323fd3033f4.png)
Oldham Council's members met on Thursday evening, but failed to find a solution as to who should lead the council
Bougatef's declaration, which came in what is called a Section 5 report, set in motion a process that could see outside intervention in the wake of no solution.
He has warned there could be 'significant' financial costs coming down the line should commissioners be required.
Commissioners are officials sent by the UK government to help run councils deemed to be failing or breaking the law, most often when a council is declared bankrupt.
Commissioners being imposed due to a political quarrel such as has arisen in Oldham is thought to be a first and could cost Â£1,200 or more a day.
Conservative councillor Beth Sharp said: "Doing nothing comes at a cost and that cost isn't being paid by us.
"It's paid for by the residents who elected us."
Services at risk
Chief executive Shelley Kipling said, while council services are continuing as they did before, the lack of a leader or elected members in key roles puts at risk how key children's and adults services are assessed
In a plea to members, she said: "I am hopeful we can find a way forward that reflects an immense amount of work that has gone on behind the scenes."
In response to a question later in the meeting, she said the government had escalated their oversight of the situation in recent weeks, telling councillors this suggested an "anticipation of a requirement for government intervention or greater more formalised support".
The government has been approached for comment.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio Manchester on Sounds and follow BBC Manchester on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external. You can also send story ideas via Whatsapp to 0808 100 2230.
summary: Oldham Council faces potential government intervention after councillors once again failed to form an administration during an extraordinary meeting. The political stalemate arose after the May elections left no party with an overall majority, resulting in a leaderless council that the top legal officer stated is breaking the law. The council's monitoring officer will now formally advise the Secretary of State of the situation, potentially bringing in government commissioners at a significant financial cost.
key_points: Oldham Council is currently leaderless and without an overall majority following the May elections.
Councillors failed to pass seven separate proposals to form an administration during a Thursday evening meeting.
The council's top legal officer declared the local authority is breaking the law because appointing a leader is a statutory requirement.
The monitoring officer is formally advising the Secretary of State, which could lead to government commissioners taking over the council.
While routine services continue, the lack of a leader threatens key children's and adults' services and risks substantial financial costs for residents.

title: Greenock: The town whose council wants migrants to move in
author: Michael Buchanan; Adam Eley
content:
![A coastal cityscape with a tall clock tower in the foreground, surrounded by historic and modern buildings. Behind it, a large white cruise ship is docked beside red industrial cranes. Beyond the harbour, green hills and mountains rise under a partly cloudy blue sky.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/305b/live/510d0290-9cca-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
The population of Greenock, on Scotland's west coast, has been falling for decades
- Published
A new shop opened along Greenock's fading High Street in May. Anik African Store has brought a small corner of Nigeria to the Scottish town, selling yams, plantain, okra and catfish.
It is not the only African food shop here - there is another just metres away, responding to the area's changing population.
Five years ago, locals say, it would have been rare to see a black person in Greenock. Now hundreds of Africans and refugees have moved to the area.
The local council has in fact come up with a plan to attract even more to this corner of the west of Scotland as a means of stemming its falling population.
Scottish people "are lovely and accommodating", says Anik's owner, Christianah Omilana, who came to the UK in 2021. "Immigrants will come when there is work", she adds.
![Christianah wears a light green hoodie and stands inside a wellâlit grocery store,  with shelves of canned goods, snacks and bulk food items behind her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/a1f8/live/cff1e2d0-9c87-11f1-a9bc-e5d8f54a68c8.jpg)
Christianah says people in Greenock have been very welcoming and friendly
The lack of work however has been a key driver of depopulation in Greenock and the wider Inverclyde area. No local authority in Scotland has been hit harder by population decline.
The number of residents in Inverclyde is 22,000 fewer than in 1981. And its current population, 78,000, is projected to fall by a further 16% over the next two decades.
Tackling the lack of people is the council's number one priority, by keeping more residents here and attracting others into the area.
It is a "lovely, friendly" town, says one of Anik's customers, Sunday, who has just moved here from Devon. He has begun a job at a hospital in Glasgow, and has come to Greenock to join his wife who works at the local hospital, Inverclyde Royal.
"If the local council can provide [jobs], everything in Greenock will change, because people [from Africa] would like to come," says Sunday.
![Grey line](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/9f2c/live/c77b7440-ec79-11f0-a422-4ba8a094a8fa.png)
Michael Buchanan and Adam Eley visited Greenock for the latest in a series of reports reflecting the range of challenges facing communities across the UK.
![Grey line](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/9f2c/live/c77b7440-ec79-11f0-a422-4ba8a094a8fa.png)
Most of Greenock's African population are working or studying in Glasgow or Paisley and have been attracted to the town by cheap housing. Many have arrived on skilled work visas, known as sponsorship, helping to bolster the health and care workforce.
Inverclyde Council's repopulation strategy is based on trying to encourage them to set down roots here, as well as attracting other legal migrants and people who've been granted refugee status to move in.
However, the lack of jobs lies at the root of the town's problems.
"It's a ghost town," says Tiffany, a mother of one, who we meet at a local parent and toddler group. "There's just nothing in it. There's nothing to do, there are no shops. There is no employment."
The 29-year-old moved away from Greenock to work but came back to bring up her child. Now, she says she is facing up to leaving once more.
"I'm struggling to find jobs that suit both childcare and myself. I've considered moving from here to Paisley because there is so much more to do there."
![A woman in a black zipâup athletic top stands indoors against light brick walls and wooden doors](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/dbd0/live/4c119c20-9701-11f1-b2ab-0dd01740f9f6.jpg)
Greenock is "a ghost town" with "no employment", says Tiffany
Rummage through Greenock's industrial history and you will find a distinct heritage - in the 19th Century its status as a global hub for refining sugar earned it the nickname "Sugaropolis". Thousands of ships were also built in the coastal town over a near 300-year period.
More recently, the computer manufacturer IBM employed more than 5,000 people at its campus near Greenock. But the site closed completely in 2016.
Indeed, in the past four years, a further 1,500 jobs have vanished. Amazon, EE and a string of other companies have gone elsewhere. Just this week, the local shipyard announced it was cutting about a quarter of its workforce. Meanwhile, supporters of Greenock Morton, the local football team, have set up a fighting fund to try to stave off financial collapse at the club.
The town has been left bereft - little wonder Scotland's First Minister John Swinney is due to visit this month, to hear the problems first-hand.
While health and social care roles employ many of the Africans, job opportunities for those born locally, and refugees, can be hard to find.
"When the work disappears, people disappear," says Muriel, one of dozens of elderly residents gathered at Lyle Gateway Community Cafe, a stone's throw from the High Street.
![Muriel and Pamela  women sit together indoors at a community space, smiling as they talk, both wear glasses and have brightly coloured tops.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/d7e6/live/922229f0-9701-11f1-b2ab-0dd01740f9f6.jpg)
Muriel and Pamela chatted to us at a cafe housed in their local church
Between games of table tennis and cheap, hearty lunches, the group remembers a vibrant town, full of people and shops they wanted to go to.
There is a despondency now, with words like "depressing" and "empty" peppering the conversation. The pensioners are sceptical too of the council's repopulation strategy. While happy for migrants to move in, they wonder how sustainable any influx would be.
The council requires hundreds more immigrants each year just to keep the population stable.
"Where would they work?" asks Pamela. "The people in Greenock can't get work [never mind] bringing in other people."
The cafe is housed in Lyle Kirk, where Jonathan Fleming has been the Church of Scotland minister for the past five years. He feels the town's depopulation crisis at first-hand. His church does "a lot more funerals than we do weddings and baptisms," he explains. "And that shift, it's a lot more dramatic than it used to be."
The church has been supporting some Iranian refugees recently and their experience is a sobering one, says Fleming. They are desperate for paid work but can't find any.
"They're wanting to contribute to the community. They want to be independent of receiving financial aid and they're not able to do it - they're actually trapped in it, in some respects."
![Jonathan stands inside a church in front of a wooden pulpit with a gold cross on a wooden backdrop.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/1a0b/live/877a11a0-9c8a-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Church minister Jonathan Fleming says he performs "a lot more" funerals than weddings and baptisms
The number of people arriving in Inverclyde from overseas has trebled in recent times, to about 750 per year since 2023. Hundreds of African migrants have now settled in the area, as well as refugees from Ukraine, Afghanistan and several other countries, many with a positive tale to tell.
As part of its repopulation plan, the council is offering English classes for those who need them and help to access skilled employment. Schools are also supported to provide an inclusive "anti-racist education".
Mo Almalarashid arrived in Greenock in 2018 as a Syrian refugee without a word of English. He says he found a supportive community and, after studying hard, he now works as a local gym instructor. "There was always people there for me," he says.
![Mo is wearing an Inverclyde Leisure shirt standing in a gym with weights and exercise machines behind him.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/1097/live/e1c7cda0-9703-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
Mo Almalarashid arrived in Greenock as a refugee in 2018, and now works as a gym instructor
There have been tensions. A local teenager was sentenced to 10 years in prison last year for planning mass murder at the local mosque. And in June, a protest outside a local hotel housing asylum seekers resulted in one woman being charged with a hate crime, and three police officers being injured.
Yet in May's Scottish Parliamentary elections, Reform UK - which campaigns strongly for lowering immigration nationally - came a distant third in Inverclyde, about 8,500 votes behind the winning SNP candidate, and despite fielding its Scottish leader in the constituency.
Other council areas will face Inverclyde's depopulation challenge in the coming years. The populations of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are all expected to begin declining within the next decade.
Stephen McCabe, who has led Inverclyde's minority Labour-led council almost exclusively since 2007, believes its repopulation plan is beginning to take effect. The population has stabilised in the past two years, he says, largely because of immigration.
Repopulation is at the heart of everything Inverclyde Council hopes to achieve, McCabe says, from housing projects and the revamping of school buildings to, perhaps most importantly, job creation.
Michael and Adam report from communities across the UK
Standing on the banks of the Clyde, he sees opportunities in the maritime, renewables and defence sectors, reimagining use of the river for the 21st Century - although for that, they will need significant Scottish and UK government support.
When asked about asylum seekers, who for the most part are not permitted to work as they await Home Office decisions, McCabe acknowledges there is "an unease, no doubt about it".
While the council has "willingly" participated in a Home Office dispersal scheme - accepting more than 200 people seeking asylum - he believes the area "has been allocated a disproportionate share", with a Home Office contractor said to have bought up a number of houses in the area.
But migrants and refugees who can work are welcome in Inverclyde, McCabe says.
"Without those people, our health service would really be struggling... The refugees who have come have brought benefits to this area. They will bring ambition. They'll bring children to this area."
Greenock's population is not just shrinking, it is also ageing. The lack of children means that one nursery is closing, while older people have greater health needs.
Add in the area's high levels of deprivation, and there is increasing pressure on public services amid a shrinking tax base. Those who remain, pay more - council tax rose by almost 8% locally this year.
![Matthew Quinn stands by a waterfront with calm blue water, coastal buildings and green hills behind him.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/0de0/live/fc19ee90-9703-11f1-870d-5d08c49babb2.jpg)
Matthew Quinn: Politicians should focus on "public services and ensuring we have a nice environment for people to live"
Yet you do not need to look far for a different vision for Greenock. Just 15 minutes down the road is the centre of Gourock, once similarly deprived, which has a small, thriving High Street with independent retailers, boosted by a recent Â£5m council investment and residents with more spending power.
Local resident Matthew Quinn, a 19-year-old former member of the Scottish Youth Parliament, says Gournock has embraced its future as a commuter town and believes other parts of Inverclyde should follow suit.
The council's focus on creating lots of jobs locally is misplaced, Matthew believes. Many people now work from home, he says, and the area's proximity to Glasgow - about 40 minutes away - should be exploited.
"If we accepted that the jobs are in Glasgow, then our focus should be on public services and ensuring we have a nice environment for people to live. Then I think we would be much more successful," he says.
"It's not that [people] are desperate to leave, it's that there's no reason to stay."
![Derek Mitchell stands in front of an old brick industrial building with tall arched windows and metal fencing.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/317e/live/491cc610-97c5-11f1-870d-5d08c49babb2.jpg)
Derek Mitchell hopes to convert a disused sugar refinery into an education hub
That is a challenge that some Greenock residents are attempting to tackle, head on.
Derek Mitchell, infused with infectious positivity, is looking to convert a former sugar refinery next to an Aldi car park into a thriving hub that will teach and enthuse young people.
A focus on science, technology, engineering, arts and maths, he says, will provide them with skills for the future.
"If you build a sense of belonging, naturally and organically, people don't want to leave."
He has purchased the building as part of a group of locals, who estimate it will need Â£5m of investment as they continue to look for partnerships.
"A lot of people are starting to do things for themselves," he says. "They see there's potential - they're fed up of waiting."
At a time when much of the UK has concerns about immigration, Inverclyde's decision to embrace migrants and refugees makes it stand out. Its lack of people is acute, its solution, striking. Other communities will soon face a similar depopulation challenge and may look to what Greenock is trying as a possible way ahead.
summary: Greenock on Scotland's west coast is facing severe population decline and an aging demographic due to decades of job losses. To combat this, the local council has implemented a repopulation strategy to attract migrants and refugees, which has already brought hundreds of new residents to the area. While some locals and migrants welcome the diversity and economic stabilization, others express skepticism about sustainability given the ongoing lack of local employment.
key_points: Greenock and the wider Inverclyde area have suffered severe population decline, with the population dropping by 22,000 since 1981.
Inverclyde Council's repopulation strategy aims to attract legal migrants, refugees, and workers to stem the population fall, helping to stabilize numbers over the past two years.
Many recent arrivals from Africa are working or studying in healthcare and other sectors, aided by affordable housing in Greenock.
A significant shortage of local jobs and high levels of deprivation remain major concerns for long-term residents and church leaders.
Despite some community tensions and local skepticism regarding job availability, the council views immigration as vital for public services and economic survival.

title: New Forest wildlife and ancient trees destroyed by A31 wildfire
author: Marcus White
content:
![A large tree stands in the middle of a scorched heath.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/3bc2/live/ad13b690-9c90-11f1-bd28-a9dd56c45ed7.jpg)
The blaze penetrated the roots of centuries-old trees in the New Forest
- Published
Ancient oak and beech trees, rare heathland and even wetland have been devastated by the recent fire that swept through the New Forest, a survey has found.
More than 1 sq km (247 acres) of the national park has been destroyed since the fire broke out on 9 August, Forestry England said.
The government agency found areas devoid of vegetation, dead wildlife and scorched bogs in an initial inspection of the damage.
It said it would take decades for the environment to fully recover.
![A blackened tree stump on ashy ground is in front of undamaged open ground and woodland.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/8d2d/live/de804180-9c9a-11f1-a5a0-114ca9d4a1bc.jpg)
The "remarkable" efforts of firefighters prevented more damage, Forestry England said
Head of planning and environment Michael Pittock said: "It is devastating to walk around the area of the wildfire and see so much destruction.
"Without the remarkable response from the fire and emergency services it could have been so much worse."
Several centuries-old trees have been lost, as the fire penetrated their root systems, Forestry England said.
Bogs, normally resilient to heat, have been burnt and partially destroyed, it added.
The lost vegetation includes pillwort, a rare wetland plant with a New Forest stronghold.
![A gloved hand holds a sand lizard near brown grass on the ground.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/8d39/live/316323f0-9c9f-11f1-a5a0-114ca9d4a1bc.jpg)
A sand lizard was among a number of creatures rescued on Wednesday
![A recently-sawn tree stump lies on a large area of scorched land.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/3226/live/06950750-9c9b-11f1-a5a0-114ca9d4a1bc.jpg)
More than 1 sq km (247 acres) of the national park has been destroyed
In a rescue mission on Wednesday, amphibian and reptile experts found dead wildlife, but also some survivors which were collected and relocated.
Forestry England said recovery plans were based on the experience gained following a large-scale heathland fire in Wareham, Dorset, in May 2020.
Heather cuttings will be used to form a protective layer over the soil and start the restoration process.
The blaze started when a van caught fire on the A31 dual carriageway between Ringwood and Cadnam.
The road through the national park has since been closed for fire damage repairs and will not open until the weekend at the earliest, according to National Highways.
![A man in a fluorescent jacket walk through an area of tufted green plants with dark stalks. Some blackened ground is visible.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/b34a/live/27c11d20-9c9a-11f1-a38b-8bb91d2ef80e.jpg)
The affected area will take take decades to fully recover
summary: A wildfire in the New Forest has destroyed more than 1 square kilometre of the national park, including ancient trees, rare heathland, and wetland. Triggered by a van fire on the A31 on 9 August, the blaze killed wildlife and scorched bogs and root systems. Forestry England stated that it will take decades for the environment to fully recover.
key_points: More than 1 square kilometre (247 acres) of the New Forest national park was destroyed by the wildfire.
The fire started on 9 August when a van caught fire on the A31 dual carriageway.
Damage includes the loss of centuries-old oak and beech trees, rare wetland plants like pillwort, and dead wildlife.
Forestry England estimates it will take decades for the affected environment to fully recover.
Recovery plans will utilize heather cuttings to protect the soil, based on experience from a 2020 fire in Dorset.

title: What happened to Harry and Meghan's American dream?
author: Shaimaa Khalil; Regan Morris
content:
Watch: How Harry and Meghan are ending their 'American dream'
- Published
When the Duke and Duchess of Sussex quit working for the Royal Family in 2020 and moved to California, they brought something even Hollywood can't manufacture: royalty.
But while Harry and Meghan enjoyed some success in showbusiness, their Hollywood reign proved short-lived and California has greeted news of their departure back to the UK with a shrug.
In pursuing their American dream, they said they were seeking more than financial independence.
In their 2021 blockbuster interview with Oprah Winfrey, Meghan described the freedom to make her own choices as "liberating".
Harry later said America offered his family a degree of privacy and freedom they "undoubtedly wouldn't be able" to enjoy in the UK - and that it was the life his mother, Diana, would have wanted for him.
The couple settled in Montecito - a celebrity enclave a few hours north of Los Angeles with neighbours like Oprah Winfrey, Gwyneth Paltrow and Rob Lowe.
Multimillion dollar podcast and Netflix deals followed.
"They were so sought after, they were names that would hit the press and command attention right away," says Stacy Jones, chief executive of Hollywood Branded, a marketing and PR agency.
![Harry and Meghan smiling next to two others, wearing cocktail attire, at a house](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/907/cpsprodpb/54f8/live/3968b500-9cf5-11f1-8cdc-014599ccd660.jpg)
Harry and Meghan with Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos and wife Nicole Avant
"There are endless parties, endless events and endless things to do if you are a celebrity inside Hollywood," she says. "But you soon realise that all those endless things are promoting something to sell."
And the royal couple had plenty to sell.
LA-based royal watcher and journalist Elizabeth Holmes, who wrote HRH: So Many Thoughts on Royal Style, says: "I think part of why this [the Sussexes leaving the US] was surprising to me was just because it did feel like they were sort of settling into their life in California."
Californians reacts to Harry and Meghan's return to the UK
Not everyone is sad to see them go. The New York Post, often scathing about the couple, greeted the news of their departure with the headline "Throne Back!", declaring that America's "long national nightmare is over".
The tabloid mockery was largely dismissive of the couple's rare achievement in Hollywood. They managed something most newcomers to Tinseltown never do: persuading some of its biggest companies to invest heavily in them.
Attracting that initial investment proved easier than sustaining it, however.
Their multi-year Spotify deal, reported to be worth up to $25m (Â£18.3m), produced Meghan's 12-episode podcast Archetypes, featuring guests such as Serena Williams and Mariah Carey.
In 2023, however, Spotify and the couple's Archewell Audio announced that they had "mutually agreed to part ways".
Their five-year Netflix deal, signed in 2020 and reportedly worth between $60m and $100m, delivered several programmes.
But it has since been replaced by a less lucrative arrangement, against the backdrop of a broader downturn across the entertainment industry.
Behind the projects, the Sussexes' production business also experienced high staff turnover, with reports that some former employees privately called themselves the "Sussex Survivors Club".
Harry, too, found commercial success, but largely when he was selling his own royal story.
His memoir, Spare, was a publishing phenomenon, reportedly coming with a $20m advance.
It sold more than six million copies worldwide, making it the fastest-selling non-fiction book on record.
As part of its promotion, Harry held a public conversation with trauma specialist Dr Gabor MatÃ©, in which he explored how his royal childhood had shaped him.
In an interview with BBC Newsnight on Thursday, MatÃ© said Harry had come across as "very personable, very sensitive" and someone doing his best to make sure "he doesn't pass on his traumas to his children".
Watch: Trauma expert unpacks Harry and Meghan's return to the UK
The Duke of Sussex remains enormously marketable when the subject is Harry himself, the Royal Family or the causes with which he has long been associated.
He became chief impact officer at the Silicon Valley coaching company BetterUp and co-created and executive-produced the Apple TV+ mental-health series The Me You Can't See, with Oprah Winfrey.
His Netflix projects have drawn heavily on his established interests.
Heart of Invictus followed wounded and injured military veterans preparing for the Games he founded, while Polo explored another of his passions.
Neither attracted anything approaching the attention generated by the couple's six-part documentary series Harry & Meghan, or his revelations in Spare.
In one of his relatively rare major public appearances, Harry also delivered the keynote address at an informal meeting of the UN General Assembly in New York in 2022, marking Nelson Mandela International Day. He spoke about his mother, his connection to Africa and Mandela's legacy.
But he seemed to struggle to break out of his royal typecast role in the US.
![a close-up photo of Harry and Meghan laughing with a dog in between them](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/7130/live/556a36d0-9cf9-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
The couple had their own Netflix documentary series called Harry & Meghan
As for former Suits actress Meghan, she branched out into a Netflix cooking and lifestyle series.
This content showed off their idyllic life with adorable "rescue chickens" and fresh-grown strawberries, against the scenic backdrop of the Santa Ynez Mountains.
With Love, Meghan was cancelled after two seasons, but it has been nominated for an Emmy in the Outstanding Lifestyle Series category.
Netflix also ended its involvement in Meghan's lifestyle brand, As Ever, earlier this year.
"Netflix produces movies. Netflix doesn't produce jam," says Jones, the brand guru.
![a phone screen showing "With Love, Meghan" series page on Netflix, in front of a TV with the show playing](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/6f59/live/de87f2f0-9cf8-11f1-a07e-5d2ec7b46104.jpg)
Meghan displayed a highly curated version of herself on her Netflix show With Love, Meghan
Critics assailed the carefully curated lifestyle presented by Meghan as tone-deaf. But in branding terms, Jones acknowledges that even negative publicity can have value if it keeps someone at the centre of the conversation.
Meghan's projects kept her visible and gave audiences something they could watch or buy.
"In moving to Britain, it looks like they are continuing to chase that proximity to the Royal Family to validate themselves or, in some cases, to commercialise," says Kinsey Schofield, whose namesake podcast focuses on the Royal Family.
"Meghan's been cosplaying as a royal selling her teas and her fruit spread through As Ever since it launched."
The Sussexes still have projects in development. They recently released a documentary about Girl Scouts and they have a scripted series in the works set in the exclusive world of polo teams, to be produced by the makers of Gossip Girl.
But their American experience overall reveals the limits of celebrity in Hollywood.
Fame may get you through the door, but it does not guarantee staying power.
![Harry and Meghan standing beside each in the stands of a baseball game, both wearing Dodgers hat, with Meghan cheering](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/0d34/live/1f988df0-9cf8-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Harry and Meghan attending a Los Angeles Dodgers game in October 2025
"Hollywood is going through an incredibly hard time right now, and it's a fractured landscape," Jones says.
Layoffs, repeated restructuring and high staff turnover have destabilised companies across the industry.
"It is pretty hard to start and launch a company and keep it going," she says. "When that company is being launched by someone who is a mega media star, it needs some really strong people supporting it."
They may no longer occupy the position they held when they first arrived in America, and they may say they're heading back to the UK to be private citizens, but it's unlikely that the couple would fade in the background.
"They will never be private citizens anywhere in their lives," Jones says.
"They are not people who can ever become background players. They are stars of their own show - or stars of someone else's show. Even if they're lower-level stars, they're still stars."
summary: After moving to California in 2020 following their departure from the Royal Family, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle secured major Hollywood deals, but ultimately struggled to sustain their initial commercial success. Despite achieving high-profile projects like Harry's bestselling memoir Spare and various media ventures, the couple faced contract changes, show cancellations, and high staff turnover. As they prepare to return to the UK, their American experience highlights the difficulties of maintaining long-term staying power in the entertainment industry.
key_points: Harry and Meghan moved to California in 2020 seeking financial independence, privacy, and freedom.
The couple secured lucrative multi-million dollar deals with companies like Netflix and Spotify, though some partnerships ended or were scaled back over time.
Harry achieved significant commercial success primarily when focusing on his royal background, notably with his record-breaking memoir Spare.
Meghan's lifestyle and cooking series, With Love, Meghan, was cancelled after two seasons, and Netflix ended its involvement with her lifestyle brand, As Ever.
Industry experts noted that while initial fame helped the couple secure high-profile investments, sustaining long-term success in Hollywood proved challenging.

title: French police attacked by migrants while stopping boat launch
author: Charles Hymas
content:
Footage has captured the moment French police officers were attacked by migrants as they intercepted the launch of a boat.
The video shows migrants wearing life jackets appearing to throw objects at the police to try to keep them away from their dinghy.
The officers then use Pava spray before slashing the inflatable boat with a knife.
Charlie Estaugh, the UK’s border security commander, claimed it was evidence of the French taking a more “bold” and aggressive approach to halting the attempted crossings.
French police say they have boarded 12 migrant “taxi boats” in their first interceptions at sea since the UK signed a new £662m deal to tackle small boat crossings.
The French have previously resisted intervening at sea because of the risk to life.
Mr Estaugh said the French and British were “piling the pressure on the criminal gangs and preventing these illegal and dangerous crossings”.
“French officers are not shy in taking bold action to prevent these launches where it is safe and lawful to do so,” he said.
The footage is designed to counter criticism after French officers were filmed by Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, standing by without intervening as a boat launched.
The Home Office said the French units prevented 185 “small boat crossing events” in the three months after the new UK-France deal.
summary: Footage has captured French police officers being attacked by migrants while intercepting the launch of an inflatable boat, responding by using Pava spray and slashing the dinghy. UK border security commander Charlie Estaugh cited the incident as evidence of a bolder French approach to stopping cross-Channel attempts following a new £662m UK-France deal. French authorities reported boarding 12 migrant taxi boats in their first sea interceptions since the agreement.
key_points: French police were attacked by migrants wearing life jackets while trying to stop a boat launch.
Officers used Pava spray and slashed the inflatable boat with a knife during the confrontation.
The UK's border security commander stated the incident shows French forces taking a bolder approach against crossings.
French police have boarded 12 migrant taxi boats in initial sea interceptions under a new £662m UK-France deal.

title: ‘Strongest El Nino in century’ to bring storms this autumn
author: Ruby Cline
content:
![A person's umbrella is turned inside from the wind in Westminster, central London](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498928536_17872590358630_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqBIhf9vY3F0gQVGEB0QvnDv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![A person's umbrella is turned inside from the wind in Westminster, central London](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498928536_17872590358630_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqBIhf9vY3F0gQVGEB0QvnDv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Britain is braced for a wet and stormy autumn because of what could be the strongest El Niño in a century.
The Met Office said the “unprecedented” oceanic heatwave would lead to storms and rain between October and December.
El Niño is a powerful natural climate phenomenon that pushes up global temperatures. The natural warming of sea temperatures is forecast to reach more than 3C in the coming months, making this year’s weather event “the largest since the 19th century”, according to the Met Office.
US scientists confirmed in June that El Niño conditions were under way in the tropical Pacific following a sharp rise in sea-surface temperatures.
Prof Adam Scaife, the head of long-range forecasting at the Met Office, said this autumn’s “extreme” El Niño would lead to rain and storms in the UK.
He told The Telegraph: “The weather map in November is looking wet and stormy on average. Mild, wet and stormy – early winter will be when El Niño peaks.”
![Spectators shelter from the rain at Headingley, Leeds](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498916494_17872590244680_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqihVibxPbOwKDCDIL8LViR75qh9cfU8a8nPeLP9jiHHc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The weather event means 2027 is forecast to be the warmest year on record.
“We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event,” Prof Scaife said.
“I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts.”
He added: “A typical El Niño leads to an equatorial Pacific sea-surface temperature rise of between one to 2C, with 2C being a really big event.
“This implies that if the forecast is accurate – and other forecast systems show similar extreme values – then 2026 will far exceed our recent experience of El Niño and its worldwide climate influences.”
El Niño events also drive an increase in global average temperature, with 2027 forecast to be the warmest year on record.
Months of drought during the summer mean Britain faces an increased flood risk because rainfall does not soak easily into the hard, dry ground.
Meteorologists have warned of increased flash-flood risks this week and next, while drought experts grapple with the longer-term implications of the dry summer.
![People play cricket at Perry Hill Park in Birmingham](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498590507_17872598014141_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Craig Snell, a senior meteorologist at the Met Office, said wetter conditions expected this week would create a risk of flooding.
He said: “Parts of the North West have seen some localised flooding, and also parts of the south coast of England over the last 24 hours or so.
“Part of that is down to the fact that the rain is falling on quite baked ground, so the water is not sinking in like it would usually do.”
The last significant El Niño was in 2015, when the UK was hit by a string of named storms.
In December 2015, hundreds of flood warnings were issued as infrastructure in York and Leeds cracked under the pressure of gushing streets.
Thousands were evacuated from their York homes when the Environment Agency was forced to open the city’s floodgates.
Dr Nick Dunstone of the Met Office said: “During large El Niño events, significantly more heat is released from the ocean to the atmosphere, leading to an increase in global average temperature, particularly in the calendar year following the winter peak of the El Niño.
“Hence, 2027 is very likely to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record.”
summary: Britain is bracing for a wet and stormy autumn driven by what the Met Office warns could be the strongest El Niño in a century. The unprecedented oceanic heatwave is forecast to peak in early winter, bringing mild, wet, and stormy conditions. Due to baked, dry ground from summer droughts, the heavy rainfall also significantly increases the risk of flash flooding across the UK.
key_points: The Met Office predicts an extreme El Niño event with sea temperature increases forecast to reach more than 3C.
The upcoming autumn and early winter are expected to bring heavy rain and storms to the UK.
Summer droughts have left the ground hard and dry, significantly increasing the risk of flash flooding from the incoming rainfall.
The climate phenomenon is expected to drive global temperatures up, making 2027 very likely to become the warmest year on record.

title: Heavy rain hits London as Sadiq Khan warns downpours could lead to 'flash flooding'
author: Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/12/50/IMG_0994.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
According to the national forecaster’s rain tracker, showers began sweeping across the capital from around 12.20pm, and more are expected to come sporadically through this evening.
As much as 32mm of rain per hour fell in parts of the capital, including Hounslow and Woolwich.
The hard, baked ground could make London more susceptible to flash flooding, as Sir Sadiq warned in a post on X.
The mayor wrote: “When heavy rain falls on hard, baked ground, water runs off much more quickly, increasing the risk of flash flooding.”
When severe flash flooding hit London in 2021, rain caused damage and disruption to homes and businesses across the city, with many Londoners forced to stay elsewhere as their homes were flooded with stormwater and sewage.
The mayor also shared government advice, telling Londoners to check the drains outside their homes and to prepare a flood kit.
summary: Heavy rain has hit London, prompting Mayor Sadiq Khan to warn that downpours could lead to flash flooding. Showers began sweeping across the capital around 12.20pm, with rainfall reaching up to 32mm per hour in areas like Hounslow and Woolwich. The mayor noted that hard, baked ground increases the risk of rapid water runoff and urged residents to prepare.
key_points: Heavy rain showers began sweeping across London from around 12.20pm.
Rainfall rates reached up to 32mm per hour in parts of the capital, including Hounslow and Woolwich.
Mayor Sadiq Khan warned that hard, baked ground increases the risk of flash flooding.
Residents were advised to check home drains and prepare a flood kit.

title: French becoming more effective in stopping small boat crossings, UK says
author: Tom Symonds
content:
French police slash migrant small boat
- Published
French police tactics are becoming more effective in stopping small boats in the English Channel from reaching Britain, the Home Office has said.
It credits French authorities with intercepting 185 potential crossings involving 4,300 migrants this summer over four separate weeks, as well as stopping 12 boats at sea using new techniques.
Footage released by French police shows officers racing across a beach in jeeps to intercept a launch. Once the boat is abandoned, an officer slashes it lengthways with a knife.
The Conservatives described the announcement as a "joke" and said Channel crossing preventions were "down by half over the past year".
Migrants can be seen throwing objects at the officers, one of whom appears to respond with pepper spray.
While Channel crossings are down about 40% compared to last year, thousands of illegal migrants are getting through with 250 arriving on Monday.
In late July a record 165 migrants reached the UK in a single boat with Border Security Command pictured towing a mega dinghy - estimated to be the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover on 23 July.
The Home Office, citing French police figures, said that since it struck a deal with France three months ago which included additional funding for authorities, 61% of small boats have been intercepted - a five per cent increase compared to last year.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the "UK-France deal is already having a real impact".
The UK-France Border Security deal agreed in April under the Starmer government, includes Â£501m over three years to strengthen operations in northern France and Â£161m for new approaches.
Previously the French authorities allowed most dinghies to head towards the UK once they had launched, because of the risk of intercepting them in deep water, while loaded with people.
Of the 12 dinghies stopped so far at sea, three interceptions took place in the last two weeks.
The techniques being used have not been disclosed by the UK or France.
Charlie Eastaugh, director of maritime and small boats at the Border Security Command, told the BBC that "last Thursday alone, the French prevented all three of the boats that tried to cross".
Speaking to the BBC at the Western Jetfoil facility in Dover used to process migrants, he said: "Two of those they prevented at sea, and one they prevented on land."
He said some had claimed bad weather was the biggest factor in a reduction of crossings this year.
"But what that demonstrates is absolutely that the French are being effective in preventing a number of these small boats."
"Clearly, every single day that one slips through the net and crosses, it's one too many, and that's why it's absolutely critical to us to not take our foot off the gas and to keep working hard with our French partners and stop this from happening."
In the last week, 425 migrants made it across the Channel on five boats during three days of good weather.
Stopping the trade in equipment for Channel crossings is the first layer of tactics being used by the UK and other countries.
Dinghies, outboard engines, and life preservers have been seized by police in Germany.
Nearer the coast, boats have been discovered buried on beaches and in cars heading for the coast.
With less equipment available, people smugglers have resorted to using bigger boats.
Earlier this month a "mega-dinghy", with 230 people on board, was intercepted in the Channel.
The second layer is to stop migrants launching from beaches.
In July last year a BBC team witnessed the police slashing an inflatable boat with a knife to prevent it being used. This technique is now being used more often.
Interception at sea is the most difficult challenge. The UK government knows if it can prevent migrant boats getting into British waters, where the Border Force is legally obliged to pick them up, the incentive to try to cross will be reduced.
The concern is that smuggling gangs will continue to adapt but Eastaugh told the BBC that changes to their methods demonstrated how hard they are finding it to operate.
"That's why the numbers we're seeing are so successful, and we're absolutely not complacent, and we must keep working this way to keep the numbers down," he said.
Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: "The only way we can stop the crossings is by having a proper deterrent. If people know they can stay in the UK, get put up in a hotel and claim benefits then they will keep risking these dangerous journeys."
Earlier this month Reform UK said if it was in power it would intercept boats crossing the English Channel and return migrants to French ports, even if France disagreed.
The French interior ministry responded by saying it would "constitute a violation of French sovereignty".
  - Published10 August
 ![A young person wearing a baseball cap and a backpack and carrying a suitcase stands in the middle of the image. To the left of the image a passport with a boarding card is held up. To the right of the image is a migrant family of a man, woman and child on a beach, walking. In the top right corner is a partial view of a UK visa document](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a530/live/da608860-cb5a-11f0-a892-01d657345866.png)
- ![Mid shot of Andy Burnham wearing a black suit and black tie with black-framed glasses. In the distance is the white cliffs of Dover.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/9549/live/c82d6200-8f02-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
- ![Migrants climb onto small boat in sea that is around waist-height. They wear orange life jackets](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/54cb/live/d39608f0-8f10-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
summary: The UK Home Office states that French police tactics are becoming more effective at stopping migrant small boat crossings in the English Channel. Under a recent UK-France border security deal, French authorities have intercepted 61% of small boats, utilizing new techniques that include slashing abandoned dinghies and intercepting boats at sea. While Channel crossings are down compared to last year, thousands of migrants continue to arrive, prompting criticism from opposition parties over the current prevention strategies.
key_points: The Home Office credits French authorities with intercepting 185 potential crossings involving 4,300 migrants over four summer weeks.
French police have used new techniques, including slashing abandoned dinghies and stopping 12 boats at sea.
