The UK-France deal agreed in April includes £501m over three years to strengthen operations in northern France and £161m for new approaches.
Conservatives criticized the announcement, arguing that Channel crossing preventions are down by half over the past year.

title: Burnham must attend first terror attack memorial day, says survivor
author: Rozina Sabur
content:
![Travis Frain with the King](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000124203352_17871579477250_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqQbIAlMgBBjstqL9vckGEln4ihL9D5G77hk2Gx25ScXg.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Travis Frain with the King](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000124203352_17871579477250_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqQbIAlMgBBjstqL9vckGEln4ihL9D5G77hk2Gx25ScXg.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The Prime Minister or the King must attend the first national day of remembrance for victims of terrorism for it to have real significance, a survivor has said.
The inaugural day of remembrance will be marked with an event in central London on Friday, and will take place in different locations across the country every Aug 21.
It follows years of tireless campaigning by survivors of terror attacks, including Travis Frain, who was severely injured as a teenager in the 2017 Westminster Bridge attack.
In an interview with The Telegraph, Mr Frain said he was “cautiously optimistic” for Friday’s event after petitioning for it for more than four years. He said he hoped the Government had listened to victims’ wishes.
“The big point behind a national day is ultimately recognition,” Mr Frain said. “We were not targeted as individuals. The vast majority of people affected by terrorism are targeted because of something far greater than themselves; because they are representative of a nation or a nation’s values.
“I think it’s only right that that same representative of the nation, whether it be the King, whether it be the Prime Minister – or in an ideal world, both – I think it’s only right that they should be there as well.”
![Travis Frain](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000194782285_17871579329330_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqLgh7iYB6BmgO3j6FNL9Qb5BjSmVWYCN1dhb2-hLMviI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
He added: “I think, frankly, without those individuals in the room, it wouldn’t be much of a national day.”
The Duke and Duchess of Gloucester will attend Friday’s ceremony on behalf of the King and Dan Jarvis, the security minister, is also expected to attend.
However, the presence of Andy Burnham or other senior government figures has not been confirmed.
Government sources stressed that the Prime Minister was acutely aware of the impact of terrorism on victims. During his time as mayor of Greater Manchester, Mr Burnham met a number of survivors of the city’s 2017 bombing.
The same year, Mr Frain, who was 19 at the time and participating in a university trip to Parliament, was hit by a car mounting the pavement on Westminster Bridge.
Five victims died in the attack and a further 50 were injured. Mr Frain suffered serious injuries all over his body, resulting in operations on his leg and hand.
![Tributes paid to those killed in the Westminster Bridge attack](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000484343383_17871582125990_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqtGQB12KHxxQCrwnTZkX0nwgWqwm85JEWpGVhFb46TTg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Friday’s event will recognise anyone affected by terrorism in the UK as well as British nationals who have suffered in terrorist acts overseas. It brings the UK into line with several European nations, including France and Belgium, and the UN, in staging annual events in tribute and dedication to the victims of terrorism.
Those affected by IRA bombing campaigns, the Manchester Arena explosion and the London terror attacks are expected to be represented. Since 1970, there have been almost 1,000 terrorist-related deaths in the UK.
In May, the UK’s terror threat level was raised to “severe”, the second-highest. The Joint Terrorism Analysis Centre, housed inside MI5, said it was a reflection of the threat from Islamist and extreme Right-wing terror.
However, Mr Frain said he feared the public were not sufficiently aware of the ongoing threat of terrorism. “I think the vast majority of people will recognise that we’re in a very unstable situation globally, but I don’t necessarily think that a lot of people see that translate domestically,” he said. “I think we need to be far more open to the public about the threats we face wherever we can.”
He added: “Having at least one guaranteed date in the diary where we know that we’re going to have an opportunity to raise awareness of extremism, of the threat of radicalisation and perhaps more importantly, what regular people can do about it, will be a really, really positive legacy in memory of those that we’ve lost.”
summary: A terror attack survivor has stated that either the Prime Minister or the King must attend the UK's first national day of remembrance for victims of terrorism for the event to hold real significance. Travis Frain, who was injured in the 2017 Westminster Bridge attack, campaigned for over four years for the memorial day, which will take place on Friday in central London. While the Duke and Duchess of Gloucester will represent the King and security minister Dan Jarvis is expected to attend, the presence of other senior government figures remains unconfirmed.
key_points: The UK's first national day of remembrance for terror victims takes place on Friday in central London and will recur annually on August 21.
Survivor and campaigner Travis Frain stated that the Prime Minister or the King must attend for the day to have true national significance.
The Duke and Duchess of Gloucester will attend the inaugural ceremony on behalf of the King.
The memorial day will honor those affected by domestic terrorism in the UK as well as British nationals impacted by attacks overseas.

title: The student survivor who shaped UK's national terrorism memorial day
author: Ewan Somerville
content:
![A man in a black jacket and with glasses, ginger hair and a beard stands on the riverside by the River Thames with Westminster Bridge and the London Eye in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a399/live/36ece130-9c95-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Travis Frain was visiting Westminster as an undergraduate at Edge Hill University when he was caught up in an attack
- Published
Travis Frain was texting his mates a photo he had just taken of Big Ben on a university trip to London when his day turned from normal to anything but.
"One of the guys in my group shouted 'look out' and as I looked up from my phone the terrorist's car was in front of me.
"It was a split second really before the car hit me. I went over the bonnet, into the air, before landing back on the ground."
This was 22 March 2017, when attacker Khalid Masood drove his car into crowds, killing four, before stabbing a police officer to death outside Parliament.
Frain, then 19, was left with multiple injuries including a fractured leg, which took two years to heal. "There will always be a part of you affected by that attack."
Now 28, he spoke to BBC News as the UK's first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism is set to take place on Friday.
'Morally correct to remember'
Mirroring similar fixtures in European countries, the UK government has said the day aims to recognise those impacted by terrorism including victims and their families, witnesses and the emergency services.
At its centre is an event in London on Friday afternoon with a two-minute silence for those lost to terrorism and readings from people affected by it. The event will be staged in locations around the UK in future years.
![Police take security measures at Westminster Bridge after a car ran over people on the bridge during a terror attack. Police tape covers the entrance to the bridge and police vans and officers are seen in the vicinity.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/a117/live/847ff560-9c93-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
The Westminster Bridge attack in 2017 came two months before another major terror attack at an Arianna Grande concert in Manchester arena
Frain, who has campaigned for this day for nearly five years, said he feels recognition and memorials for terror victims "often go under the radar".
"As a society, it is right and morally correct that we should be remembering those lost to terrorism," he said, adding that victims were "often not targeted as individuals but as representatives of something far greater - the nation, the nation's values; the values we're all meant to hold I'm sure."
At the same time, the day will be about encouraging people to "keep an eye on each other" as "we all have a role to play" in stopping terrorism, he added.
In May, the UK's terror threat was raised to "severe", meaning an attack is highly likely. A record nearly 10,000 people were referred to Prevent, the government's anti-terrorism scheme, in the year to September 2025.
![Travis Frain lays on a hospital bed with his leg strapped while King Charles is at his bedside.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/2d5b/live/0c4a8820-9c94-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Travis Frain was visited by Charles, then Prince of Wales, while in hospital
The idea for a national day for terror victims and survivors came about after a Home Office review, external found many needed more support.
But many who have campaigned for the day still feel more needs to be done to help survivors.
A report, released on Friday by the Survivors Against Terror (SAT), said while psychological support for victims had improved, no progress had been made to the state compensation scheme for terror victims, the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority.
SAT's co-founder Brendan Cox, whose wife MP Jo Cox was murdered by a neo-Nazi in 2016, welcomed the national day but warned "survivors also want it to be a moment of accountability".
"We're not talking large sums of money, we're talking about a process that dehumanises people where if you're a survivor of a terror attack, you can only claim for the first three injuries you have despite the fact you have 80 or 90 or 100 pieces of shrapnel in your body," Cox said.
"At the moment we still have members who don't have the resources to build a downstairs toilet following attacks that have left them struggling to walk," added Lisa Ghiggini, who survived the Fishmonger's Hall attack in 2019.
The Ministry of Justice, which is responsible for the taxpayer-funded scheme, where victims self-classify the type of incident, said Â£180m was paid out last year for all types of violent crime including terrorism.
![A young man kneels in front of the floral memorial at Victoria station during the commemoration. Colourful flowers, posters and pictures of Manchester bee icons are shown.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/14d8/live/160a6210-9c97-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Many in Manchester have paid their respects to the victims of the Manchester Arena attack in 2017
The chosen date for the national day of 21 August coincides with the UN International Day of Remembrance and Tribute to the Victims of Terrorism, which began in 2017.
While the UK event will take place in London for its debut year, the Home Office has said people across the country can mark it at home by observing a moment of reflection and sharing posts about the day on social media.
Frain said he knows of many terror survivors who can never return to London, as they remain too harrowed what they experienced in attacks.
He returned to Westminster Bridge just two days after the 2017 attack - while still injured - to "desensitise" himself and he plans to return to the capital on Friday with a similar defiance.
He hopes the King, another royal, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, or a senior cabinet minister will turn up to hear from survivors.
"It's those individuals that provide the national aspect - it can't just be victims in a room talking to one another."
summary: Travis Frain, a survivor of the 2017 Westminster Bridge terror attack, has campaigned for nearly five years to help establish the UK's first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism. Following a Home Office review that highlighted the need for more support, the inaugural event takes place on Friday to recognise those impacted by terrorism, including victims, families, witnesses, and emergency services. While campaigners welcome the national day, they emphasize that more action is needed regarding accountability and improvements to the state compensation scheme.
key_points: Travis Frain was 19 and a university student when he was struck by a car during the 2017 Westminster Bridge attack.
The UK is holding its first national day for victims and survivors of terrorism, coinciding with the UN International Day of Remembrance.
The national day aims to recognize those affected by terrorism, including victims, families, witnesses, and emergency services.
Campaigners and groups like Survivors Against Terror warn that despite better psychological support, the state compensation scheme for terror victims remains flawed and dehumanising.

title: Leaders attack ‘demotivating’ plan to make pupils who fail GCSEs retake maths and English
author: Richard Adams; Sally Weale
content:
The government’s plans to make young people continue studying maths and English if they fail GCSEs could be demotivating and ineffective, according to education experts and school leaders after retake pass rates slumped this year.
Only one in seven students in the age group retaking GCSE maths after a previous failure got a grade 4 or above this summer, while only one in six managed to pass English, meaning the majority will have to retake the exams next year if they remain in education or training.
The lower than expected results for older students came against a more positive national picture in which students in year 11 achieved record high grades in GCSE examinations across England.
While seven in 10 of 16-year-olds achieved pass grades in maths and English, the remaining 620,000 year 11 students face retaking GCSE maths or English next year after failing to reach grade 4.
Lucy Powell, the education secretary in England, said the government would be sticking with plans for a new “stepping stone” qualification aimed at those who got a grade 2 or worse in their first attempt at GCSEs.
Powell described the current policy as “a hamster wheel” and said: “There’s got to be a better way to give young people the skills and confidence that they need to succeed, not just branding them a failure, and also allowing them to gain other qualifications that show they have a strong foundation in English and maths.
“So that’s why I want to bring in a new level-one qualification so they’ve got a strong foundation in English and maths that gives them that passport to go on for further study or an apprenticeship or a training place.”
But the plan, first announced in last year’s skills white paper, has been met with scepticism by experts and school leaders, who warned that the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) was likely to increase as long as GCSE failure rates remained high.
Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “This year’s post-16 resit results reinforce the fact that the government policy of force-feeding them a relentless diet of GCSE English and maths in post-16 education is simply not working.
“Tinkering at the edges of the qualification system will not solve this problem. As long as we continue to grade students in this way in these gateway subjects of English and maths, we will continue to damage their future prospects.
“If the government is serious about tackling the Neet crisis it must grasp this nettle and rethink how we assess English and maths.”
Lee Elliot Major, a professor of social mobility at the University of Exeter, warned that the new qualification would “need a strong fairness test to ensure this doesn’t create a two-tier system in which pupils from under-resourced backgrounds are disproportionately directed onto lower-level routes.
“With around a third of young people not achieving the grade 4 benchmark in both English and maths, the system itself needs reform. This is the cruel injustice of narrow expectations: we need different pathways, but not different ceilings.”
The Department for Education’s consultation positions the new “stepping stone” qualification as preparation for a later GCSE resit, meaning young people will still face multiple examinations while they remain in education.
Paul Whiteman, head of the National Association of Head Teachers, said: “We have long called for an end to the current policy which forces students into dispiriting rounds of repeated, demotivating resits.
“What is needed are more appropriate and engaging alternatives to GCSEs in English and maths at key stage 4 which enable students to study for qualifications that better suit their needs and aspirations.”
This year, the results revealed a strong performance in maths among boys in England, with a new high of 24% achieving grade 7 or above, while 20.5% of girls reached the same level. However, girls maintained their lead in top grades across all subjects, with 25.5% of their exam entries being awarded grade 7 or above compared with 20.7% of boys.
The proportion of exam results at the top grade, 9, remained at 5.2%, unchanged from 2025.
GCSEs in England award grades on a scale of 9 to 1, while many in Northern Ireland and Wales continue to award letter grades with A* at the peak. Education policy is devolved to UK national governments, making it difficult to directly compare GCSE results between them due to different content, marking and regulation.
In Northern Ireland 31.5% of entries by 16-year-olds gained A or grade 7 and above, a slight improvement over last year, while 84.4% gained C or grade 4 and above.
In Wales, 20.2% of grades for 16 year-olds were awarded A or better, and 63.7% of entries gained at least a C, slightly below the 2025 pass rate.
summary: Education experts and school leaders have criticized government plans requiring students who fail GCSE maths and English to retake them, arguing the policy is demotivating and ineffective. Recent data showed only one in seven retaking maths and one in six retaking English achieved a passing grade. While education secretary Lucy Powell defended plans for a new "stepping stone" qualification for students with grade 2 or worse, critics warn the current system risks increasing the number of young people not in education, employment, or training.
key_points: Only one in seven students retaking GCSE maths and one in six retaking English achieved a grade 4 or above this summer.
Education secretary Lucy Powell plans to introduce a new level-one "stepping stone" qualification for students who receive a grade 2 or worse.
School leaders and experts warn that forcing students into repeated GCSE resits is demotivating and fails to address broader issues.
About 620,000 year 11 students failed to reach grade 4 in maths or English and face retaking the exams next year.

title: 'Relentless' GCSE resit cycle 'simply not working', union says
author: Beth Rose
content:
![Students queue to get their results at Llanishen High School on August 20, 2026 in Cardiff, Wales.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/af3e/live/90ab23d0-9cb3-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
- Published
The "relentless" cycle of pupils in England failing and then resitting their GCSEs in maths and English is "simply not working", a leading education union has said.
The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) said a "significant proportion" of students fall short of passing those subjects, and that most who retake those exams "face the miserable experience of falling short once again".
Thursday's results data showed nearly one in four maths and English GCSEs in England were taken by students aged 17 and older, mostly young people resitting exams they had previously failed.
The government said it wanted to stop the "endless treadmill of unnecessary resits".
It said it would introduce a new "stepping stone" qualification from 2028 at Level 1 - one level below GCSEs - for students who do not achieve a pass in GCSE maths or English.
Currently, many courses and jobs remain dependent on students securing GCSE passes in those subjects.
But those that miss the grade can find themselves in a continuing loop of resits as they try and try again to pass.
Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of ASCL, said the fail-resit cycle was like "force feeding" students a "relentless diet of GCSE English and maths".
"This limits their education and career options and is very likely to be a factor in the large number of young people who end up not in employment, education or training," he said.
Pass rates for students aged 17 and older in English and maths are much lower than 16-year-old students taking the exams for the first time, bringing down overall GCSE grades for all ages across England, Wales and Northern Ireland as a result.
While resitting is not a requirement, according to the Department for Education (DfE), colleges will generally enter students into exams when they think they are ready.
For Marianne, from Cambridgeshire, results day has been a "mixed bag" as both of her sons, Tobias and Jake, collected GCSE results.
While Jake achieved a grade 8 in maths, his older brother, Tobias, did not get the pass he wanted after sitting the exam for a fifth time.
![Tobias has long hair and glasses and is standing outdoors in front of rolling countryside under a cloudy, overcast sky.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/00f8/live/69fa1510-9ca5-11f1-a5a0-114ca9d4a1bc.jpg)
Despite picking up good A-level results last week, Tobias is stuck in a GCSE resit loop with maths
"He was very upset," Marianne said.
"He turns up for his lessons, he puts great effort in, there's just something about maths he doesn't get. What do we do now?"
Last week Tobias, collected A-level results in which he achieved a B in history and two Cs in politics and criminology - but his ambitions to apply to university to become a history teacher are on ice without that pass in maths.
"It's horrendous making him keep doing it. I don't think it's fair, the pressure on them to keep resitting it," mum Marriane said.
The new stepping stone qualification would offer an alternative route for students like Tobias to keep moving forward.
Although the details are scant, the DfE said a student could be directed to it once they had sat maths and English GCSE but did not achieve a pass.
It said it would "give students the essential knowledge and skills" before they resit their GCSEs, and then "only be entered into exams when they are ready".
It is hoped it would provide a solution for students like Abdi, 17, from east London, who failed to pass his exams in maths and English for the third time.
"I have to get my retakes right next time, or they won't let me complete my course at college," he said.
"My school has provided extra classes to help prepare for the exams, but you have to be self-disciplined because juggling resits and college is not easy."
![Adbi, with dark afro-style hair holds a crumpled printed document and wears a dark tunic with gold embroidered trimgainst a wall lit by blue LED lights.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/a1ed/live/2ab01a30-9caf-11f1-84cf-fd4cfd9d6c84.png)
Abdi plans to resit his maths and english GCSEs in November after learning he did not pass them for the third time
Catherine Sezen, from the Association of Colleges, said the stepping stone qualification sounded positive, but that it should become an option for students long before they fail their GCSEs.
"We have to look at what happens probably from reception right the way through, because young people who don't achieve very well in their SATs at 11 are really unlikely to achieve a grade 4 at 16."
She said this year's resit figures were "disappointing and slightly demoralising for everybody" but not a "huge surprise".
"I think we're still also seeing the legacy of the pandemic," she said.
"These young people would have been in Years 6, 7 and 8, and so possibly haven't necessarily got the basic foundations in these subjects which are really fundamental."
But the resit cycle is not always an inevitable one.
Amandeep, 17, did not pass her maths or English language GCSEs this time last year.
But on results day on Thursday, the student at Sandwell College, in the West Midlands, found out she had passed with a grade 5.
"I teared up, I thought my patience had paid off," she said.
"It happened for a reason, it was meant for me this year."
Amandeep's results mean she is now able to move on to study a T-level in health and social care.
![Amandeep stands in a college atrium wearing a black varsity-style jacket, with registration tables, pink bunting, and groups of people in the background](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/9288/live/85bb2f50-9ca5-11f1-a5a0-114ca9d4a1bc.jpg)
Amandeep was one of the resit students who managaged to get the grades she needed for her next step in life
While the majority of resit students are aged 17 to 19, some are also mature students.
Wynne Hindle, 52, a grandmother from Sudbury, in Suffolk, celebrated having passed her GCSE maths on Thursday after taking it for a fifth time and achieving a grade 4.
"I was very happy and shocked to pass," she said.
"I just wanted to achieve something and I'm a resilient person."
Hindle, who previously worked as a nanny and nursery nurse, now hopes to work in a school and said it was all "part of a journey".
She said her message to others who might be stuck in the resit cycle is: "Keep at it".
summary: The Association of School and College Leaders has criticized the relentless cycle of students repeatedly failing and resitting GCSE maths and English exams as ineffective and damaging to career options. Data shows nearly one in four maths and English GCSEs in England are taken by students aged 17 and older. In response to the issue, the government plans to introduce a new Level 1 "stepping stone" qualification starting in 2028 for students who do not pass.
key_points: Nearly one in four GCSE maths and English exams in England were taken by students aged 17 and older, mostly consisting of resits.
The Association of School and College Leaders stated that most students who retake exams fall short again, creating a miserable and limiting experience.
The government plans to introduce a new Level 1 "stepping stone" qualification in 2028 to help students who fail GCSE maths or English before they retake the exams.
While many students struggle in the resit loop, some successfully pass after multiple attempts, allowing them to progress to courses or jobs.

title: Academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism suspended by his university
author: Chris Osuh
content:
Nathan Cofnas, the academic who made plagiarism allegations against Prof Jason Arday before his death, has been suspended by a university.
Arday, 41, resigned from his role at the University of Cambridge this month after coverage of Cofnas’s accusations of plagiarism. The allegations, which were not proven in any formal investigation, triggered questions about Arday’s achievements.
There has been stiff criticism of Cambridge over its handling of the affair, but also of the coverage by some media. The university’s chancellor, Chris Smith, described it as a “racist feeding frenzy”. Arday, who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, was found dead in Battersea, south London, on Friday.
![Flowers are tied to the gates along with a photo of Jason Arday](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/7166f637b6c872ffb2089527262bb3ef4ec57e4e/0_0_6000_4000/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The “American anti-woke” blogger Cofnas is a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University’s department of philosophy and moral sciences, according to his website.
In a post on X on Thursday, Cofnas said: “I am under investigation by my university for discriminating against Arday.” He added in a separate post: “I was just suspended by Ghent University. They will almost certainly fire me.”
Ghent University confirmed his suspension after saying they had been “shocked” by Arday’s death and that it “should prompt reflection”, adding that the institution “opposes discrimination, hatred and racism”.
In a joint statement on Wednesday, Ghent University’s rector, Petra De Sutter, and vice-rector, Herwig Reynaert, said: “We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial. However, that freedom is not unlimited.
“It goes hand in hand with responsibility and may be restricted in order to protect the rights of others. For this reason, the university takes the recent public statements made by a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University regarding this matter very seriously.
“Ghent University has decided to take appropriate action within its powers and the applicable framework.”
after newsletter promotion
The rector and vice-rector said that while it was “important to be transparent”, they did not want to “pre-empt any potential decisions at this stage”.
In an update on Thursday, a spokesperson said: “Ghent University formally notified the staff member concerned of the launch of a preliminary disciplinary investigation.
“As part of this process, the university is assessing whether there are sufficient grounds to refer the case to the competent disciplinary body for further consideration. Pending this preliminary investigation, Ghent University has suspended the staff member as a precautionary measure.”
Earlier this week, organisers said more than 30,000 people had attended a vigil for Arday in Trafalgar Square, central London.
Cofnas was sacked from his role at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, in 2024. In blog posts, he had said that, in a meritocracy: “Blacks would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment.” In a piece titled “Don’t Scapegoat Women”, published in January this year, Cofnas claimed “women but not men can get people fired by pointing and crying”.
He added: “To meet de facto quotas, employers have had to reach deeper into the pool of less qualified female candidates. For obvious reasons, affirmative action hires often have a chip on their shoulder. Many of them turn to social justice activism to distract from the fact that they aren’t as good at their job as the straight white men who earned their position based on merit, or weren’t hired at all.”
summary: Nathan Cofnas, the academic who previously made unproven plagiarism allegations against Professor Jason Arday, has been suspended by Ghent University. Arday recently resigned from the University of Cambridge and was later found dead in London. Ghent University officials stated they are launching a preliminary disciplinary investigation following public statements made by Cofnas regarding the matter.
key_points: Nathan Cofnas was suspended by Ghent University as a precautionary measure during a preliminary disciplinary investigation.
Cofnas previously made unproven plagiarism allegations against Professor Jason Arday before Arday's death.
Ghent University's rector and vice-rector stated that academic freedom comes with responsibilities and is not unlimited.
Arday resigned from the University of Cambridge earlier this month and was found dead in south London on Friday.

title: Putin takes aim at UK in anti-Nato game of fear
author: Andrew Rettman
content:
Western Europe has become so used to Russia’s petty violence on its territory that even assassinating a British defence-firm CEO might not give president Vladimir Putin the “shock” he needs to reassert authority, amid daily humiliations in the Ukraine war.
US intelligence warnings that he was planning to attack a Baltic state or Poland in the “coming months” to fix his strongman image prompted a snap Nato drill involving some 50 military aircraft in the Baltic Sea on Wednesday (20 August), in order to flex deterrence.
But Putin’s foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, also renewed threats on Tuesday of a strike on the UK, because it had supplied long-range drones to Kyiv.
Lavrov spoke of “consequences”, but Kremlin propagandists, Vladimir Kornilov and Vladimir Solovyov, went on TV urging Russian people to get behind anything and everything, up to a nuclear strike.
And for Artem Voitovych, from the Olgian Strategies defence consultancy firm in Ukraine, there was another reason why a Russian escalation with Nato was becoming more likely – China.
“Chinese president Xi Jinping also wants to see how Nato would deal with a direct attack, due to his own agenda in the South China Sea,” he said, referring to Beijing’s territorial claims against Western allies in Asia, including Taiwan, as well as Japanese and Philippine islands.
“Now, they [the Chinese] have their own clown [Putin], their own puppet, to do it for them,” Voitovych said, given Russia’s dependence on Chinese tech-support in the Ukraine war.
And if Putin did outflank the US intelligence warning by going after the UK instead of a Baltic target, he had various options.
The most realistic ones, for defence experts, would be designed to fall below Nato's threshold for a united 'Article 5' armed response.
These were, in order of escalation: harassing British diplomats in Moscow; a 'deniable' cyber-strike on vital British infrastructure (such as energy facilities) or economic interests; cutting UK undersea telecommunications cables; sabotage attacks on British warehouses, trains, or ports shipping weapons to Ukraine; and the assassination of a British defence-firm CEO.
"Psychological pressure on diplomats could involve KGB-type, almost schoolboy-type tricks, such as moving things around in their flats when they're not home, to show that they've been visited," said Katia Glod from the New Eurasian Strategies Centre (NEST) think-tank in the UK, referring to Russia's Soviet-era spy service, which is now called the FSB.
Russia has already carried out cyber attacks on UK car maker Jaguar-Land Rover and retailer Marks & Spencer, halting production lines and online shopping services.
It has cut cables in the Baltic Sea and its agents burned down a warehouse storing Ukraine-bound equipment in east London in 2024, as well as starting fires in facilities in Estonia (last Saturday), Germany, and Poland in the past two years.
It has plotted to kill two German defence CEOs (Rheinmetall chief Armin Papperger and Donaustahl boss Stefan Thumann), German and US intelligence has said, and for Jamie Shea, a former senior Nato official, it was "highly likely" a British one could be targeted as well.
"Russia has infiltrated a number of GRU [military intelligence] hit squads into the UK for this purpose … and there's no reason why only German CEOs would be targeted," said Shea, who now teaches war studies at Exeter University in the UK.
But the problem with these options, from Putin's point of view, Shea added, was that they were all "happening already", meaning that Nato security services were ready for them, while the Western and Russian general publics had become blasé.
"Western intelligence services are clearly now on high alert to track and stop Russian plots," said Shea.
"It would be just more of the same," said Glod.
![](https://static.euobserver.com/2026/08/52524711052_0dbb51955d_o-2400x1600.jpg)
'Shock effect'
Katja Bego, from British think-tank Chatham House, also said: "They [the Russians] need a shock effect, to come up with something new".
"They feel backed into a corner and need to signal both domestically and internationally that they have an answer to this [Ukraine's drone strikes deep in Russian territory]," she said.
A more hawkish option could be to arm and pay a proxy force in Iraq or Syria to kill British soldiers stationed in the Middle East, said NEST's Glod.
summary: Russian officials and propagandists have renewed threats against the UK over its supply of long-range drones to Kyiv, while US intelligence warns of potential Russian attacks on Baltic states or Poland. Experts suggest that if Russia escalates against the UK, it may use sub-threshold tactics such as cyber-attacks, sabotage, or targeting defense executives. However, analysts note that these methods are already familiar to Western security services and may lack the desired shock value for Vladimir Putin.
key_points: Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov threatened the UK with consequences over long-range drone supplies to Kyiv, while Kremlin propagandists advocated for severe escalation including a nuclear strike.
US intelligence warnings of a potential Russian attack on a Baltic state or Poland prompted a snap NATO military drill in the Baltic Sea.

Experts believe potential Russian actions against the UK could fall below NATO's Article 5 threshold, including cyber-attacks, cutting undersea cables, infrastructure sabotage, or assassinating defense-firm CEOs.
Russia has already conducted prior sabotage and cyber-attacks across Europe, including burning down a Ukraine-bound equipment warehouse in London in 2024.
China reportedly wants to observe how NATO reacts to direct attacks due to its own regional territorial agendas, using Russia's dependence on Chinese tech-support.

title: What Harry and Meghan’s move back to the UK could mean for their tax bill
author: Madeleine Ross; Steve Bird
content:
![Prince Harry and Meghan attending UK trials for the Invictus Games in Australia, in 2018](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000470079451_17872433757500_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq15XUfPwoY7svuJOpueeorV5NUcTKNHKqy85KLqtvPLE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Prince Harry and Meghan attending UK trials for the Invictus Games in Australia, in 2018](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000470079451_17872433757500_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq15XUfPwoY7svuJOpueeorV5NUcTKNHKqy85KLqtvPLE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
As the Duke and Duchess of Sussex prepare to relocate back to the UK, they will be keenly aware of the risk of unwelcome attention from the taxman.
With an international property and investment portfolio, millions of pounds in the bank from lucrative Netflix deals, as well as money bequeathed by the late Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother and Diana, Princess of Wales, their estimated £48m net worth is bound to be of interest to HMRC.
Within hours of The Telegraph revealing Prince Harry and Meghan were planning a return to Britain, there was speculation they could benefit from a tax break offered to those who have stayed away for more than five years.
But the complexities of the US and British tax systems – as well as the perks and perils of being multi-millionaires – will mean their financial advisers will have their work cut out.
How their financial outlook has changed
Inevitably, the devil will be in the details of their financial affairs since 2020, when they announced they were leaving the UK and stopped receiving financial support from the Royal family.
The couple were clear that Prince Harry’s inheritance from his mother was the reason they were able to move to the United States. Now, six years on, their finances are apparently robust enough for them to retain a £10.3m property in the US, a £6.3m home in Portugal, as well as setting up home in England.
In his 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, shortly after leaving Britain, the Duke hinted at how they would initially tackle the financial challenges ahead.
“I’ve got what my mum left me, and without that, we would not have been able to do this,” he said, sitting beside his then-pregnant wife in the Santa Barbara sunshine.
“It’s like she saw it coming and she’s been with us through this whole process.”
Since that interview, their financial outlook has certainly changed – with the couple’s affairs further complicated by a raft of US investments, entertainment deals and a jam-making business. It means the English and American couple will have to work out carefully how far they sever their links with the US.
While the family is moving their base to the UK – and Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet are to start school here in a matter of weeks – reports suggest they won’t cut all their ties to California.
Property portfolio brings complications
The couple are likely to keep the £10.3m 9-bedroom and 16-bathroom Californian mansion, bought in 2020, and the Portugal home at the golf and leisure resort in Costa Terra, south of Lisbon, which they acquired in 2023 for £6.3m.
That international property portfolio complicates their tax status (keeping that Montecito home will mean a property tax bill of approximately £110,000 a year to be paid in California).
The Duchess’s American citizenship also lands them with an extra bill. Because the US taxes its citizens on their worldwide income, no matter where they live, the Duchess will probably still have to pay American taxes, unless she relinquishes her citizenship.
To do this, as a multi-millionaire, she would have to pay an “exit fee” to the US government. If she remains a US citizen, the couple will have to do an annual audit of their finances to work out how much tax is owed in each country.
![The entrance to a private road leading to the couple's Montecito home](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498899257_17872430799920_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqyuLFFzXshuGqnr8zPdDWXhbQKbwj1ZsnNMhuR7O6ySI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Jennifer McNally, partner at tax firm Crowe, said: “The tax position is unlikely to be straightforward, and it may be that Harry and Meghan’s positions are not identical.”
Experts warned that the couple could even have to pay tax in both the UK and the US this year, as a result of moving halfway through the tax year.
Ms McNally said: “As the UK and US tax years are not aligned, they may be considered dual UK and US tax resident for a period or indefinitely.”
Complicating matters further is Portugal – where the couple own a home. Portugal offers those who have invested £215,000 in property or businesses the opportunity to live there.
If they spent more than 183 days a year there and their main family and business ties were Portuguese, they would become tax residents there, rather than in the UK.
![The family in the pool at their Portuguese property](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000496219366_17872437341190_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqGnvE-VNXSbhg1qqFSd7eP_4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
But the fact the couple intend to put their children in a British school makes it unlikely.
Portugal also offers a so-called golden visa for wealthy individuals who invest a minimum of €250,000 (£214,000) in the country, allowing them to come and go as they please and travel freely within the EU. It is not known if the Duke and Duchess have taken advantage of this, but it does not come with any tax breaks.
Their foreign homes will also mean they have to pay more in stamp duty if they buy another property in the UK. Second-home owners pay higher stamp duty rates, bringing the total tax bill on a £10m house to £1.6m.
The tax breaks that won’t come their way
Meanwhile, the Duchess is no longer able to be a non-dom for tax purposes, because of changes introduced in April last year.
She will also be unlikely to benefit from a replacement tax break for foreigners because she has lived in the UK in the past decade.
The “Foreign Income and Gains” perk – “Fig” for short – offers 100 per cent tax relief on foreign income and assets and can be claimed for four years.
However, having lived in Frogmore Cottage in Windsor after her royal marriage in 2018 – so, within a 10-year time limit – she is barred from this tax break.
![Living at Frogmore Cottage until 2018 makes Meghan ineligible for certain tax breaks](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000193875283_17872437275360_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq5UkwdrNdLmi7F8HLRonNAIX55UGE1-QmdhXTcMmlCx4.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Dhana Sabanathan, a tax partner at law firm Michelmores, said: “If they had remained non-UK tax resident for 10 consecutive tax years before returning, they could have enjoyed relief on their non-UK income and gains for the first four years of their return.”
The couple’s return from the US after less than 10 years away could also mean a bigger inheritance tax bill on their Californian and Portuguese estates.
Ms Sabanathan said: “Staying away for 10 years could have also enabled Harry to protect his non-UK assets from UK inheritance tax.”
But the Duchess may well be able to take advantage of the change of non-dom rules in 2025, which mean that wealthy foreigners pay lower rates of tax on money brought into the UK until 2028. If she took money from her US portfolio and invested it in the UK, she would only pay 12 per cent tax, rather than the 45 per cent top income tax rate.
The Duchess has a considerable US investment portfolio. Since 2020, she has put money into Clevr Blends, a wellness drinks company, and invested in the luxury handbag company Cesta Collective, as well as a haircare company Highbrow Hippie, a menopause startup called Midi Health and an AI-powered fashion company called OneOff.
In 2021, the couple announced they had joined investment firm Ethic, which now manages a $10bn (£7.4bn) fund, as “impact partners”, ploughing in some of their own money.
![The Duchess of Sussex making her own jam in her home in Montecito](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000447754644_17872440338910_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqkZdGXfzOPVSbO-9sH583RKS-UyG44at75VysheuSlvg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The Duchess has also launched a lifestyle company of her own, As Ever, selling $12 (£9) jams and $64 (£47) scented candles.
But if she chose to relocate the company – which was earlier known as American Riviera Orchard – to the UK, or open a British office, the Duchess would have to register the company here, and file tax returns.
Capital gains conundrum
The timing of their return more than five full years after their exit could mean a lower capital gains liability as investors and entrepreneurs.
Those who stay out of the UK for more than five years, as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have done, will not face capital gains bills on assets they owned before their departure.
This rule is in place to stop wealthy business people from moving out of the UK for short periods, only to sell shares or holdings while overseas, and then return without paying a penny of tax on the deals.
![Some speculate that the family's timing of leaving California may have been influenced by tax issues](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000453992647_17872435027110_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-f615DnU9pEmsfZIAMglH89luWBnPl6Sn_iGFrIRcxE.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Nimesh Shah, of accountancy firm Blick Rothenberg, said: “It might be a complete coincidence, but leaving in March 2020 just at the end of the old tax year, and coming back this year. That’s a beautiful period for tax purposes.”
He said: “From my perspective, you wouldn’t advise it any better than that. It’s the perfect timeframe to be outside of these rules.”
However, the Sussexes would have paid tax in California if they sold assets while over there that they had previously acquired in the UK.
Because California’s capital gains tax is higher than Britain’s – amounting to as much as 37.1 per cent, compared with 24 per cent in this country – they would have been unlikely to face a UK tax bill upon their return in any case.
Harry’s family riches
Prince Harry was the beneficiary of considerable inheritances before his marriage.
Diana, Princess of Wales, left her sons the bulk of £12,966,022, after an £8,502,330 inheritance tax bill was paid.
In her will, she stipulated that her estate, which comprised stocks and shares, jewellery, cash from her £17m divorce settlement, dresses and other personal belongings, should be held in trust to be shared equally between Prince Harry and Prince William.
The will stated that her sons would be entitled to their entire share of the capital on reaching the age of 25, but after her death the executors changed the terms of the will to raise the inheritance age to 30.
The money was shrewdly invested by royal advisers which saw it grow to an estimated £20m by the time Harry could access it in 2014.
Another income stream came from the late Queen Mother. In 1994, she had set up a trust containing around £19m for her great grandchildren – which included William and Harry.
![Diana, Princess Of Wales, Prince William and Prince Harry visiting a theme park](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498851838_17872434823930_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqv3hxuICTza90rxjOncu1SDDAfwB3lrD912jpbltkVmM.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
It is understood the brothers split £6m of this trust at the age of 21, with Harry taking the majority of that cash to apparently “compensate for not becoming sovereign”.
When they reached 40, it was also suggested they were allowed to split another £8m. However, the other grandchildren were expected to receive a portion of that sum.
There is perhaps one other fortunate element to the timing of their planned return.
The capital gains tax rate in the US would have been far higher than the UK’s current rate of 24 per cent. But Andy Burnham has been rumoured to favour an increase in capital gains taxes.
So the couple may have a golden window within which to sell off assets – for example, so they can buy a British house – both avoiding the higher US capital gains rates and dodging any proposed increase the Treasury may be planning.
As is invariably the case with personal tax matters, HMRC declined to comment.
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are planning a relocation back to the UK, which presents a complex set of international tax implications across the UK, US, and Portugal. While their timing of staying away for over five years may protect them from certain capital gains liabilities, their property portfolio, business investments, and prior UK residency mean they will face mixed tax outcomes. Financial experts note that navigating dual residency, US citizenship obligations, and ineligible tax breaks will make their financial return far from straightforward.
key_points: The couple retains a multi-million-pound international property portfolio, including homes in California and Portugal, alongside their planned UK residence.
Meghan Markle's US citizenship means she will likely continue to owe taxes on worldwide income unless she formally relinquishes her citizenship and pays an exit fee.
Having lived in the UK at Frogmore Cottage within the last decade makes Meghan ineligible for certain foreign income tax breaks and could increase inheritance tax exposure.
Their return after more than five years away may protect them from capital gains liabilities on assets they owned prior to their 2020 departure.

title: UK, France, Germany, Italy and Canada condemn Israel's West Bank settlement project
author: Ruth Comerford; Tom McArthur
content:
![Wide view of a highway near the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim in the area of the so-called E1 project in Jerusalem, in the occupied West Bank, taken in February 2026.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/980/cpsprodpb/e405/live/b1ef1300-9be4-11f1-ba30-ddd78081057f.jpg)
File photo of the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim in the occupied West Bank next to the so-called E1 project in East Jerusalem, taken in February 2026
- Published
Israel's plans to open up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank have sparked fresh condemnation by major Western powers.
In a joint statement, the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Canada called the decision "unacceptable", external and urged Israel to "retract the plans immediately".
All settlements are illegal under international law and, under international pressure, Israel held off for decades on plans to build in E1 to the east of Jerusalem.
Many of its allies and Palestinians argued this development would deal a major blow to hopes of a two-state solution, effectively cutting the West Bank in two and isolating east Jerusalem.
"At a time of grave instability in the West Bank with unprecedented levels of violence by settlers against civilians, and serious restrictions on the Palestinian economy, this decision is even more concerning", the statement from the European allies and Canada published on Thursday said.
"Not only will they [the plans] take us further from peace, but they further undermine Israel's international standing," the statement added.
In a separate statement, the UN secretary general also said the E1 plan posed an "existential threat" to a contiguous Palestinian state - and so did Belgium's foreign minister.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's condemnation earlier on Thursday had drawn "ouright" rejection by the Israeli foreign minister.
![Map showing Israeli settlements and built-up Palestinian areas in the West Bank around Jerusalem â highlighting the E1 settlement in red. Other Israeli settlements are marked in blue and Palestinian areas in light purple. The municipal boundary of Jerusalem is outlined in red. An inset map shows the regionâs location within Israel and Jordan.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/48fd/live/00ce0160-790a-11f0-a20f-3b86f375586a.png)
Despite an Israeli court challenge to the plans by Bedouin Palestinians living in the area and Israeli peace groups, on Wednesday the Israeli housing ministry issued a tender for 1,234 of the 3,401 housing units approved by the Israeli government last August.
It covers about 12 sq km (4.6 sq miles) between East Jerusalem and the settlement of Maale Adumim.
At the time of their unveiling, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich - an ultranationalist and settler - said the idea of a Palestinian state was "being erased".
The deadline for bids is 19 October, just days before Israel's general election on 27 October, making it much harder for any future government to overturn any tenders issued.
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
Despite the fierce international opposition, successive Israeli governments have allowed settlements to grow.
However, expansion has risen sharply since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu returned to power in late 2022 at the head of a right-wing, pro-settler coalition, as well as the start of the Gaza war, triggered by Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
Opponents of the E1 project have warned that it would effectively block the establishment of a Palestinian state because it would cut off the north of the West Bank from the south, and prevent the development in the centre of a contiguous Palestinian urban area connecting Ramallah, East Jerusalem and Bethlehem.
- ![Wide view of a highway near the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim in the area of the so-called E1 project in Jerusalem, in the occupied West Bank, taken in February 2026.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/980/cpsprodpb/e405/live/b1ef1300-9be4-11f1-ba30-ddd78081057f.jpg)
  - Published1 August
 ![Yehuda Shimon, a large, bearded man wearing glasses, gestures with his hand](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/678b/live/ea29f390-8c56-11f1-b8ee-9b3c26ad07bb.jpg)
summary: Major Western powers, including the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and Canada, have strongly condemned Israel's plans to open tenders for building settlement homes in the E1 area of the occupied West Bank. Critics warn that the project would cut the West Bank in two, isolate East Jerusalem, and severely damage the prospects of a two-state solution. Despite international opposition and legal challenges, the Israeli housing ministry issued a tender for over 1,200 housing units.
key_points: The UK, France, Germany, Italy, and Canada issued a joint statement calling Israel's E1 settlement plans unacceptable and urging an immediate retraction.
The Israeli housing ministry issued tenders for 1,234 housing units between East Jerusalem and the Maale Adumim settlement.
Opponents and international allies warn the E1 project threatens a contiguous Palestinian state by cutting the West Bank in half.
All settlements are considered illegal under international law, though Israel disputes this.

title: Harry and Meghan: the key moments, conflicts and controversies since their US move
author: Guardian staff reporter
content:
Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, will reportedly return to Britain after six years of living in the US, a move that triggered a long period of strained relations with King Charles III, the Prince and Princess of Wales and others in the royal family.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex and their two children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are expected to relocate to the UK this month.
The family will reportedly live at a private, non-royal residence outside London, but they plan to maintain their home in California and another property in Portugal.
Here is a timeline charting the major moments since the family moved to the US in 2020.
2020
January
Harry and Meghan announce they will step down as working royals. The decision comes after a period marked by open warfare with the media over claimed intrusion and bullying.
“We intend to step back as ‘senior’ members of the royal family and work to become financially independent, while continuing to fully support Her Majesty the Queen,” the couple say.
June
The couple moves to Meghan’s native California, settling in the wealthy seaside enclave of Montecito near Santa Barbara. Media reports put the 2020 purchase price of their 16-bedroom home at $14.7m.
2021
March
Harry and Meghan are interviewed by Oprah Winfrey on CBS.
In a series of stunning revelations, Meghan accuses the royal family of fostering an atmosphere of racial hostility so intense that she came close to suicide while pregnant with Archie. Meghan also claims members of the royal family had openly expressed concerns about how dark Archie’s skin would be.
In response, Queen Elizabeth issues a statement: “The issues raised, particularly that of race, are concerning. While some recollections may vary, they are taken very seriously and will be addressed by the family privately.”
![Prince Harry and Meghan are interviewed by Oprah Winfrey](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5edd035b0acac397640f40589f799e9945762ffb/0_0_3500_2627/master/3500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
June
The couple’s second child, Lilibet, is born in California. She is named after the family nickname for the Queen.
2022
August
Harry files a lawsuit against the Home Office and the Metropolitan police over his security arrangements in the UK since he stepped down as a working royal.
September
While Harry and Meghan are visiting London, Queen Elizabeth dies. They stay in Britain for her funeral. Ahead of the funeral, Harry and Meghan join William and Kate in meeting wellwishers outside Windsor castle.
![Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, attend the state funeral and burial of Queen Elizabeth](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1158b4c9e21b3f552cfb23a1dfb032821e161b2b/0_0_4576_3074/master/4576.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
2023
January
Harry publishes his memoir Spare, detailing his relationship with his family.
Among the most notable revelations, Harry recounts what he says was a physical attack by William as their relationship fell apart over his marriage to Meghan. Describing a confrontation at his London home in 2019, Harry says William called Meghan “difficult”, “rude” and “abrasive”.
May
Harry attends his father’s coronation alone after Meghan and his young children opted not to attend and to remain in California. He walks into Westminster Abbey alone and is seated two rows behind William.
![Prince Harry at the coronation ceremony of King Charles III in Westminster Abbey](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/456937fe5376fa01de79b121c59174bde6c9eed5/0_0_6000_4000/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
![Prince Harry departs Westminster Abbey during the Coronation of King Charles](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b710c127ff23fb0f5fe5b1f0539c76bfdefeae6f/0_0_5732_3822/master/5732.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
2024
February
Buckingham Palace announces King Charles has been diagnosed with a form of cancer and will postpone public engagements to undergo treatment. Harry is photographed arriving at his father’s London residence for a brief meeting.
2025
April
Appearing at a high court appeal over the changes to his police protection, Harry’s lawyer warns his “life is at stake”. The Home Office, defending the appeal, says that Harry’s “bespoke” security arrangements are designed to accommodate his “unique set of circumstances”.
May
Harry loses the legal challenge over his security arrangements, allowing the government to proceed with a “bespoke”, and cheaper, level of protection for his family. Three senior judges reject Harry’s claim he had been “singled out” for “inferior treatment”.
Later that same day, Harry says he wants reconciliation with his family, explaining that his father no longer speaks to him due to the security row.
Speaking in California, Harry says: “I can’t see a world in which I would be bringing my wife and children back to the UK at this point … I miss the UK. And it’s really quite sad I won’t be able to show my children my homeland.”
August
Harry and Meghan sign a fresh deal with Netflix. The couple, who struck a five-year deal in 2020 reportedly worth $100m (£78m), had collaborated with Netflix on a number of projects. Media reports had suggested that poor viewing figures for some of the projects meant that Netflix would not extend the deal.
![Harry and Meghan on a Netflix show](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/7d0ab19bfa3f0ba7619134002faf68f442846c91/404_24_1961_1307/master/1961.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
2026
June
Buckingham Palace says Harry will not be staying at the palace during a visit to London, despite the Duke of Sussex’s team earlier announcing publicly he had accepted an invitation to do so.
July
Harry and other high-profile British figures lose their privacy lawsuits against the Daily Mail’s publisher. Harry and the group face a legal bill of up to £50m after losing their case.
![Prince Harry arrives at the Royal Courts of Justice in London](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/35b8b876fc218baf5a79485d8f195a0f896855f9/0_0_4996_3546/master/4996.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
July
King Charles meets in private with Harry and his family, having not seen the children for four years. According to reports, Harry, Meghan, Archie and Lilibet were hosted by Charles and Queen Camilla at the king’s private residence in Gloucestershire.
August
The couple reportedly plan to move with Archie and Lilibet from California to Britain for an extended period. The children will begin school there in September, but the couple will not return to royal duties, according to reports.
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are reportedly planning to relocate from California back to Britain with their two children after six years of living in the US. Their move follows a turbulent period marked by strained relations with the royal family, legal battles over security, and media controversies. Despite returning to the UK to live at a private residence, they plan to maintain their properties in California and Portugal and will not return to working royal duties.
key_points: Prince Harry and Meghan are reportedly moving back to Britain with their children after six years in the US.
The family will live at a private residence outside London while maintaining homes in California and Portugal.
Their time in the US was marked by major conflicts, including a 2021 Oprah interview alleging racism and Harry's 2023 memoir detailing family rifts.
Harry lost a legal challenge regarding his UK security arrangements and faced setbacks in privacy lawsuits against the Daily Mail's publisher.
King Charles met privately with Harry, Meghan, and their children in July 2026, marking a step toward reconciliation after years of strained relations.

title: Harry and Meghan’s security funding on UK return is private matter, Burnham says
author: Caroline Davies
content:
Security arrangements for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex while living in the UK are a “private matter”, Andy Burnham has said, after news that Harry and Meghan intend to relocate to Britain from the US this month.
The UK prime minister refused to be drawn on security funding, saying: “This is a private matter. It’s a matter for Harry and Meghan, and we wish them well in the moves that they’re making.”
The couple, who moved to North America more than six years ago, will make their home in a non-royal residence outside London. Their children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are already enrolled at British schools and due to start in September.
King Charles, who was told of the decision on Sunday, is said to welcome the opportunity to see more of his family in a personal capacity. There will be no change in their status as private individuals and non-working royals who do not carry out royal engagements. There is said to be no half-in, half-out option.
Security funding has been a long-running source of tension between Harry and the Home Office, the government department that would decide on such measures. The Times has reported that there are no plans to provide the couple and their family with taxpayer-funded armed protection.
Last year, Harry lost a protracted court battle over what security he and his family would be entitled to while visiting the UK after automatic taxpayer-funded security was withdrawn when the couple stood down as working royals.
During the legal challenge against the Home Office, Harry said in his witness statement: “The UK is my home. The UK is central to the heritage of my children and a place I want them to feel at home as much as where they live at the moment in the US. That cannot happen if it’s not possible to keep them safe when they are on UK soil. I cannot put my wife in danger like that and, given my experiences in life, I am reluctant to unnecessarily put myself in harm’s way too.”
A senior judge later ruled that his “sense of grievance” over the decision about his security was not sufficient as grounds for an appeal.
The prince later told the BBC that he “can’t see a world” in which he would bring his family to the UK.
He was understood to be already awaiting a fresh risk-management assessment, but his new circumstances may now have to be factored in. Decisions on the security of royals are taken by the royal and VIP executive committee, an independent body overseen by the Home Office. The prime minister does not decide about security for the royal family.
After the couple left the UK, Harry was granted a “bespoke” security arrangement. He may no longer qualify for the level of protection he previously had as a working royal but he is a high-profile figure and former military serviceman who has served in Afghanistan, which may be considered in any assessment.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “The UK government’s protective security system is rigorous and proportionate. It is our long-standing policy not to provide detailed information on those arrangements, as doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals’ security.”
In the US, the Sussexes paid for their own private security team.
![Prince Harry and Meghan react to a crowd of people taking photos of the couple on their phones](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/50433cc3f085face8b2018017b5f18395137cfb5/0_0_6000_4001/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
There has been no statement from the Sussexes on why they are choosing to return to the UK, but a source close to them said they had had a great time during their visit in July, and that “stars are aligning with work” to make this a good time to move. This may include Harry’s Invictus Games, which are to be held in Birmingham next year.
The couple intend to retain their properties in Montecito, California, and in Portugal. Meghan is expected to run her lifestyle brand As Ever from the UK, but it is not yet known whether she will begin undertaking charity visits as a non-working royal or embark on other ventures.
Harry has recently made it clear that he would like to spend more time with his father, who has cancer. Next year also marks the 30th anniversary of the death of his mother, Diana, which will include commemorations and events in the UK. Harry and his family stayed at home of Diana’s family, the Spencers, in Althorp, Northamptonshire, during their visit to the UK last month.
A YouGov poll of 5,810 adults carried out the day after the Sussex’s surprise news, showed 33% believe Harry and Meghan should not return to the UK, while 45% do not know. Less than a quarter (21%) are in favour of the Sussexes relocating to the UK.
summary: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex intend to relocate from the US to a non-royal residence outside London this month, with their children enrolled in British schools starting in September. Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated that security arrangements are a private matter, while reports indicate there are no plans to provide taxpayer-funded armed protection. King Charles reportedly welcomes the move, though the couple will remain private individuals and non-working royals without a half-in, half-out option.
key_points: Harry and Meghan plan to relocate back to the UK from the US with their children.
The UK prime minister stated that security funding for the couple is a private matter.
Reports indicate there are no plans to provide taxpayer-funded armed protection for the family.
The couple will retain their status as private individuals and non-working royals.
King Charles was informed of the decision and welcomes the opportunity to see more of his family.

title: Tinder conman from Denbighshire jailed for taking Â£68,000 from victims
author: Sarah Easedale
content:
![Mugshot of Joseph Gibson.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/d8cf/live/05eda8f0-9c89-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Joseph Gibson told his victims lies including that he had cancer and was ex-special forces
- Published
A fraudster who claimed to be a special forces soldier-turned multimillionaire cancer patient has been sentenced to more than three years in prison.
Joseph Gibson, 35, took almost Â£68,000 from his four victims, two of whom he had met on dating app Tinder, and convinced one they were in a relationship.
Gibson, from Penbryn Nant, in Ruthin, Denbighshire, lied that he had been worth hundreds of millions of pounds, had served in the Special Boat Service, and owned yachts.
He was sentenced to three years and two months at Bristol Crown Court on Thursday, after pleading guilty to four charges of fraud by false representation.
A proceeds of crime hearing, to recover his assets to repay his victims will take place in March.
Joseph Gibson was sentenced to three years and two months
The court heard one victim was persuaded to send Gibson money for business opportunities, hospital expenses and online trading.
She lost more than Â£5,600 and said she had suffered "anxiety and emotional distress".
Another, known as SC, handed over more than Â£30,000 when Gibson claimed he could make substantial returns through investments and trading.
She lost Â£21,000 after getting only about Â£9,700 back and said she had been left "heavily in debt".
Another, JH, invested on the back of Gibson's claims he was a successful businessman.
She gave him Â£28,000 and got Â£10,000 back and said it had affected her relationships with her children.
The fourth victim, a retired super yacht captain known as PH, invested Â£23,350 and said he had suffered "severe" emotional impact.
In text messages released after the case, Gibson claimed he had homes in Sandbanks, Bath, Dubai, Singapore and Mayfair in London, as well as 21 rental properties.
He wrote: "Mate I have everything I want, I have amazing houses, cars, boats, helicopters."
Gibson also said he had made Â£1.1m through financial trading, adding: "I am trading a five million account on my phone from a hospital bed."
In one exchange, he asked a victim about their preference for clothing and shoe brands.
After being asked the spending limit, Gibson replied: "In January I was valued at 440m if you need me."
Gibson's barrister had asked Judge Jaron Crooknorth to defer sentencing, saying it would give him time to earn money with which to repay the victims.
But the prosecution raised concerns over his finances and his credibility, saying there had been hundreds of thousands of pounds going through his accounts, but it had been spent on cars and overseas travel.
Crooknorth told Gibson his offending was "serious, sophisticated and sustained" and had involved deception from his "first contact" with his victims.
He said between July 2020 and October 2021, Gibson used false names, had invented business opportunities, and used fake bank statements to show apparent substantial wealth to persuade them to hand money over.
"Joseph Gibson, you are simply a fraudster," Crooknorth said.
"It has taken years for you to admit that.
"Pity those who have had the misfortune to have you come into their lives, prey on their affections, steal their money, steal their goals and fracture their relationships."
![Joseph Gibson wearing a dark suit and white shirt leaves court.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/85c5/live/fac6e4d0-9cad-11f1-84cf-fd4cfd9d6c84.jpg)
Gibson was sentenced to three years and two months in prison
The judge said Gibson had been of previous good character and admitted his offending, albeit shortly before his trial.
He added that the defendant would get little reduction in his sentence for remorse.
"You are sorry for the position you have found yourself in," Crooknorth said.
He told the court he had Â£40,000 in savings but it emerged he had only Â£15,000.
Gibson told Crooknorth he could save Â£5,000 per month for compensation and asked for his sentence to be deferred for a further nine months to fully repay his victims.
The judge said: "You have tried to persuade this court that you have more money than you have. You have not shown evidence of that money to me.
"You have sought to deceive this court into believing that you had it."
He said the victims had suffered "significant financial and emotional harm" as a result, with some left heavily in debt and with damaged relationships.
The judge said Gibson had previously tried to persuade the court he had not deliberately deceived the victims, but said the evidence had shown "deception was central" to his offending.
He said that there was little mitigation other than he had no previous convictions and had expressed some remorse, and he said that only immediate custody was appropriate.
Lead investigator Jenny Williams, of Avon and Somerset Police said: "Joseph Gibson is a confident and manipulative man who developed an extensive web of lies for his own personal gain.
"The impact of fraud on victims can often be profound and long-lasting, and those duped by Gibson have been left with significant debt, a loss of trust and the difficult task of rebuilding their lives.
"His deception has left his victims struggling to come to terms with the extent of his dishonesty."
summary: Joseph Gibson, a 35-year-old fraudster from Denbighshire, was sentenced to three years and two months in prison after pleading guilty to four charges of fraud by false representation. He conned four victims out of nearly £68,000 by lying about being a multimillionaire cancer patient, former special forces soldier, and successful businessman. The judge described his crimes as serious, sophisticated, and sustained, noting that his victims suffered significant financial and emotional harm.
key_points: Joseph Gibson was sentenced to three years and two months in prison at Bristol Crown Court.
He stole nearly £68,000 from four victims, two of whom he met on Tinder.
Gibson lied about having cancer, serving in the Special Boat Service, and owning vast wealth including yachts and properties.
A proceeds of crime hearing will take place in March to recover assets to repay the victims.

title: Asylum seekers told rape and harassment illegal in UK in new Home Office booklet
author: Jennifer McKiernan
content:
Asylum seekers told rape and harassment illegal in UK in new Home Office booklet
![Home Office The image is of a cropped poster with a pink background and the Home Office logo. In the top right hand corner, a label reads: Asylum Consequences of Behaviour. In large font, the poster reads "it is illegal to harass people" and in smaller print below, text reads: "In the UK, everyone has the right to feel safe in public. You must never: Make sexual comments to strangers, even as a compliment."](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/b4a0/live/b9488090-9c71-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png.webp) Home Office
Asylum seekers have been told that rape, sexual harassment and domestic abuse are illegal in the UK, in guidance for new arrivals published by the Home Office.
A nine-page online booklet covers respect in public, sex and consent, and gender equality, with guidance on how UK laws and customs may be different from their home countries.
The Conservatives said any asylum seekers breaking UK law should be deported and Reform said the publication showed the government "knows that they are a menace".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the government had "a very clear principle that if you break UK law, you will be removed from the country".
He said the number of removals of illegal immigrants from the UK "are significantly up" and that he was working to ensure that foreign national offenders are removed from the prison system.
He added: "It follows that if we're taking this approach, it's made explicitly clear what the UK law is and what the societal norms of the UK are and that's why this approach is being taken."
The booklet sets out how asylum seekers must understand UK law, because the consequences of breaking the law mean "you could get in trouble with the police, lose your asylum support, or it could affect your asylum claim."
A section on gender explains that women in the UK have equal rights to men, and do not need the permission from a husband, father, brother or any other man to do things like work, study, travel, or make decisions.
Another section on sex and consent sets out how both people must agree to sex or sexual contact of any kind, and consent cannot be given if someone is asleep, drunk, or unable to respond.
"If you have sex with someone who does not want to, this is called rape. Rape is a serious crime," the document says.
"It is still rape if: You are married to the person or in a relationship. They agreed once, but changed their mind."
![Home Office Two pages from Home Office guidance for asylum seekers. The first one says "Domestic abuse is illegal. In the UK, it is illegal to hurt, threaten or control your partner or family. This includes: hitting, pushing or any physical violence, threatening or verbal abuse, controlling their money or where they go, honour-based violence or abuse."
