The second one says: "In the UK, both people must say 'yes' to sex. This is called consent. If you have sex with someone with someone who does not want to it is called rape. Rape is a serious crime. It is still rape if: you are married to the person or in a relationship, they agreed once, but changed their mind."](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/43bb/live/14fc69c0-9c71-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.png.webp) Home Office
And a section headed Respect in Public outlines how it is not acceptable to whistle or make kissing noises at people on the street, nor "make sexual comments to someone, even if you think it is a compliment".
The guidance also contains contact details for organisations for victims and those seeking help with the issues raised.
The Home Office spokesman added: "Returns of failed asylum seekers have reached their highest level since 2010 under this government."
The latest government figures show nearly 70,000 illegal migrants and foreign criminals have been returned or deported from the UK since Labour came to power in July 2024.
The BBC understands nearly 10,000 foreign criminals, including murderers and rapists, have been removed since the last election – a 36% increase on the previous 21 months.
![Home Office Two pages from Home Office guidance for asylum seekers, the first one says: "It is illegal to harass people. In the UK, everyone has the right to feel safe in public. You must never: make sexual comments to strangers, even as a compliment, approach someone repeatedly if they are not interested, follow someone or block their path." The second one says: "Do not photograph or film people in public. In the UK, you should not take pictures or videos of someone without their permission. This includes taking pictures or videos in public spaces, like streets or parks, or in private spaces like at home. Sharing sexual pictures or videos of someone without their permission is as serious offence."](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/a403/live/2b00f7f0-9c70-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png.webp) Home Office
The Home Office said: "We expect everyone who comes to the UK to abide by our laws. If they do not, they will face consequences, including the refusal of their asylum claim and removal from the UK."
Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: "Instead of trying to train these mainly young, male illegal immigrants behave in a civilised way towards women, they should be deported."
Philp called for deportations of asylum seekers, rather than attempting to change existing behaviour.
"Immigrants are coming from places and societies where attitudes towards women can be completely incompatible with Western society," he said.
"Too many communities are failing to properly integrate and become part of our culture, leaving frankly backwards standards to prevail."
In a two minute video posted on social media, Reform UK's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf labelled the document "a disgrace", saying: "I genuinely cannot believe what I have just read.
"The government has just published a handy guide for illegal migrants on how not to be a rapist, not to be a paedophile, how not to beat women and how to leave babies alone.
"That again may be really hard to believe but that is exactly what they have just done."
But Green Party peer Baroness Jenny Jones called on Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to apologise for what she claimed was a "grave error of judgement".
"This is a dangerous and unnecessary move by the Home Office which feeds into right wing tropes," she told Sky News, adding: "We support consent education, but it needs to be universal."
A Labour spokesperson declined to comment. The Liberal Democrats were also contacted for comment.
Jacqueline McKenzie, head of immigration and asylum law at Leigh Day, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the material from the Home Office is "problematic, it's inflammatory but done well it could be useful".
"Something that could be quite good if done well and not done in a patronising way could be useful, but I'm very suspicious at the fact that the government has put this in the public domain."
Sussex Police and Crime Commissioner Katy Bourne told the same programme that the government was "finally recognising that there's an issue" but questioned what action would be taken.
The Conservative politician said: "Giving somebody a pamphlet saying 'Be a good boy and don't blow kisses at girls in this country and, by the way, girls and women have to say yes if you approach them' is not going to cure something that is societal, it's a cultural issue."
Louise Calvey, executive director of the Asylum Matters charity, said: "By singling out people seeking sanctuary as in particular need of basic instruction not to commit abuse or sexual violence, the government is fuelling hostility, suspicion and racism, instead of doing any real work to promote understanding or safety."
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, “Get the latest political analysis and big moments, delivered straight to your inbox every weekday”. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/6fad/live/133a6af0-dc98-11ef-bc01-8f2c83dad217.png.webp)
Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to read top political analysis, gain insight from across the UK and stay up to speed with the big moments. It'll be delivered straight to your inbox every weekday.
summary: The Home Office has published a new online booklet for asylum seekers outlining UK laws regarding rape, sexual harassment, domestic abuse, and gender equality. The guidance warns that breaking UK laws can result in police action, loss of asylum support, or removal from the country. While the government defends the approach as a clear statement of societal norms and legal consequences, the publication has drawn mixed reactions from politicians and charity representatives.
key_points: A nine-page Home Office booklet informs new asylum seekers that rape, sexual harassment, and domestic abuse are illegal in the UK.
The guidance explains gender equality, consent laws, and expectations for public behavior, such as prohibiting street harassment and unauthorized photography.
Breaking UK laws can negatively impact an individual's asylum claim, lead to a loss of support, or result in deportation.
The publication has sparked debate, with critics from charities and some political figures calling it inflammatory or patronizing, while supporters emphasize the importance of enforcing UK laws.

title: GCSE results: almost one in four boys in England get top grades in maths
author: Richard Adams; Sally Weale
content:
Almost one in four boys in England received top grades in maths while results in English improved across the board, helping to propel improved GCSE results for this year’s cohort of 16-year-olds.
The stronger performances in maths helped pupils taking GCSEs in year 11 reach a record level for higher grades in England outside the Covid pandemic years, when exams were replaced by teacher assessments.
The overall results for 16-year-olds nudged slightly higher compared with last year, with the proportion receiving grades 7, 8 and 9 – equivalent to grades A and A* – rising by 0.1 of a percentage point to 23.1%. The proportion of nearly 700,000 16-year-olds in England who got a grade 4 or better – equivalent to a C or higher – also rose to 70.7%, compared with 70.5% in 2025.
Some of the strongest performances appeared to come in the compulsory subject of maths, where 22.3% received 7s or better, including 24% of boys and 20.5% of girls. But girls did worse than last year in lower grades, dropping from 71% awarded 4 and above to 70.7%, while boys improved further to 72.8%.
Richard Harry, the executive director of qualifications and assessment at the Welsh exam board WJEC, said the maths results for 16-year-old boys in England “may be the highest in recent years”.
Coming after last week’s A-levels also showed stronger results in maths, Harry said it was difficult to know what was driving the improvement: “Since coming out of the pandemic we’ve been maintaining the standard in maths at both GCSE and in A-level and I think we’re confident that the outcomes we’re seeing this year reflect the level of attainment that learners have achieved.”
Girls continue to outperform boys at GCSE, but the gap is closing and is now 2.9 percentage points lower than it was in 2019. Harry urged caution, however. “The gap is only very slightly narrower this year – it’s a very small change. I think it would be difficult to speculate too much around the differences for such small changes.”
![Three boys look at sheets of paper with their results; they look happy.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3788565696a0fad27ff13cf3a5cf59b82e98ad99/0_0_6000_4000/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In English, the other compulsory subject, results bounced back after dipping last year, with 66.1% of boys getting 4s and above while girls improved to 76.8%.
Many of the pupils receiving GCSE results this summer were in year 5 when schools were largely closed due to Covid-19 restrictions, disrupting their final years of primary schooling.
Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “It should be remembered that these young people experienced significant disruption earlier in their education … That so many have done so well in their GCSEs and other level 2 qualifications is an example of triumph over adversity both for them and for their schools.
“However, a significant proportion of students continue to fall short of a grade 4 GCSE pass in English and maths both at the age of 16 and in subsequent resits in post-16 education where most face the miserable experience of falling short once again.
“This limits their education and career options and is very likely to be a factor in the large number of young people who end up not in employment, education or training (Neet).”
The results came as more than a million candidates in England, Wales and Northern Ireland received their grades on Thursday morning. Scotland published its equivalent results earlier this month.
Twenty-two per cent of UK entries were awarded the top grades of 7 or A and above this year, up by 0.1 percentage points on last year. That was higher than in 2019, the last year before the pandemic, when 20.8% of entries achieved the top grades.
Myles McGinley, managing director of the Cambridge OCR examination board, noted that alongside maths many more pupils were taking business studies, with the number of entries rising by a third in five years.
after newsletter promotion
“This looks like an increasingly entrepreneurial generation, fascinated by how business works. The founders of some of the next great unicorn businesses may well be among those achieving GCSEs in business studies today,” McGinley said.
![A group of girls, most wearing headscarves, stand around a table as a woman hands out their results.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/802f8e0acc2d8fbd5877fccdf55a10586bbc8069/0_0_7413_4942/master/7413.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
One of the key areas of concern after the results will be the high failure rates for those students in England forced to resit English and maths GCSE after previously failing to secure a pass at the age of 16.
It is a longstanding problem and the government has already proposed the introduction of a “stepping stone” qualification to help better prepare students who are struggling, but frustrated school leaders said more fundamental change was needed.
Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the NAHT school leaders’ union, said: “We have long called for an end to the current policy which forces students into dispiriting rounds of repeated, demotivating resits. The curriculum review focus was on ensuring students are better prepared for resits and introducing a stepping-stone qualification.
“Today’s data shows why more fundamental changes to this policy are needed, with only 18.8% of students aged 17 and over achieving a grade 4 in English, and 13.6% of students achieving a grade 4 in maths – both down on last year, when these figures were 19.7% and 15.3% respectively.
“What is needed are more appropriate and engaging alternatives to GCSEs in English and maths at key stage 4 which enable students to study for qualifications that better suit their needs and aspirations.”
Concern will also focus on persistent regional differences. London was once again the highest performing area with 28.6% of grades 7 and above, up 0.2 percentage points from last year. In the north-east, the lowest performing region, 17.7% of grades awarded were 7 and above, down 0.1 percentage points from last year.
Carl Cullinane, the director of research and policy at the Sutton Trust education charity, said there had been “no progress” in addressing regional imbalances in GCSE performance, with the gap between London and the rest of the country continuing to grow.
The Sutton Trust also pointed out that the gap between state comprehensives and private school pupils getting the top grades may have narrowed slightly by 0.9 percentage points, but it remained big, at 27 percentage points.
summary: GCSE results for 16-year-olds in England improved slightly this year, driven by stronger performances in maths and a bounce back in English. Nearly one in four boys in England received top grades in maths, reaching a record level for higher grades outside of pandemic years. However, persistent challenges remain, including regional attainment gaps between London and the north-east, and low pass rates for students forced to retake English and maths exams.
key_points: The overall proportion of entries receiving top grades (7, 8, and 9) in England rose by 0.1 percentage points to 23.1%.
In compulsory maths, 24% of boys and 20.5% of girls received a grade 7 or better.
London remained the highest-performing region with 28.6% of top grades, while the north-east was the lowest at 17.7%.
Resit pass rates for students aged 17 and over declined, with only 18.8% achieving a grade 4 in English and 13.6% in maths.
Entries for business studies rose by a third over five years, reflecting growing interest among students.

title: Burnham says fly-tippers will be forced to pay for the clean-up when they dump waste illegally – UK politics live
author: Tom Ambrose; Vivian Ho; Kiran Stacey; Aletha Adu; Caroline Davies; Rowena Mason
content:
National Crime Agency brought in to tackle organised gangs behind illegal dumps
Andy Burnham has said fly-tippers will be forced to pay for the clean-up when they dump waste illegally.
The prime minister laid out his plans to crackdown on waste crimes as he visited an illegal dump in West Yorkshire.
He told broadcasters:
We’ve begun a much more networked approach to this, where we’re bringing the National Crime Agency in to work with the Environment Agency, increasing the penalties and bearing down now on the organised crime that lies behind some of what you see behind me.
Asked why the National Crime Agency was involved, the prime minister said:
It’s building the intelligence as to who is behind this, the networks that are orchestrating what is a very serious crime, and then using the Proceeds of Crime Act to make them pay for the clean-up.
It cannot be right that we leave the situation to build, the public purse then exposed in relation to the clean-up.
But actually we should be getting in much earlier, apprehending them, using all of the intelligence that comes through that investigation to make sure the polluter pays.
Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, the equalities minister has said, as she warned that young men were being sucked into violent misogyny by the “cesspit” of social media.
Bridget Phillipson said she was increasingly worried about how commonplace misogyny and racism had become, fuelled by online interactions and statements by politicians she said would not have been acceptable a few years ago.
She accused senior MPs from Reform and the Conservatives of having made racist statements in recent years, and accused the police of not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough.
Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast, she said: “I worry that we are at kind of a ground zero in terms of attitudes around violence against women and girls.
“Things that not very long ago felt totally unacceptable are becoming normal. I think we’re seeing that in terms of attitudes towards women, and I think we see that in terms of attitudes around racism.”
She accused the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, and Reform’s economic spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, of having made racist statements in recent years.
Bridget Phillipson has suggested her sweeping reforms to special educational needs provision could be adapted to give parents greater protections if they are unhappy about the service being provided for their children.
The former education secretary told the Guardian ministers were open to making changes to the plans, which were announced earlier this year but which have since been subject to consultation.
Under Andy Burnham, Phillipson has been moved to the women and equalities brief, but she said that before she left the education department the plan had been to make moderations to the plans after the consultation process.
Parents and some MPs have particularly expressed concern that under the new system, parents who are denied an Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) will not be able to demand that local authorities move their child to a particular school.
Phillipson said however that some of the legal protections in the new system could be strengthened to give parents more confidence.
“The consultation was a genuine one and, you know, final decisions are still to be taken,” she told the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast.
“I do obviously recognise the enormous kind of nervousness that many parents will be experiencing if their children are in that system,” she said.
And she added: “I can only speak to where I kind of left things … It was clear to me through the passage of that consultation, through the events we did right across the country, hearing directly from parents, through all of the conversations I had, that there were areas where there would need to be more finessing of some aspects of the policy.”
Labour MP for Bradford West Naz Shar and Environment Agency staff show Andy Burnham an illegal rubbish dump near Bradford City’s football ground.
Labour MP for Bradford West Naz Shar (L), and Environment agency staff show Britain's prime minister Andy Burnham (C), an illegal rubbish dump near the Bradford City football ground in Bradford, northern England on 20 August 2026. Photograph: Scott Heppell/AFP/Getty Images
Education Lucy Powell on Thursday addressed the GCSE gender gap, which shrank to its narrowest point this century.
Almost one in four boys in England received top grades in maths while results in English improved across the board.
“The white working-class review that was recently done, that was one things it found, that more boys need to see the purpose of education, they need to see the line of sight into work,” Powell told the Press Association.
“I just spoke today here at Harper Green to some young lads doing the construction qualification they’ve now put on here, and that’s exactly what they said to me, is that they feel it’s engaging, they understand the purpose of it, they want to use their hands and their skills in different ways.
“So that’s giving them a reason to come to school and then they’ll engage in the other subjects as well.”
Andy Burnham told reporters that funding for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s security arrangements on their return to the UK was a “private matter”.
Harry and Meghan are expected to return to live in Britain later this month. After six years in the US, they will be moving with their two children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, to a non-royal residence outside of London.
After stepping down as senior royals, the Sussexes are no longer eligible to receive taxpayer-funded protection while in the UK, other than when within royal residences. Prince Harry, 41, has previously stated that he would not feel safe bringing his family back to the UK without police protection.
When questioned about their security arrangements, the prime minister said: “Well, this is a private matter.
“It’s a matter for Harry and for Meghan, and we wish them well in the moves that they’re making.”
The Guardian’s Rowena Mason has more on Richard Tice, business spokesperson for Reform UK, and his defence of the party’s decision to suspendTimMontgomerie:
Reform UK has been stalling in the polls in recent months following questions about Nigel Farage’s financial affairs, with a personal £5m gift from Thailand-based billionaire Christopher Harborne currently under investigation by parliament’s standards watchdog.
The party has also faced splits over the actions of Zia Yusuf, its home affairs spokesperson, who branded a senior Tory a “traitor”, and the decision to suspend Tim Montgomerie, a high profile activist who had defected from the Conservatives.
Montgomerie had been critical of Farage’s decision not to attend the count when he won the Clacton byelection, and said the leader had show a “too dominant aggrieved tone”, arguing that “you don’t skip your own victory count without a much better explanation”.
The Reform member, who had posed with Farage when he joined the party, was informed earlier this week of his suspension.
Asked at a press conference whether the party had become too thin skinned and unable to take criticism, Tice said it was “far from” the case and Reform was beginning to climb again in the polls.
He added: “We’re not afraid of competition, voters have got more choice and none of us have ever claimed we are perfect … we get lots right, we make mistakes, we push on.”
National Crime Agency brought in to tackle organised gangs behind illegal dumps
Andy Burnham has said fly-tippers will be forced to pay for the clean-up when they dump waste illegally.
The prime minister laid out his plans to crackdown on waste crimes as he visited an illegal dump in West Yorkshire.
He told broadcasters:
We’ve begun a much more networked approach to this, where we’re bringing the National Crime Agency in to work with the Environment Agency, increasing the penalties and bearing down now on the organised crime that lies behind some of what you see behind me.
Asked why the National Crime Agency was involved, the prime minister said:
It’s building the intelligence as to who is behind this, the networks that are orchestrating what is a very serious crime, and then using the Proceeds of Crime Act to make them pay for the clean-up.
It cannot be right that we leave the situation to build, the public purse then exposed in relation to the clean-up.
But actually we should be getting in much earlier, apprehending them, using all of the intelligence that comes through that investigation to make sure the polluter pays.
The prime minister has defended new government advice that will tell asylum seekers that rape and domestic abuse are serious crimes.
Speaking to reporters on a visit to an illegal waste dump in Bradford, West Yorkshire, Andy Burnham said:
As a government, we have a very clear principle: if you break UK law, you will be removed from the country and we have seen that in relation to immigration, where removals are significantly up.
I’m currently working to ensure that foreign national offenders who can be removed from the prison system are removed from that system.
So it follows that if we’re taking this approach, it’s made explicitly clear what the UK law is and what the societal norms of the UK are, and that’s why this approach is being taken.
The guidance, published on Wednesday, forms part of a Home Office document entitled ‘Understanding Behaviours And Expectations In The UK’, which also provides guidance on gender equality and respect in public.
Britain's prime minister Andy Burnham is shown an illegal rubbish dump near the Bradford City football ground in Bradford, England, Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026, after he announced a new crackdown on illegal waste dumping and action to clear up communities. Photograph: Scott Heppell/Pool AP/AP
Richard Tice defended Nigel Farage after the Reform UK leader chose not to attend the official count for the Clacton byelection.
The party’s deputy leader said Farage led a “brilliant campaign” and secured an “incredible result”.
Asked at a press conference whether Reform was coming across as thin-skinned, Tice said: “Far from it … we get more scrutiny than everybody else.
“But isn’t it interesting, Nigel’s success in Clacton, getting a thousand more votes than he secured (previously), despite a much, much lower turnout.
“That was an incredible result through hard work, through a brilliant campaign.”
He added: “We’re going back up in the polls, and we’re back ahead of Labour. We’re not afraid of competition. In a sense, democracy demands competition, and voters have got more choice. That’s a good thing. None of us have ever claimed we’re perfect.”
Reform’s deputy leader has defended the suspension of party supporter Tim Montgomerie.
Speaking to reporters, Richard Tice said:
With regard to other matters, Tim, and things, we’re a fast-growing political party.
There’ll be a range of views, and sometimes we’ll agree, and sometimes we’ll have a debate and discussion.
That’s what you do in business. That’s what you do in a boardroom. That’s what you do when you’re brainstorming.
But what we’ve always said is that actually, when you are, when you’re having your discussions about those things, in the nicest possible way, as you would in a boardroom or in a brainstorming session in a company, you keep it behind closed doors, and then you go out and sell a great message.
That’s what we’re doing.
Deputy Leader of Reform UK Richard Tice during a Reform UK Press Conference in Enfield, London. Photograph: Victoria Jones/Shutterstock
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced a new crackdown on illegal waste dumping during a visit to West Yorkshire, stating that the National Crime Agency will be brought in to target organized gangs and use the Proceeds of Crime Act to make polluters pay for clean-ups. In other political developments, equalities minister Bridget Phillipson warned that racism and sexism have become normalized in Britain, and Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice defended the party's recent actions and the suspension of activist Tim Montgomerie.
key_points: Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated that fly-tippers and organized criminal gangs behind illegal waste dumps will be forced to pay for clean-ups using the Proceeds of Crime Act.
The National Crime Agency is being brought in to work with the Environment Agency to build intelligence on waste crime networks.
Equalities minister Bridget Phillipson warned that racism and violent misogyny have become increasingly normalized, fueled by social media and online interactions.
Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice defended the suspension of Tim Montgomerie following criticism of party leader Nigel Farage.

title: GCSE results: girls still ahead but gender gap narrows as hundreds of thousands of pupils receive grades – as it happened
author: Mabel Banfield-Nwachi; Taz Ali; Tom Ambrose; Sally Weale; Richard Adams
content:
The proportion of GCSE students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland achieving at least a grade 4 (equivalent to a C) has fallen slightly this year, to 67.3% from 67.4% in 2025. This is the same as the proportion recorded in 2019, before the pandemic.
While it is a minor decrease, it still means nearly a third of teenagers are not achieving basic English and maths skills when finishing school. In England, students who fail to reach a grade 4 or equivalent in English or maths GCSEs have to retake them.
More students aged 17 and above took English and maths this year, likely due to the resits policy in England. But results show the pass rate has worsened for this cohort, falling by 1.4 percentage points for English and 1.7 for maths compared with last year.
That’s all from us on the GCSE results live blog today, thanks for following along.
Here are the main developments from today:
The proportion of GCSE students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland achieving at least a grade 4 (equivalent to a C) has fallen slightly this year, to 67.3% from 67.4% in 2025. This is the same as the proportion recorded in 2019, before the pandemic.
The overall results for 16-year-olds in England nudged slightly higher compared with last year, with the proportion receiving grades 7, 8 and 9 – equivalent to grades A and A* – rising by 0.1 of a percentage point to 23.1%.
The proportion of nearly 700,000 16-year-olds in England who got a grade 4 (equivalent to a C) or better also rose to 70.7%, compared with 70.5% in 2025.
Pupils collect their GCSE results at Egglescliffe School, in Eaglescliffe, North Yorkshire. Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA
Girls continue to outperform boys at GCSE, but the gap is narrowing. Almost a fifth (19.6%) of boys’ GCSE entries in England, Wales and Northern Ireland were awarded a grade 7 or higher (equivalent to an A) compared with nearly a quarter (24.4%) of girls’ entries, a 4.8 percentage point gap, down from 5.1 last year. Overall, 70.2% of girls achieved a pass rate (grade 4 and higher) compared with 64.4% of boys, a 5.8 percentage point gap, a decrease from 6.2 last year.
In England, London remains on top for pupils achieving a grade 7 or above, at 28.6%. This is a slight increase from last year, when 28.4% of GCSE students in the capital achieved the top grades. North-east England had the lowest figure, with 17.7% of GCSE entries awarded at least a 7, down from 17.8% in 2025.
In a message to students, prime minister Andy Burnham said the government is creating “more opportunities” for young people to “choose the path that’s right for them”. He added: “Whatever your results, remember there isn’t just one route to success.”
Education secretary Lucy Powell said the government is looking at changing the resits policy in England, noting that only one in five students who resit English and maths were passing them. “For some, they’re doing it many times over,” she added. “So we’re branding them a failure after failure after failure. It’s knocking their confidence.
Among those celebrating their GCSE results today were quadruplets Ellen, Eric, Layla, and Rose Lamb, who all attended Aureus School in Didcot, Oxfordshire.
Quadruplets Rose, Eric, Layla and Ellen Lamb receive their GCSE results at Aureus School in Didcot, Oxfordshire. Photograph: David Collins Photography
Ellen achieved one grade 9, five grade 8s, three grade 7s, and one grade 6. She is heading to Oxford City College to study A-levels in biology, chemistry and maths and hopes to become a paediatrician.
“I’ve really enjoyed the sense of community at Aureus,” she said. “The teachers have always been incredibly supportive, and encouraged me to challenge myself both academically and personally.
“Some of my favourite memories include our Year 11 prom, taking part in the school production, and celebrating after completing our GCSE exams.”
Eric is going on to study dance, while Layla will be studying English, history and psychology at sixth form and Rose will study history, sociology, and English A-levels.
Gender and golf course studies are examples of “Mickey Mouse” degrees, Suella Braverman has said.
Asked to name a specific degree which falls under Reform UK’s definition of a “Mickey Mouse” course that should be avoided, the party’s education spokesperson said:
In terms of Mickey Mouse courses, listen, this has been well-chronicled for many years. Whether it’s gender studies, whether it’s golf course studies, I think I’ve seen there’s not a necessity. There’s not a value in many of these degrees.
Now I know that might be uncomfortable to those people who have those qualifications, but the reality is you’ve got to ask yourself: what are your graduate outcomes looking like?
Have you really spent three years of your life in the best possible way, and was it worth £50,000 worth of debt.
Young people are coming out of university unable to get on to the housing ladder, unable and unwilling to get married, unable to start a family. Why? Because they’re starting off with their hands behind their backs because they’ve been sold a line that university is the pathway to success.
Reform: don't waste time 'studying for a pointless degree at a mediocre university'
Tom Ambrose
Suella Braverman has urged young people getting their GCSE results not to “waste your time studying for a pointless degree at a mediocre university”.
The Reform UK education spokesperson made the comment as she set out the party’s plans to create 600,000 more apprenticeship starts a year by the end of the first term of a Reform government.
Suella Braverman during a Reform UK Press Conference in Enfield, London. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA
As she set out the policy, Braverman addressed students receiving their exam results, telling them:
My advice to those young people today getting their results, my advice to those grandparents and those parents looking at the young people in their families who may be getting their results today: Be careful, don’t get ripped off by the great university scam.
Don’t waste your time studying for a pointless degree at a mediocre university. If you want to work hard, if you want to move forward, earn a wage, and have opportunities in your life, take up and look for apprentices.
And a Reform UK government will ensure that those opportunities exist. Your success is our country’s success. We’re on your side, and when I said I wanted a skills revolution, I meant it.”
For more UK politics news, follow our live blog here:
Chris Zarraga, director of Schools North East which represents 1,150 schools in the regions, said there was some “genuinely encouraging news” in today’s results.
At grade 4 and above, the gap between the north-east and London has narrowed and is back to around where it was before the pandemic.
But the picture at the highest grades remains concerning. The gap at grades 7 to 9 has increased again this year and remains wider than it was in 2019.
The movement each year might look relatively small, but the important point is its persistence. Year after year, this divide remains; and is then reflected in student destinations, employment rates, and HE progression rates.
We have to understand what these figures are telling us. There is not a north-south divide in the quality of schools, nor in the talent, potential or aspirations of young people.
There is a structural divide in the circumstances and opportunities surrounding them.
Schools in the north-east are working incredibly hard to overcome those circumstances.
But schools cannot independently fix poverty, stretched public services, shortages in special educational needs and disabilities (Send) support, transport barriers, unequal access to enrichment or very different local economic opportunities.
These inequalities are neither inevitable nor acceptable. The government needs to treat them as a system challenge and address the conditions around schools as well as what happens inside them.”
PA has reported a heartwarming story about a Sudanese refugee who passed his GCSEs in English and maths.
Nasser Hamid, 20, of Ipswich, achieved grade 4 in both subjects, collecting his maths results today after having passed English earlier this year.
He studies at Suffolk New College, where he is also taking an IT course.
On finding out he now has his English and maths qualifications, he said: “I feel proud – it is one of the proudest moments in my life – this is the result I was waiting for to step forward.
“Thanks to Suffolk New College, without their help I wouldn’t be standing here.”
Nasser Hamid, a student who fled war-torn Sudan to live in the UK, said that passing his GCSE exams in maths and English is ‘one of the proudest moments in my life’. Photograph: Suffolk New College/PA
Nasser is an aspiring football referee, after an injury ended his dream of being a professional player. He recently oversaw a charity football match at Ipswich Town’s ground, Portman Road, and said he would love to referee at a future World Cup.
He also officiates at Saturday and Sunday league games.
He urged others in a similar position to “just believe in yourself”.
“With discipline and hard work, you can achieve your goals,” he said.
Nasser said he was “pushing forward to be an engineer”.
“I’m on track,” he said.
“Next, I’m going to do an access course and then (hopefully) go to university to study engineering.”
David Squire, head of maths at Suffolk New College, said: “I’ve never been prouder of a learner in my life.”
On subject choice, statistics and business studies may have grown in popularity this year – up 11% and 8% respectively – but computing has dipped 7%. Myles McGinley, managing director of Cambridge OCR, explained: “The emergence of AI could be leading to students thinking they don’t need to know how to code.
“But I would say maybe that’s something that would be up for debate. I think potentially computer science is more important than ever in the age of AI.
“And while vibe coding might be all the rage, I think AI won’t be able to replace a solid understanding of how software works, how technology can solve real-world problems and how it can create a good user experience.”
One of the key areas of concern following today’s GCSE results will be the high failure rates for those students in England forced to resit English and maths GCSE after previously failing to secure a pass at the age of 16.
It is a longstanding problem and the government has already proposed the introduction of a “stepping stone” qualification to help better prepare students who are struggling but frustrated school leaders said more fundamental change is needed.
Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the NAHT school leaders’ union, said: “We have long called for an end to the current policy which forces students into dispiriting rounds of repeated, demotivating resits.
“The curriculum review focus was on ensuring students are better prepared for resits and introducing a stepping stone qualification.
“Today’s data shows why more fundamental changes to this policy are needed, with only 18.8% of students aged 17 and over achieving a grade 4 in English, and 13.6% of students achieving a grade 4 in maths – both down on last year, when these figures were 19.7% and 15.3% respectively.
Pupils celebrate their GCSE results at
Leeds Grammar School, in Leeds, Yorkshire. Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA
“What is needed are more appropriate and engaging alternatives to GCSEs in English and maths at key stage 4 which enable students to study for qualifications that better suit their needs and aspirations.”
Girls continue to outperform boys at GCSE, but the gap is closing and is now 2.9 percentage points (pp) lower than it was in 2019. Richard Harry, executive director of qualifications and assessment at the Welsh exam board WJEC, urged caution however.
“The gap is only very slightly narrower this year – it’s a very small change,” he said. “I think it would be difficult to speculate too much around the differences for such small changes.”
Concern will also focus on persistent regional differences, with London once again the highest performing area with 28.6% of grades 7 and above, up 0.2pp from last year. In the north-east, the lowest performing region, 17.7% of grades awarded were 7 and above, down 0.1pp from last year.
Carl Cullinane, director of research and policy at the Sutton Trust education charity, said there had been “no progress” in addressing regional imbalances in GCSE performance, with the gap between London and the rest of the country continuing to grow.
“Forthcoming curriculum and assessment reforms, and future government spending decisions, must have a laser focus on closing gaps in attainment and progression across the country.”
The Sutton Trust also pointed out that the gap between state comprehensives and private school pupils getting the top grades may have narrowed slightly by 0.9pp, but it remains vast at 27pp.
London widens lead over other regions for top grades
Looking at the results in England on a regional level, London remains on top for pupils achieving a grade 7 or above, at 28.6%.
This is a slight increase from last year, when 28.4% of GCSE students in the capital achieved the top grades.
North-east England had the lowest figure, with 17.7% of GCSE entries awarded at least a 7, down from 17.8% in 2025.
This means the regional gap has widened between the highest and lowest proportions of pupils achieving a grade 7 or above, from 10.6 percentage points last year to 10.9 points this year. It is the largest gap since the start of available data in 2010, according to analysis by PA.
Here’s what the data says about the other regions:
North-west England: 18.9% of entries received a grade 7 or above, up slightly from 18.8% in 2025.
London – north-west gap: The gap widened to 9.7 percentage points, from 9.6 in 2025, close to the recent record of 9.9 points in 2024.
East Midlands: 18.2% of entries received a grade 7 or above, 10.4 percentage points behind London, up from 10.3 in 2025.
West Midlands: 18.3% of entries received a grade 7 or above, 10.3 percentage points behind London, up from 9.9 in 2025.
Wider regional divide: The gap between London and both the East and West Midlands has widened to its largest level since at least 2010.
Here some pictures on the newswires of students picking up their GCSE results today:
Prosper Okoroafor (centre) at the Ark Greenwich Free School, Woolwich, south London. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA
Farzana Fatimah reacts as she reads her GCSE results with her mother at Plashet City of London Academy. Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images
Ethan Rillon celebrates his GCSE results with his sister Angela Rillon (left) and his mother, Jan Rillon, at Hazelwood Intergrated College in Newtownabbey, North Belfast. Photograph: Mark Marlow/PA
Iris Hamilton-Potter and friend Poppy Plant receive their GCSE results at Llanishen High School in Cardiff, Wales. Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty Images
Education secretary Lucy Powell speaks with students collecting their GCSE results at Harper Green School in Farnworth, Bolton. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA
Ellie Anns, Isabella Bruce, Izzy Phillips, Belle Bosham, Susanna Dat and Luci Tedeschi at St Gabriel's School in Newbury, Berkshire. Photograph: David Hartley/Shutterstock
The gap in GCSE results between boys and girls in England, Wales and Northern Ireland has shrunk again this year.
Almost a fifth (19.6%) of boys’ GCSE entries were awarded a grade 7 or higher (equivalent to an A) compared with nearly a quarter (24.4%) of girls’ entries, a 4.8 percentage point gap, down from 5.1 last year.
Overall, 70.2% of girls achieved a pass rate (grade 4 and higher) compared with 64.4% of boys, a 5.8 percentage point gap, a decrease from 6.2 last year.
These are the narrowest leads enjoyed by girls since at least 2000, which is the earliest archive data available, PA reported.
The proportion of GCSE students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland achieving at least a grade 4 (equivalent to a C) has fallen slightly this year, to 67.3% from 67.4% in 2025. This is the same as the proportion recorded in 2019, before the pandemic.
While it is a minor decrease, it still means nearly a third of teenagers are not achieving basic English and maths skills when finishing school. In England, students who fail to reach a grade 4 or equivalent in English or maths GCSEs have to retake them.
More students aged 17 and above took English and maths this year, likely due to the resits policy in England. But results show the pass rate has worsened for this cohort, falling by 1.4 percentage points for English and 1.7 for maths compared with last year.
'Concerning' fall in language GCSE entries, says British Academy
The British Academy, the national organisation for humanities and social sciences, said its analysis of GCSE results today shows business and psychology are up but languages face another year of decline.
Among its key findings were:
French seeing its sharpest fall since 2018, with a 5.4% decrease in take-up this year.
Other modern languages, which includes Arabic, Chinese and Urdu among others,are also down by 4%.
Spanish growth may be slowing down, with a 0.3% increase compared to 2.6% last year and 6.2% the year before.
German is up 0.2%, a very small increase compared to its long-term decline of 12.5% over the past 5 years.
The highest growing subjects in Shape (the acronym for social sciences, humanities and arts) was business studies, with a 7.9% increase.
Sociology and psychology continue to rise, by 4.8% and 3% respectively.
Susan Smith, president of the British Academy, said: “This year’s GCSE entries show that young people continue to be inspired by subjects providing insight into people, economy and society.
The growth of business studies, sociology and psychology, in particular, show increasing appetite for skills nurtured by the social sciences, arts and humanities."
However, the continued fall in language entries is concerning. Languages are vital for diplomacy, trade and cultural understanding. AI translation is no match for the human communications skills and capabilities we need to navigate an increasingly interconnected, but divided and volatile world. Yet, losing languages at this level has a domino effect across the entire education system, and once this expertise disappears, it will be very hard to recover.
As government reflects on future education pathways, we urge ministers to seize every opportunity to give all young people access to a broad, balanced curriculum, delivering the critical thinking and creativity that employers value and the UK needs.”
Here are some statements from the prime minister and the education secretary on the GSCE results today.
Andy Burnham said:
Congratulations to everyone collecting their results today, you should be proud of the hard work that got you here.
Whether the next step is sixth form, a college course, an apprenticeship, a T Level, work, or something else entirely, we’re ensuring that there are more opportunities than ever to choose your own path to get on in life. I’m determined to bring back hope and give every young person the chance to fulfil their potential.
Lucy Powell said:
Massive congratulations to everyone collecting their results today – be proud of what it took to get here, and thank you to the teachers and families who backed you every step of the way.
More of you are hitting top grades in maths, and technical pass rates are climbing in every region. That’s proof there is no wrong door, only different routes that suit everyone’s individual ambition.
But there’s more to do to put academic and technical qualifications on an equal footing, so we’re introducing V Levels and expanding T Levels and apprenticeships, so wherever you’re headed next, there’s a path that works for you.”
Andy Burnham and Lucy Powell speaking to apprentices at the Alstom factory in Derby. Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/AFP/Getty Images
summary: Hundreds of thousands of pupils across England, Wales, and Northern Ireland received their GCSE results, with the overall pass rate falling slightly to 67.3%. Girls continue to outperform boys, though the gender performance gap has narrowed slightly compared to previous years. Meanwhile, education leaders have raised concerns over declining pass rates and high failure figures for older students required to retake English and maths exams.
key_points: The proportion of students achieving at least a grade 4 dropped slightly to 67.3%, matching pre-pandemic levels from 2019.
Girls continue to outperform boys, though the attainment gap between genders has decreased.
Pass rates for students aged 17 and over retaking English and maths worsened, falling by 1.4 and 1.7 percentage points respectively.
London remained the top-performing region for top grades (7 and above), while the north-east recorded the lowest figure.

title: Prince Harry and Meghan's UK security a private matter, Burnham says
author: Sofia Ferreira Santos
content:
![Prince Harry and Meghan sat next to each other and smiling in Colombia in 2024](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/42ad/live/498598d0-9c8d-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Prince Harry and Meghan are planning to move back to the UK, BBC News understands
- Published
Security arrangements for The Duke and Duchess of Sussex on their return to the UK are a "private matter," Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.
He added: "It's a matter for Harry and for Meghan, and we wish them well in the move that they are making."
It comes after it emerged that the couple intend to relocate with their children from the US to the UK later this month to a private, non-royal residence outside London.
Security for the couple has long been a point of tension, with Prince Harry losing a legal challenge last year over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.
The couple's children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are enrolled to start at a British school in September.
King Charles was told of the move on Sunday. There are no current plans for either Prince Harry or Meghan to resume their roles as working royals.
The Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties in early 2020, before settling in California in March that year.
They were last in the UK in July to visit the King and Queen Camilla, in what was seen as a key development in their relationship.
The Palace described the meeting at the King's private home in Gloucestershire as a "private family occasion".
It was the first time the King had seen his grandchildren in person in more than four years, and the couple's first visit to the UK together since 2022.
It is understood that July's visit had to be adjusted after the duke's request for police protection was rejected.
Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge in which he sought to overturn a decision that had downgraded his security after his move to the US.
At the time, he told the BBC that he "can't see a world" in which he would bring his family to the UK due to the downgrading of his protection.
It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.
Royal expert Robert Hardman told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme it was likely that some of their past security issues "have been resolved" but details - or who is going to foot the bill - are still unknown.
This breaking news story is being updated and more details will be published shortly. Please refresh the page for the fullest version.
You can receive Breaking News on a smartphone or tablet via the BBC News App. You can also follow @BBCBreaking on X, external to get the latest alerts.
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan are planning to relocate from the US to a private residence outside London with their children later this month. Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated that their security arrangements are a private matter. King Charles was informed of the move, though the couple has no plans to resume working royal roles.
key_points: Prince Harry and Meghan intend to move back to the UK with their children later this month.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated that the couple's UK security is a private matter.
King Charles was informed of the relocation on Sunday.
The couple has no current plans to resume their duties as working royals.

title: Supercars torched in wedding ‘firebomb attack’
author: Tom McArdle
content:
Two supercars were set alight in a suspected firebomb attack at a wedding in Birmingham.
A McLaren and a Ferrari went up in flames after a hooded assailant threw at least three petrol bombs at the vehicles outside Royal Shalimar, a Pakistani wedding venue in Sparkbrook, on Wednesday evening.
CCTV footage from the incident shows the vehicles burning and several smaller fires breaking out nearby, including one at the front of the venue, at around 8.50pm.
Staff members tackled the flames as emergency services arrived.
The footage, posted on social media, showed several figures dressed in black standing opposite the venue, before what appeared to have been petrol bombs were hurled at the cars.
The figures could then be seen fleeing the scene after men ran out to confront them.
summary: Two supercars, a McLaren and a Ferrari, were destroyed in a suspected firebomb attack outside a wedding venue in Birmingham. A hooded assailant threw at least three petrol bombs at the vehicles, causing fires that were tackled by staff members. Emergency services responded to the incident, which was captured on CCTV footage.
key_points: A McLaren and a Ferrari were set on fire in a suspected petrol bomb attack.
The incident occurred on Wednesday evening outside a wedding venue in Sparkbrook, Birmingham.
CCTV footage showed a hooded assailant hurling the devices before fleeing the scene.
Venue staff members tackled the flames prior to the arrival of emergency services.

title: GCSE results: Girls’ lead over boys drops to record low
author: Albert Tait; Ollie Corfe
content:
![Florence Davies (L) looks at her results at Llanishen High School in Cardiff](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498909399_17872139606290_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqERCyFNcLUIKPeqT28e10m15NUcTKNHKqy85KLqtvPLE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Florence Davies (L) looks at her results at Llanishen High School in Cardiff](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498909399_17872139606290_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqERCyFNcLUIKPeqT28e10m15NUcTKNHKqy85KLqtvPLE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Girls’ lead over boys at the top GCSE grades has narrowed to its smallest on record.
Female pupils continue to outperform boys at the highest grades and at pass level, but the gender gap has fallen to a record low.
The proportion of boys achieving a grade 7 or above rose from 19.4 per cent in 2025 to 19.6 per cent this year – their best performance since 2011, excluding the pandemic-affected years.
Meanwhile, girls’ share declined from 24.5 per cent to 24.4 per cent, their lowest since 2019, meaning the gap is at a record low for the second year running, down to just 4.8 percentage points.
The trend – seen in both GCSEs and A-levels – has been linked to girls’ worsening mental health, with the number of girls being diagnosed with problems rising since the coronavirus pandemic.
Across the board, the proportion of GCSE entries awarded top grades in the UK has risen slightly to 22 per cent, up from 21.9 per cent in 2025.
However, the pass rate – grade 4 or above – for English and maths has declined for the fifth consecutive year since the pandemic, dragged down by record numbers of students failing their resit exams.
Female pupils have historically outperformed boys in achieving both top GCSE grades and passing grades, with experts believing they were more suited to modular exams, which involve splitting courses into separate units and sitting an exam at the end of each one.
However, the phasing out of modular exams from 2012 in favour of linear exams – when students sit all their exams at the end of the two-year programme – saw the gender gap largely stabilise in the years leading up to the Covid pandemic and even start to decrease.
When it was deemed impossible to hold examinations during the pandemic, the enforced switch to teacher assessment took the gap in top grades to new heights, reaching eight percentage points in 2020 and nine in 2021.
Since then, however, girls’ share of top grades has fallen for five consecutive years, whereas boys have improved their share in 2025 and 2026.
This means the gender gap for top grades has now reached just 4.8pp, marking the first time it has been below 5pp on record going back to 2001.
![Pupils at the all-boys London Nautical School shook hands as they opened their results on Thursday](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498912424_17872157177370_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqolk963VRNCok71xFe0ekZkikPYR0xYwuEBLwP9UFqPg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The gender gap for passing grades has also fallen slightly from 6.2 points in 2025 to 5.8 points in 2026.
It emerged last week that a similar trend is present for A-levels, where boys have now opened up a record lead in achieving top grades after years of being outperformed by girls.
For both GCSE and A-level, the trend has been linked to girls’ worsening mental health, with their absence rate at school increasing far more sharply since the pandemic than for boys.
A Telegraph analysis of Department for Education data revealed last week that girls’ absence rate increased by 35 per cent from the 2019-20 academic year to 2025-26. In comparison, the rate for boys increased by 29.9 per cent.
Girls have also seen a greater increase in absence specifically because of illness, which has risen by 21 per cent since 2019, compared with 16 per cent for boys.
Persistent absence – missing at least a tenth of all classes – has also risen far more quickly for girls, jumping from 12.8 per cent in 2019 to 18 per cent. The 41 per cent increase is greater than the 34.6 per cent rise for boys in the same period.
Another reason for the declining gap is that boys’ share of top grades has improved more than girls’ in the most popular subjects.
In combined science - the most popular subject with just over a million entries - boys improved their top grade share from 8.6 per cent to 8.8 per cent while the girls’ share decreased slightly from 10.03 per cent to 10 per cent.
The next most subscribed subject was maths (more than 912,000 entries), with boys improving their top grade share by 0.5 percentage points, whereas girls rose just 0.2pp. In English language (more than 882,000 entries), both genders declined but girls by 0.3pp and boys by 0.2pp.
Despite the gender gap decreasing, experts remain concerned that boys are still performing far worse than girls.
Prof Alan Smithers, an academic at the University of Buckingham who forecasts exam results every year, questioned earlier this week whether girls might have an “inherent advantage” at GCSE and called for the gap to be investigated.
summary: The gender gap between girls and boys achieving top GCSE grades has dropped to a record low of 4.8 percentage points. While female pupils continue to outperform males overall, girls' share of top grades has declined for five consecutive years while boys have improved. This narrowing trend in both GCSEs and A-levels has been linked by experts to girls' worsening mental health and sharper increases in school absence rates since the pandemic.
key_points: The proportion of boys achieving grade 7 or above rose to 19.6 per cent, while girls' share declined to 24.4 per cent.
The gender gap for top GCSE grades has fallen below 5 percentage points for the first time in records dating back to 2001.
The pass rate for English and maths declined for the fifth consecutive year due to record numbers of students failing resits.
Girls' absence rates, illness-related absences, and persistent absence have increased more sharply since the pandemic compared to boys.
Boys improved their share of top grades more than girls in popular subjects like combined science and maths.

title: United Utilities 'extremely sorry' after burst pipe led to flooding
author: Dan Wareing
content:
![A street is flooded, and a man in crouching down in the water. There is a truck parked up on the side of the street.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/395/cpsprodpb/23fc/live/628f3400-9c68-11f1-827b-69a6492daae1.jpg)
Homes on Elm Vale in Fairfield were evacuated after a burst water main caused flooding
- Published
A water company has said it is "extremely sorry" for the disruption caused by a burst pipe which led to flooding and forced people to evacuate their homes.
Repairs are under way on Prescot Road in Fairfield, Liverpool, after a water main burst on Wednesday evening, United Utilities (UU) said.
People on the neighbouring street, Elm Vale, were told to leave their properties and a reception centre was set up to provide shelter.
UU said some customers may notice changes in water pressure, external at busy times during the repair work or some temporary discolouration of their water.
![A hole in the road with green cables over it - surrounded by metal fencing. Workers in yellow outfits and white hats stand nearby](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/8d00/live/e4d174a0-9c68-11f1-827b-69a6492daae1.jpg)
United Utilities managed to divert the water around its network
The water firm said it had "isolated the burst" and "moved water around our network and will also be using our Water on Wheels tankers to top up supplies in the area".
"We are extremely sorry for the disruption caused by this major water main burst in Liverpool," a spokesperson added.
'Natural sediments'
It said the temporary discolouration of the water was due to "using different routes through our network to keep water flowing to homes and businesses".
"If your water looks discoloured, don't worry - this can happen when natural sediments in the pipes are disturbed," a spokesperson said.
UU said customers whose properties had been damaged "as a direct result of the burst" would be compensated.
They thanked locals for "their patience, understanding and kindness" towards its workers.
Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service (MFRS) said crews were alerted just after 17:30 BST.
![Road Closed sign next to traffic cones and yellow fencing - with fencing around a hole where repairs take place](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/c02d/live/024d5e40-9c69-11f1-827b-69a6492daae1.jpg)
There are several road closures while work is carried out
A full evacuation of Tudor Court took place due to flood water in the basement.
MFRS said the council provided 16 tonnes of stone to assist with water diversions.
The leak had stopped by 23:22 and UU restored supplies by using the network to bypass the damaged pipe, it added.
There will be road closures and traffic disruption in the area while work takes place to carry out repairs.
![A digger lifts up a mound of earth as workers in fluorescent yellow and orange stand nearby with white safety helmets on](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/8032/live/54be6080-9c77-11f1-8413-79a38c9f8909.jpg)
Work continues to try and fix the burst pipe
Listen to the best of BBC Radio Merseyside on Sounds and follow BBC Merseyside on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external. You can also send story ideas via Whatsapp to 0808 100 2230.
summary: United Utilities issued an apology after a burst water main on Prescot Road in Liverpool caused severe flooding and forced residents on Elm Vale and Tudor Court to evacuate. Emergency repairs and water diversions began on Wednesday evening, with the leak stopped by late night. Customers may experience temporary water pressure changes, discolouration due to disturbed sediments, and ongoing road closures while work continues.
key_points: A burst water main in Fairfield, Liverpool, led to flooding and home evacuations on Elm Vale and Tudor Court.
United Utilities stated it is extremely sorry for the disruption and confirmed repairs are under way.
Water supplies were restored using network bypasses and Water on Wheels tankers, though temporary discolouration and pressure changes may occur.
Customers whose properties suffered direct damage from the burst will be compensated.
Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service and the council assisted with the response, and road closures remain in place during repairs.

title: Burnham announces plans to clean up worst three illegal waste dumps
author: Jennifer McKiernan; Jenny Kumar
content:
![Andy Burnham is wearing a dark-coloured jacket, light blue shirt and glasses. He has short black hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/1916/live/fe3e8cc0-9c68-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
- Published
Three of the country's worst illegal dumps are due to be cleaned up using taxpayers' money, the government has announced.
Sites in Kent, Surrey and West Yorkshire will be assessed for clearance, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying the "toxic dumps have blighted communities for too long".
Fines for waste offences will also rise from Â£300 to Â£5,000 to deter, catch, and punish those who dump illegally, and the Environment Agency will have more powers to seize assets bought with the proceeds of crime by those involved.
But opposition parties said illegal dumps were a small part of a much bigger issue with smaller scale fly-tipping and landfill all posing big problems for communities.
Burnham is looking to build on work started by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to tackle waste crime, with an action plan published in March detailing a series of measures - including using drones to map illegal waste sites.
The government said the new sites identified for clearance contain around 22,000 tonnes of illegally dumped waste.
They are: Power Station Road, on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent; Aymer Close, in Runnymede, Surrey; and Midland Road in Bradford, West Yorkshire.
West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester will be the first areas with new region-led approaches to waste crime.
The government said this will give mayors and council leaders the lead in co-ordinating councils, police, regulators, and other enforcement agencies.
Burnham said: "The days of making easy money out of waste are over. We're giving authorities the powers to hunt down the people responsible. We will seize their assets and shut their operations down."
A new "waste crime crackdown group", chaired by Environment Secretary Angela Eagle, will bring regulators and law enforcement together in a bid to dismantle criminal operations.
Eagle said: "We are cleaning up sites, but we are also stopping the cycle, driving faster prevention and disruption, better intelligence, and stronger coordination across the system."
A Green Party spokesperson agreed a crackdown was needed, but highlighted that smaller-scale dumping was a bigger issue and called for extra ring-fenced funding.
"We also need to boost the circular economy, so households and businesses are better able to reuse, repair, repurpose and recycle goods and make manufacturers and producers responsible for the safe disposal for the goods and packaging they produce," they added.
Liberal Democrat environment spokesperson Tim Farron welcomed tougher fines but said waste crime was only one part of a bigger problem, and called for an independent review of the waste system.
"Andy Burnham needs to wake up and smell the landfill," he said.
"New mayoral powers won't cut it if the National Crime Agency isn't empowered to clear these illegal sites, and stop legal sites spiralling out of control.
"We need an independent review of the whole system to crack down on these organised gangs once and for all."
The Conservatives and Reform UK have been contacted for comment.
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âGet the latest political analysis and big moments, delivered straight to your inbox every weekdayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/6fad/live/133a6af0-dc98-11ef-bc01-8f2c83dad217.png)
Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to read top political analysis, gain insight from across the UK and stay up to speed with the big moments. It'll be delivered straight to your inbox every weekday.
summary: The government has announced plans to use taxpayers' money to clean up three of the country's worst illegal waste dumps in Kent, Surrey, and West Yorkshire. Prime Minister Andy Burnham also revealed measures including raising waste fines from £300 to £5,000, granting the Environment Agency asset-seizure powers, and introducing region-led approaches for mayors and council leaders. Opposition parties welcomed the crackdown but argued that illegal dumps represent only a small part of a broader waste crisis involving fly-tipping and landfill issues.
key_points: Three major illegal dumps containing about 22,000 tonnes of waste in Kent, Surrey, and West Yorkshire will be cleared using taxpayers' money.
Fines for waste offences will increase from £300 to £5,000.
The Environment Agency will receive expanded powers to seize assets purchased with the proceeds of crime.
West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester will pilot new region-led approaches giving mayors and council leaders coordination authority.
Opposition parties noted that illegal dumps are part of a wider issue and called for broader systemic reviews and additional measures.

title: Travelodge boss steps down after security issues in rooms
author: Faarea Masud
content:
In an interview with the BBC, Travelodge chief executive Jo Boydell says she only became aware of the assault during the court case almost three years later
- Published
The boss of hotel chain Travelodge, Jo Boydell, is stepping down as the group addresses safety issues after a sexual assault at one of its hotels.
A woman staying at a hotel in Maidenhead, Berkshire was sexually assaulted in December 2022 after a man lied to staff to get a key card to her room, triggering an independent review of security measures at the hotel giant.
Kyran Smith was jailed for seven years and six months for the attack.
Boydell, who stood down on 17 August, has been replaced on an interim basis by Ray Reidy. In a statement, Reidy said: "We remain focused on the safety and well-being of our guests and will continue taking the actions necessary to strengthen the business.
"We will also continue to engage proactively and constructively with government and the wider hospitality industry on the issue of safety and security."
Following the court case against Smith, the BBC was contacted by many people over concerns about security failures at the hotel.
Earlier this month, a domestic violence victim told the BBC how she was attacked in her hotel room after Travelodge reception staff gave a key to her abuser.
The woman said she was "failed" by the chain and described it as one of the "most traumatic nights of my life" after the man kicked the door off its hinges.
Boydell had been criticised for the company's handling of issues with its safety and security.
In March, the then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer wrote to Boydell urging her to "seriously engage" with the government over security at its hotels.
In another incident, a couple in Scotland woke to find a shirtless man in their hotel bedroom after he was mistakenly given a key card to their door.
In yet another case in April, a group of hotel guests said they were given keys to other people's rooms twice in one week at a Travelodge branch in Newham, east London.
John Nowell, who was part of a corporate group staying at the hotel, told the BBC that his key card allowed him into a room where the occupant was in the middle of a shower.
summary: Travelodge chief executive Jo Boydell has stepped down following criticism over security issues and safety failures at the hotel chain. The leadership change comes after multiple incidents where guests were mistakenly or fraudulently given key cards to occupied rooms, including a 2022 sexual assault in Maidenhead. Ray Reidy has taken over as interim chief executive while the company focuses on strengthening guest safety.
key_points: Travelodge CEO Jo Boydell stepped down on August 17 and was replaced on an interim basis by Ray Reidy.
The leadership change follows security failures, including a December 2022 sexual assault where a man obtained a key card by lying to staff.
Other reported incidents involved staff mistakenly giving key cards to abusers, strangers, and other guests.
In March, then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer urged Boydell to seriously engage with the government regarding hotel security.
