title: Students wait for GCSE and BTec grades as app launches for 750 schools in England
author: Hazel Shearing
content:
![A teenage boy with short light brown hair sits indoors, holding and looking at a black smartphone. He wears a light grey sweatshirt over a white shirt. The blurred background features a painting on the wall and a blue sofa behind him.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/b521/live/5e586fc0-9bc6-11f1-98c6-93bfcdb08681.jpg)
- Published
Pupils in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive GCSE, BTecs and other Level 2 results on Thursday, with some grades in England available through an app that is rolling out for the first time.
Schools and colleges will distribute grades in person, but from 11:00 BST pupils at more than 750 schools in England will also be able to see their grades on their phones.
Results this year come as the government in England plans to boost technical education and address a growing number of English and Maths GCSE resits.
Last year, 67.4% of all GCSE entries were graded 4/C or above.
The pass rate for National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher exams in Scotland rose across the board at the start of the month.
And top A-level results increased slightly again last week â with 28.5% of all grades across England, Wales and Northern Ireland marked at A* or A.
Students will get results for BTec Tech Awards, BTec Firsts and BTec Level 2 Technical courses on Thursday, as well as for Cambridge Nationals.
Last year, more than 360,000 results for vocational and technical qualifications were given out.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants to make more technical subjects available to teenagers, and has announced plans for schools and colleges in England to offer subjects like manufacturing and AI in addition to core academic learning from Year 10.
![The image shows a table comparing old GCSE letter grades with the newer number grades. It has two columns, a grey column for the old letter grades and a red column for the number grades. The table runs from A* at the top, matching grade 9, down to U at the bottom.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/800/cpsprodpb/b1f2/live/0539b590-9bb5-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
This year, pupils at more than 750 secondary schools in England will be able to see their results on their phones.
The Department for Education (DfE) says pupils will still go into school to get their results in envelopes first, but they will also be able to access their results through the Education Record app from 11:00 BST.
A record of their results will stay in the app for colleges and future employers to review, in a move the government hopes will reduce paperwork for students and teachers.
In England, pupils who do not get at least a grade 4 in GCSE English and maths must continue studying for it alongside their next course, whether this is A-levels, a T-level, or something else.
Resitting is not a requirement, according to the DfE, but colleges will generally enter students into exams when they think they are ready.
GCSE English and maths resits take place in November and May or June.
Last year, nearly a quarter of maths and English GCSEs were taken by people aged 17 and older. Some will have been mature students sitting exams for the first time, but most were young people resitting papers.
A government-commissioned report in May cited research suggesting that half of 18 to 25-year-olds in England without level 2 qualifications - including GCSEs at grade 4/C and above - have spent time not in employment, education or training.
Skills minister Baroness Jacqui Smith said in October that the DfE planned to introduce a new qualification as a "stepping stone" to GCSE resits, helping students who "too often have been on this demoralising roundabout of taking exams and failing them".
Data shows that girls are more likely than boys to pass GCSEs, but last year the gap between them was the lowest on record - with girls' pass rates dropping and boys' pass rates rising very slightly.
There was also a regional divide. The gap between the highest and lowest-performing regions shrank, but remained higher than before the Covid pandemic.
Disparities in GCSE results are often framed through the lens of a North-South divide, but there are also challenges facing children in coastal and rural parts of England.
For example, in South West England, 40% of children eligible for free school meals obtained a grade 4 in maths and English at GCSE compared with 56% of the same cohort in London.
This is the third year that grading has returned to pre-pandemic standards across all three nations.
The proportion of GCSE passes rose in 2020 and 2021 when exams were cancelled and results were based on teachers' assessments.
That was followed by a phased effort to bring them back down to 2019 levels.
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/d048/live/80825d90-55a8-11f1-b682-cf91850925ea.png)
summary: Pupils in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland are set to receive their GCSE, BTec, and other Level 2 results. Alongside traditional in-person collection, students at more than 750 schools in England will also be able to access their grades via a new Education Record app starting at 11:00 BST. This year's results follow recent increases in top A-level grades and Scottish exam pass rates.
key_points: Students in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland will receive GCSE and BTec results on Thursday.
An app is rolling out to over 750 schools in England, allowing students to view their grades on their phones from 11:00 BST.
The government plans to introduce technical education options and address growing numbers of English and Maths GCSE resits.
Grading has returned to pre-pandemic standards for the third consecutive year across all three nations.

title: Downpours continue for UK with risk of flash flooding
author: Ben Rich
content:
![A discarded flood warning sign sits in a field of long dry grass](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/097c/live/a609a580-9bd7-11f1-bb4d-1147ef2e78e5.jpg)
- Published
Heavy showers and thunderstorms will continue to affect large swathes of the UK on Thursday, bringing the threat of flooding and travel disruption.
A Met Office yellow thunderstorm warning remains in force across northern England and north Wales until 10:00 BST on Thursday.
The downpours will drift southwards and eastwards during the day, affecting other parts of Wales, the Midlands, East Anglia and southern England.
Drivers are being warned that the return to wet weather could lead to slippery conditions as well as the risk of flooded roads.
Temperatures are also forecast to drop with some places expected to remain below the August average over the next few days.
Low pressure drifts eastwards
After a summer that has largely been dominated by high pressure, low pressure has now taken control.
Unstable air underneath the low has allowed big storm clouds to develop, capable of delivering torrential downpours accompanied by hail and thunder.
During Thursday morning, northern England and north Wales will bear the brunt of the thunderstorms.
![A map showing the Met Office yellow warning area, stretching from Newcastle in the north to Holyhead in the south](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/596/cpsprodpb/27a3/live/025d34a0-9bd8-11f1-bb4d-1147ef2e78e5.jpg)
The Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms remains in force until 10:00 BST
Within the Met Office yellow warning area, 15-20mm of rain could fall in just an hour, with 30-50mm possible in a six hour period.
Flash flooding is possible, especially in areas where the ground remains very hard after the prolonged hot, dry spell.
Lightning and hail will bring additional hazards.
Showers are expected to ease from the north during the morning, migrating southwards into other parts of Wales as well as central and southern England where a few downpours could still be heavy and thundery.
As ever with showers, some places will see more rain than others.
Scotland and Northern Ireland will also have showers but they should be less intense, with a lower chance of thunder.
Tricky driving conditions
Motoring experts warn that wet weather after a prolonged dry spell can cause dangerous driving conditions.
RAC road safety spokesperson Rod Dennis says: "Oil, fuel and rubber deposits that have built up over many weeks will now have been mixed together by the light rain, instead of being washed away, which means drivers are at greater risk of skidding on greasy roads.
"If heavier rain arrives, motorists may have to contend with the danger of flash floods in some areas."
Drivers are being advised to reduce their speed and leave extra space between them and the vehicle in front.
No end in sight for the drought
Even as rain has returned, experts are warning that the drought gripping large swathes of the UK will not immediately come to an end.
It will need a sustained period of persistent rainfall to replenish water stocks and we are unlikely to know whether this has happened until late in the upcoming winter.
However, it is worth adding that while most areas have seen rainfall well below normal this summer - with some locations having a two month dry spell - that has not been the case everywhere.
Aultbea in the Scottish Highlands has recorded 389.6mm of rain so far this summer - more than one and a half times the seasonal norm, and only 10.2mm short of its wettest summer on record.
Temperatures fall below average
As northerly winds develop across the UK, temperatures are set to drop.
Thursday afternoon is expected to bring highs of 13-23C.
It is expected to be the first day since 29 June when temperatures will fail to reach 25C anywhere in the UK.
Friday is set to be cooler still with temperatures widely remaining below the August norm.
![A weather chart showing Friday afternoon's temperatures - ranging from 12C in Lerwick to 21C in Plymouth, London and St Helier](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/665/cpsprodpb/a793/live/20358a90-9be2-11f1-ba30-ddd78081057f.jpg)
Daytime highs of 15-23C would be typical across the UK in August
Friday night will also be the chilliest for quite some time with temperatures widely dropping into single digits.
Parts of Scotland and northern England could see lows of 3 or 4C.
Chilly nights will continue to feature over the weekend although daytime temperatures will rebound a little as high pressure tries to build - meaning less rain and more sunshine.
You can keep up to date with your local forecast on the BBC Weather website and app.
summary: Heavy showers and thunderstorms are continuing to affect large parts of the UK, bringing risks of flash flooding and travel disruption. A Met Office yellow thunderstorm warning is in place, while low pressure drives the unsettled weather and causes temperatures to drop below the August average. Experts warn that the current rainfall will not immediately end the ongoing drought, and drivers face hazardous road conditions.
key_points: A Met Office yellow thunderstorm warning is in force for northern England and north Wales.
Flash flooding is possible, particularly where ground remains hard from dry weather.
Wet weather following a dry spell creates greasy road conditions and skidding risks for drivers.
Temperatures are dropping below the August average, with chilly single-digit lows expected in some areas.
Experts state that a sustained period of persistent rainfall is needed to end the UK drought.

title: ‘Burnham’s writing cheques, this one might bounce’: homeless people doubt PM’s plan
author: Amelia Gentleman; Jessica Murray
content:
As Andy Burnham set out his plan to end rough sleeping on Tuesday night, volunteers from homelessness charity Under One Sky were offering hot drinks, sandwiches, socks, underwear and soap to dozens of rough sleepers around Tottenham Court Road in central London.
Among those sleeping on the streets, the prime minister’s plan was met with widespread scepticism born from long familiarity with similar political declarations.
“You can never end rough sleeping. I think he is taking on a monumental task,” said a former construction worker in his 50s, who did not want to be named.
He was living in a hostel after struggling to find work over the past few years, and was reluctant to sign on for unemployment benefits. “[Burnham] has committed himself to the target; if he doesn’t fulfil it, there will be problems. I wouldn’t have done that,” he said.
Many said it was hard to follow the news without regular internet access, but several were aware that Burnham had made a commitment to end rough sleeping when he came to power.
“He has made a pledge? You mean he has said some words?” said one man in his 60s who has been sleeping intermittently in a tent in front of a furniture shop for several years.
He was reluctant to say why he was homeless, only that he had previously owned a restaurant before losing his house. He chose to stay in his spot on the street because of the easy access to a nearby hospital, and said he was not looking for any help from the government.
“I don’t want to go to a hostel because they’re full of people with drug problems. I’ll sort myself out,” he said.
Burnham has likened his plan to the “Everyone In” scheme launched during the Covid pandemic, which housed thousands of rough sleepers, mainly in hotels, during lockdown.
“We got people out of the cold because, as a country, we decided it had to be done. We can do it again,” Burnham said in an article for the Guardian on Tuesday.
But many working in the homelessness sector said it will not be easy to recreate this feat. Adam Soliman, a deputy manager at St Mungo’s, a homeless charity, ran a Holiday Inn branch that was used to house rough sleepers during the pandemic.
He said while the scheme was successful at getting people through the door, it did not help them to stop rough sleeping in the long term, largely because there were no permanent homes for people to move to.
“Bringing people in is great and gives them a sense of safety, but if there’s no move-on options, we’re just putting a plaster on the issue,” he said.
![Andy Burnham speaks with a service user in a kitchen](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/005564418b463e2c1ede6b5bfa90519a436155d2/0_0_4762_3175/master/4762.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“Is there going to be more affordable housing for people? Is there going to be more money for mental health services?
“It’s great to get everyone in by Christmas, but on 1st January, what’s the plan?”
He also said there are many people, often with mental health or addiction problems, who refuse to engage with services for many years.
Lesley Howard, head of homelessness at charity Change Grow Live, which helps substance misusers, said the answer would not be found by “throwing more money at the issue”.
“We need to think it through and we need to make sure there’s longer-term funding because these things take time,” she said.
“During the pandemic, we had a lot of hotels that were open for people to go into. That’s not going to be the offer this time – is it going to be night shelters? That’s not necessarily an offer everyone will accept.”
Government guidance states councils should use studio flats, shared houses, supported accommodation, B&Bs, hostels and night shelters to house rough sleepers over the coming months.
Near the bars of Soho, a man who had recently been released from prison said there were lots of ex-prisoners on the streets.
“We saw that it can be done overnight; they did it during Covid. There are so many buildings up and down the country that are empty,” he said.
But he remained sceptical about whether Burnham would succeed. “He says he is going to eradicate homelessness. He is writing cheques at the moment, and this one might bounce.”
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent pledge to end rough sleeping has been met with widespread skepticism from rough sleepers and homelessness charity workers in London. While Burnham has compared his goal to the successful "Everyone In" pandemic initiative, sector experts warn that a lack of permanent housing, long-term funding, and move-on options makes the new target extremely difficult to achieve. Many individuals living on the streets also expressed doubt or reluctance to utilize government housing services.
key_points: Andy Burnham announced a plan and commitment to end rough sleeping, likening it to the "Everyone In" pandemic scheme.
Rough sleepers interviewed in central London expressed deep skepticism and doubt regarding the prime minister's ability to fulfill his pledge.
Charity workers from organizations like St Mungo's and Change Grow Live noted that temporary housing solutions fail in the long term without permanent affordable housing and sustained funding.
Some individuals experiencing homelessness are reluctant to use hostels or government services due to safety concerns, drug problems, or personal preference.

title: Andy Burnham to donate 15% of PM salary to homelessness fight
author: Liam Geraghty
content:
“There are things that we can do. We proved it in the pandemic. We should do it again now and it should just be what we do all the time.”
Burnham made a pledge to end rough sleeping his first instruction after being unveiled as prime minister last month.
This week he laid out his first steps on how he intends to achieve a milestone that has eluded governments since the New Labour years. Burnham’s approach echoes the Everyone In scheme that saw rough sleepers taken off the streets during the Covid pandemic.

title: Prince Harry and Meghan ‘moving back to Britain this month’
author: Nadeem Badshah
content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are planning to return to live in Britain, six years after leaving for the US, it has been reported.
The couple and their two children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are expected to relocate later this month to a non-royal residence.
The property is believed to be outside London, and the children are enrolled to start school in September, the Daily Telegraph reported.
King Charles was informed on Sunday that his son and daughter-in-law would return to Britain, according to the Telegraph.
It comes after the Sussexes, who have lived in California since 2020, had a reunion with the king last month at Highgrove in Gloucestershire.
The king is said to welcome the opportunity to see more of his family in a personal capacity but there will be no change in their status as private individuals after relinquishing their official working roles within the royal family.
The Prince and Princess of Wales are said to have also been informed of the decision.
The couple are expected to retain their homes in Montecito, California, and Portugal, where they went on holiday earlier this summer.
The duke and duchess’s security arrangements have not been disclosed.
The long-running issue over their security meant that Prince Harry did not bring Meghan, 45, or their children to events in London last month, as had been originally planned.
Prince Harry, 41, has previously stressed he would not feel safe bringing his family back to the UK without police protection.
In May 2025, after losing a legal challenge over his security in the UK, the Duke of Sussex said: “I can’t see a world in which I would bring my wife and children back to the UK at this point.”
In an interview with the BBC after the ruling, Prince Harry said he “would love a reconciliation” with the royal family.
He said: “There have been so many disagreements between myself and some of my family,” but he had now “forgiven” them.
“I would love reconciliation with my family. There’s no point continuing to fight any more, life is precious.”
Prince Harry added the dispute over his security had “always been the sticking point”.
Asked whether he had asked the king to intervene in the dispute over security, he said: “I never asked him to intervene – I asked him to step out of the way and let the experts do their jobs.”
Last month, the Duke of Sussex and six other co-claimants lost their privacy case against the publishers of the Daily Mail in London. The claimants, who included Doreen Lawrence and Elton John, sued Associated Newspapers Ltd over allegations of unlawful information gathering. Their claims were dismissed in their entirety by Mr Justice Nicklin.
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are reportedly planning to move back to Britain from California this month with their two children. King Charles and the Prince and Princess of Wales were reportedly informed of the decision following a recent family reunion at Highgrove. The couple's return comes despite ongoing disputes regarding their UK security arrangements, and their official working roles within the royal family will remain unchanged.
key_points: Prince Harry and Meghan are reportedly moving back to Britain this month with their children, Archie and Lilibet.
King Charles and the Prince and Princess of Wales were informed of the relocation plan.
The couple plans to live in a non-royal residence outside London and enroll their children in school for September.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are expected to retain their homes in California and Portugal.
Security arrangements for the family have not been disclosed, following previous legal challenges regarding UK police protection.

title: Prince Harry and Meghan moving back to UK
author: Daniela Relph; Olivia Ireland
content:
![Prince Harry and Meghan waving as they arrive at the Australian National Veterans Arts Museum in Melbourne, Australia on 14 April 2026.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/1aa9/live/d0abf130-9c1d-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
- Published
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are planning to move back to the UK, BBC News understands.
As first reported by the Daily Telegraph, external and the Sun,, external Prince Harry and Meghan intend to relocate from the US later this month to a private, non-royal residence outside London.
The couple's children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are enrolled to start at a British school in September.
King Charles was told of the move on Sunday. There are no current plans for either Prince Harry or Meghan to resume their roles as working Royals.
The Sussexes and their children visited the King at his Highgrove home in July this year, but it is understood the move was not discussed.
The BBC understands the King was unaware of the move before last weekend but he welcomes the opportunity to see more of the Sussex family in a private and personal capacity.
But there will be no expected change to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.
Prince William and Princess Catherine have also been informed of their plans.
The couple's move from California comes after they left the UK and royal duties in early 2020.
Family relations had been strained since, with July's visit to the King and Queen Camilla being a key development in their relationship.
The Palace described the meeting at the King's private home in Gloucestershire as a "private family occasion".
It was the first time the King had seen his grandchildren in person in more than four years.
Prince Harry and Meghan had not been in the UK together since 2022, when they attended the funeral of Queen Elizabeth II.
Security for the couple has long been a point of tension, with the July visit being reconsidered because the duke's request for police protection was rejected.
Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.
The Duke had sought to overturn a decision that had downgraded his security after he stopped being a working royal and moved to the US with the Duchess.
Prince Harry had previously said that worries about safety have prevented him from coming to the UK and bring his wife and children.
![Thin, purple banner promoting the Royal Watch newsletter with text saying, âInsider stories and expert analysis in your inbox every weekâ. There is also a graphic of a fleur-de-lis in white.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/ef34/live/a99f61b0-109d-11f0-b234-07dc7691c360.png)
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan are planning to relocate from the US back to the UK later this month to a private residence outside London. Their children, Archie and Lilibet, are enrolled to start at a British school in September. King Charles and Prince William's family have been informed of the move, though the Sussexes will remain private individuals with no plans to resume working royal roles.
key_points: Prince Harry and Meghan intend to move back to the UK from the US later this month.
The couple's children are enrolled to start at a British school in September.
King Charles was informed of the relocation last weekend and welcomes seeing more of the family.
There are no plans for Prince Harry and Meghan to resume their roles as working royals.

title: Exclusive: Harry and Meghan plan move back to Britain
author: Victoria Ward
content:
![Prince Harry and Meghan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498866743_17871632651010_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwWPw2b5__oFarkj5WlWIJuI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Prince Harry and Meghan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498866743_17871632651010_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwWPw2b5__oFarkj5WlWIJuI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are planning to move back to Britain, The Telegraph can reveal.
The family intends to relocate from the US later this month to a private, non-royal residence thought to be outside London.
Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, the couple’s children, are enrolled to start at a British school in September.
There are no current plans for either the Duke or Duchess of Sussex to reprise their official working roles within the Royal family. However, the move raises the prospect that they could do so in the future.
The King was informed of the move on Sunday. It was not discussed when the Sussexes visited him at Highgrove in July, it is understood. He was said to be naturally pleased for the opportunity to see more of his family on a regular basis, both in a private and personal capacity.
However, the King is clear that the Duke and Duchess’s status as non-working royals and private individuals, in keeping with their previously expressed wishes, will remain unchanged.
The Prince and Princess of Wales have also been informed of the move.
![The Duke and Duchess with their children, Lilibet and Archie](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000453992647_17871459552520_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqCu-rHd-sgjqZvaAjQdr_s9luWBnPl6Sn_iGFrIRcxE.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The Duke and Duchess’s security arrangements have not been disclosed, but there has been no announcement of any change. Prince Harry has previously made it clear that he would not feel safe bringing his family back to the UK without police protection, something he has been fighting for for several years.
The British state has so far steadfastly refused to provide him with police support.
The couple will retain their homes in Montecito, California, and Portugal, while the Duchess will continue to run her lifestyle brand As Ever – which sources insist is thriving – from their new base.
Sources suggested that the UK would be their primary home for an extended period, although it had not yet been decided whether to make the move permanent. The locations of the home and school have not been made public for privacy reasons.
The decision comes more than six years after the couple quit royal duties and moved abroad in search of financial independence, agreeing not to use their HRH titles.
In a statement released in 2021, following a 12-month review of their situation, Elizabeth II confirmed that the couple would not “continue with the responsibilities and duties that come with a life of public service”.
She had made it clear that they could not maintain a “half-in, half-out” approach to royal duties while also pursuing commercial opportunities. The Duke and Duchess responded by saying: “We can all live a life of service. Service is universal.”
Prince Harry was stripped of his honorary military titles but has continued to support a handful of charities. The couple believe they have since proved that the “half-in, half-out” model does work.
After moving to the US, the Duke and Duchess made a series of incendiary allegations that shook the Royal family to its core.
They suggested that senior royals were racist by asking questions about the colour of their unborn son’s skin. The Duchess of Sussex also revealed that she had had suicidal thoughts and had struggled with her mental health after joining the Royal family.
![The Duke and Duchess](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000473770726_17871504877150_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqvoXbRQehuJNQprvLCxGprovjVPZKjB48ONGNjYqQH1M.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
She said in a 2019 television interview that British friends had warned her before marrying Prince Harry that the tabloids would destroy her life, and she described the British way of dealing with emotions as “probably really damaging”.
In a 2022 magazine interview, she alleged that she would “never be able to do school pick-up and drop-off” in Britain “without it being a royal photo call”.
While the Duke has started building bridges with his father, his relationship with his brother, Prince William, remains deeply fractured.
The pair are not thought to have spoken for years. Both the Prince and Princess of Wales are said to feel deeply betrayed by the revelations made in the Duke’s memoir, Spare, and in various television interviews.
![The Prince and Princess of Wales with Harry](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/royal-family/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498851847_17871526761720_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqMG9jYnib85FJIfCc-bQYcSXF5qJfRX82QwtVzSKzjL8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
However, Prince Harry has long made it clear that he misses the UK and is desperate for his children to experience British life and culture.
The move will also enable him to dedicate further time to his charitable organisations.
Invictus 2027 takes place in Birmingham next July, and the Duke fervently hopes that the King will join him to open the event.
![Harry at the Invictus games](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000494697482_17871505462100_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqaBJSHwufYM_Fh0ArUj1hel5NUcTKNHKqy85KLqtvPLE.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
His relationship with his father has improved in recent months, with the pair chatting regularly on the phone.
When the Duke and Duchess returned to the UK last month, they enjoyed a long-awaited reunion with the King and Queen at Highgrove, the monarch’s Gloucestershire home.
It was a significant moment and marked the first time Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet had seen their grandfather in four years. The meeting was considered a key step on the road to reconciliation.
The Sussexes have already sought to build a base in Europe, buying property in Portugal, at the prestigious Costa Terra resort in Melides, in 2023. The country is popular with US emigrants and offers a so-called golden visa granting EU residency in exchange for an investment of at least €250,000 (£216,000), provided the visa holders stay in the country for seven days a year.
summary: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are planning to relocate from the United States to a private residence in Britain later this month, with their children enrolled to start at a British school in September. The King and the Prince and Princess of Wales have been informed of the move, though the couple will remain non-working royals. The UK is intended to serve as their primary home for an extended period, while they also retain properties in California and Portugal.
key_points: Prince Harry and Meghan are planning to move back to Britain from the US later this month.
Their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, are enrolled to start at a British school in September.
The King was informed of the move and is pleased to see more of his family, but the couple's status as non-working royals will remain unchanged.
The couple will keep their homes in Montecito and Portugal while using the UK as their primary residence for an extended period.

title: My kids are petrified going to Shepherd's Bush, says Laila Cunningham after stabbing
author: Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Laila Cunningham tells how she has brought up her children](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/9ec17174-20a8-5108-b76c-a892fc39daa3/thumbnail-360.webp)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
![Bus driver Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa died after being shot on Monday evening in Clapham (Metropolitan Police/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/12/18/10d77b27d5b3de0bfdc57923c38f4a4cY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg2NjQxNDg4-2.85545879.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
“My own kids swim in Shepherd’s Bush. They’re now petrified of going there. And as their mum so am I.
“We were there last weekend. It increasingly feels like nowhere is safe.
“Sadiq Khan can keep telling us London is safe, but that means very little to families living with this fear,” she added.
But Sir Sadiq has rejected claims of a “lawless London” with high numbers of shootings and stabbings.
Earlier this week, he hit out at Donald Trump and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK who have sought to argue that the capital is plagued by crime.
He posted on X: “The loudest voices online aren't always the most accurate.
“New data shows our homicide rate is lower than every US state, while murder rates are at record lows.
“The evidence is clear: our approach to tackling crime and its causes works. It’s driving down violence right across the capital.”
![Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan said the research ‘proves we were right to act’ (Victoria Jones/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/07/6cf18c2a55353082ea87aedde5a23035Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MTQ0ODM2-2.75224103.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Scotland Yard said a man, aged 48, had been arrested on suspicion of murder and attempted murder after a woman was fatally stabbed in Shepherd’s Bush, west London.
Read More
Police were called to reports of a stabbing shortly before 8.30am on Tuesday, 18 August, at an address on Askew Road, Shepherd’s Bush.
Officers attended the scene with the London Ambulance Service where two women, aged 52 and 32, were found with stab wounds.
Despite the best efforts of medical professionals, the older woman was pronounced dead at the scene.
Her next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by specially-trained officers.
The 32-year-old woman was taken to hospital.
Detective Inspector Richard MacKenzie, who is leading the investigation, said: “We believe this to be an isolated incident within a residential address, but we know it will cause concern locally.”
There were 97 homicides in the capital in 2025, down 36 per cent from 153 in 2019 and 11 per cent fewer than the 109 in 2024.
The Met said last year also had the lowest killings since 95 took place 11 years ago in 2014.
The force stated that 2025 saw a homicide rate of 1.1 per 100,000 people - safer than comparable global cities such as New York at 2.8, Paris (1.6), Toronto (1.6), Berlin (3.2), Los Angeles (5.6), Chicago (11.7), and Philadelphia (12.3).
Just days ago, detectives investigating the murder of 25-year-old Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa renewed their appeal for information.
The Transport for London bus driver died on Willington Road, Clapham, at around 10pm on Monday, 10 August.
Following the shooting, officers arrested a 22-year-old man on suspicion of murder after he attended hospital with a gunshot wound.
He was later discharged and released with no further action following further police enquiries.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/16/01M0AJ3H1BBYM2JA29BGJV0VQD.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Separately, detectives launched a murder investigation after a man in his 40s was found inside a vehicle with gunshot wounds at around 3am on Tuesday August 18.
summary: Following a fatal stabbing in Shepherd's Bush, local concerns about safety have grown, with residents expressing fear despite London Mayor Sadiq Khan defending the capital's safety record and citing declining homicide rates. Police arrested a 48-year-old man on suspicion of murder and attempted murder after two women were stabbed at a residential address on Askew Road. Meanwhile, detectives are also investigating separate fatal incidents involving firearms, including the shooting of a bus driver in Clapham.
key_points: A 52-year-old woman was killed and a 32-year-old woman was injured in a stabbing on Askew Road in Shepherd's Bush.
A 48-year-old man was arrested by Scotland Yard on suspicion of murder and attempted murder regarding the Shepherd's Bush incident.
Mayor Sadiq Khan rejected claims of a lawless London, stating that data shows record low murder rates and a lower homicide rate than every US state.
Police are conducting separate investigations into other fatal incidents, including the shooting of bus driver Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa in Clapham.

title: Hounslow murder investigation launched as woman dies after fire
author: Jess Warren
content:
![A general view of Berkley Avenue in Hounslow.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/521/cpsprodpb/7d82/live/7d47bb80-9bf2-11f1-8470-d18257d2d589.png)
A 48-year-old woman died in hospital following a fire at a residential address in Hounslow
- Published
A murder investigation is under way after a 48-year-old woman died in a fire in west London.
Officers were called to a residential address on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow, at about 01:15 BST on Wednesday following reports of the blaze, the Metropolitan Police said.
Six men and three women were taken to hospital, where the 48-year-old woman died. Another woman, 40, is in a life-threatening condition.
The Met said no arrests had been made but officers believed the fire may have been started deliberately. Det Ch Insp Neil John said: "Our inquiries are progressing at pace as we work to establish the full circumstances surrounding the fire."
John said the force's thoughts were "first and foremost with the victim's family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time, as well as everyone who has been injured".
The remaining seven people have been discharged after receiving treatment for minor injuries.
John said the force understood the incident to be isolated to a residential address, but officers would remain in the area and provide updates as the investigation continues.
A London Ambulance Service spokesperson said: "We were called at 01:18 BST today to reports of a fire on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow.
"We sent resources to the scene including ambulance crews, a paramedic in a fast-response car, an incident response officer and paramedics from our hazardous area response team.
"We treated nine patients and took them all to hospital."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: A murder investigation has been launched after a 48-year-old woman died in hospital following a residential fire on Berkeley Avenue in Hounslow. Police and emergency services responded to the blaze at about 01:15 BST on Wednesday, taking nine people to the hospital. Authorities believe the fire may have been started deliberately, though no arrests have been made at this time.
key_points: A 48-year-old woman died following a fire at a residential address in Hounslow.
A 40-year-old woman remains in a life-threatening condition in the hospital.
Six men and three women in total were taken to the hospital for treatment.
Police believe the fire may have been started deliberately, and no arrests have been made yet.
Emergency services including the Metropolitan Police and London Ambulance Service responded to the scene at approximately 01:15 BST.

title: Russia is threatening escalation against Britain: Here’s how they could do it
author: David Blair; Roland Oliphant
content:
“You send a message that you are capable of penetrating a Western airport and Western Europe, and potentially it might be extremely damaging, but you stop short of causing any real damage. That would serve the purpose, because the purpose we have seen since 2022 in Russian sabotage operations was always to raise the costs of supplying support to Ukraine and raising the costs of protecting critical infrastructure.”
Given that Russia is also doubtless seeking to divide British society and stir up as much trouble as possible, there are plenty of other methods that have already been tried elsewhere. In France, Russian agents have variously deposited pigs’ heads outside mosques, defaced synagogues and vandalised the country’s Holocaust memorial. They even left mock coffins under the Eiffel Tower. The French government has also blamed Russia for trying to frighten tourists away from Paris by spreading the story in 2023 that the city’s hotels were infected with bed bugs.
Many of those operations could be traced back to a Russian company called the Social Design Agency, which is close to the Kremlin, according to leaked documents published by Delfi, an Estonian news website.
Last month, British police officials warned that both Russia and Iran were trying their best to inflame social conflict. “Their ultimate goal is destabilising our democracy, sowing division and chaos, and disturbing our peace,” said Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing.
Assassinate Britons inside Britain
Likelihood: Medium
Russian intelligence has a long record of murdering – or trying to murder – people on British soil. But, so far, the targets have always been Russian exiles whom the Kremlin would consider traitors. The former spy Alexander Litvinenko, for instance, suffered an agonising death in 2006 when two Russian agents poisoned him with radioactive polonium in a London hotel. Later, in 2018, two GRU officers attempted to kill Sergei Skripal, a Russian defector, with Novichok nerve agent in Salisbury. Skripal survived, but his erstwhile assassins carelessly discarded their lethal substance, which killed Dawn Sturgess, an innocent British mother of three.
If Russia wished to escalate, it could expand its target list to include British citizens involved in arming Ukraine. Once again, events in Germany may provide a guide. In 2024, the CIA uncovered a Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, the German defence giant.
His British counterpart would be Charles Woodburn, the chief executive of BAE Systems, the biggest British defence company and a supplier of advanced drones to Ukraine. But Woodburn – and others like him – will presumably be well-protected against any threat.
Indeed, killing people in Britain might be harder than doing so elsewhere in Europe. “It should not be completely ruled out, but Britain has built experience because of the Litvinenko and Skripal cases,” says Katia Glod, the deputy head of foreign policy at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre. “It’s harder to do that in Britain today than in Germany or France, which are probably more penetrated by [Russian] spies.”
Attack British facilities in Ukraine
Likelihood: High
This is probably the most likely option for any Russian escalation. Britain’s effort to supply Ukraine relies on a network of physical facilities inside that country. The existence of some has been publicly disclosed. In March, the Ministry of Defence said there were four “maintenance, repair and overhaul” facilities in Ukraine, where “UK companies with British and Ukrainian workforces” were engaged in reconditioning armoured fighting vehicles and artillery.
BAE Systems, meanwhile, announced in 2023 that it was establishing a “local presence” inside Ukraine. If Russia knows where any of these facilities are located, striking them with missiles or drones – and probably killing any Britons working inside them – would be a straightforward way of retaliating against Britain.
“They probably would try to start with something on Ukrainian territory,” says Soldatov. “They are actually quite creative at identifying what belongs to which country in Ukraine, so they might attack some facilities which they think might have some connections to Britain.”
What about British diplomatic premises, such as the embassy in Kyiv? Russia is less likely to take that step because it has plenty of embassies of its own and therefore retains an interest in preserving the immunity of diplomatic premises.
As for the drones that Britain is sending to Ukraine for long-range strikes on Russia, one option would be to target them as soon as they enter the country. Moskovsky Komsomolets, a Russian daily, recently pointed out that the drones in question are delivered as finished products and suggested targeting the containers the moment they crossed the border into Ukraine. That would require precise intelligence about the timing of drone consignments and the exact lorries in which they are carried.
Whether the Russians have acquired such detailed information is unknown. If they have, using this intelligence to destroy the British-supplied drones before they can take off would be the most logical response.
Direct military strikes on Britain with missiles or armed drones
Likelihood: Low
As Ukrainian attacks cripple oil refineries, giant warehouses and arms factories across Russia, the Kremlin must be sorely tempted to hit back against one of its enemy’s principal allies. At this moment, almost everywhere in Europe and particularly in Britain, advanced weapons are being made for Ukraine to use against Russian soldiers on the frontline and increasingly against targets in Russia itself.
Tempting but still unlikely. With its force bogged down in Ukraine and its arms-making capacity stretched to the limit, the last thing that Russia needs is to provoke a retaliatory attack from Nato. If a Russian missile or drone were to slam into a British arms factory, killing scores or hundreds of people inside, the danger is that Britain might invoke Article V, the mutual defence clause of the Nato treaty, and Putin’s difficulties would suddenly become even greater.
“I don’t think the military logic would allow that option,” says Glod. “I don’t think the Kremlin discounts the possibility of a Nato kinetic strike back and it wouldn’t be able to counter that because of its stretched military production.”
Despite the blood-curdling words of the Russian embassy in London – though it is notable that the threatening statement did not come from a higher level, such as the foreign ministry in Moscow or the Kremlin itself – the most likely outcome is that Russia will step up the existing campaign against Britain. Its operatives will probably do more of the same, running the gamut of sabotage, drone incursions, cyber attacks and disinformation, while staying just below the level of triggering open armed conflict.
“In many ways,” says Galeotti, referring to the embassy statement, “the language is an expression of impotence because, yes, Putin does have escalatory options, but they all have massive costs and risks for Russia.”
summary: Russia is considering potential escalations against Britain to raise the costs of supporting Ukraine and to destabilize British society through operations such as sabotage and disinformation. While methods like hybrid warfare, attacks on British facilities in Ukraine, or targeting UK-supplied weapons are possible, direct military strikes on Britain remain unlikely due to the risk of triggering NATO's mutual defense clause. Consequently, Russia is expected to continue utilizing covert tactics like sabotage and cyber attacks that remain just below the threshold of open armed conflict.
key_points: Russian sabotage and influence operations aim to raise the costs of supporting Ukraine and sow division in Western societies.
Potential escalation tactics include targeting British citizens involved in arming Ukraine or attacking British maintenance and repair facilities located within Ukraine.
Direct military strikes on British soil are considered unlikely because they risk triggering NATO's Article V mutual defense clause.
Russia is most likely to intensify its existing campaign of sabotage, drone incursions, cyber attacks, and disinformation.

title: Burnham hits back after Russia threat over Ukraine’s ‘use of British drones’
author: Athena Stavrou
content:
Andy Burnham has insisted Britain will continue to “support Ukraine 100 per cent” despite Russia threatening “consequences” for strikes made with British-built drones.
Russia’s embassy to the UK said reports that Ukrainian forces had used unmanned aircraft manufactured by two UK companies “confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis”.
It accused Britain of “seeking to contain Russia and inflict maximum damage on it by proxy” and warned that the deeper its involvement becomes, “the higher the price it will pay”.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” it said.
But the prime minister hit back, saying Britain would not be deterred by the threats. Asked what his message to Vladimir Putin was after Russia accused the UK of escalating the war, Mr Burnham said: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100 per cent against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin.
“We are providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself, and that’s been the British position all the way through this conflict by previous prime ministers.
![During a visit to Wolverhampton bus station, Andy Burnham was asked what his message to Vladimir Putin was after Russia accused the UK of escalating the war and warned of consequences](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/18/12/2026-08-18T112027Z_2032056839_RC2W0NAWW3SC_RTRMADP_3_BRITAIN-POLITICS-BURNHAM.JPG)
“It remains the case with me. We are not fair weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”
His defiant stance comes after a government minister insisted that Britain would continue to supply Ukraine with military equipment and continue to “stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine”, despite Moscow’s warning.
Work and pensions minister Lilian Greenwood told Sky News on Tuesday: “The Russians should be clear that our resolve remains completely steadfast in backing our friends in Ukraine and providing them with the equipment that they need.
However, Russia’s warning has raised questions over Putin’s willingness to strike Britain, risking Nato intervention in Russia.
Andrey Fedorov, former deputy foreign minister of Russia, said there was a feeling in Moscow that Nato will not hit back at Russia, even if the UK is attacked.
“Taking into consideration current instability within Nato, current problems within Nato, it’s quite possible that Nato will do nothing,” he told BBC Radio 4.
“[It] will make a statement, or will use Article Four, but not Article Five. It’s linked first of all to Donald Trump, who is still the keeper of the keys in Nato.”
Former Tory defence secretary Grant Shapps told The Independent Nato “undoubtedly has genuine problems”, not least the political divisions within the West, but Putin “would be a fool to mistake disagreement for weakness in a moment of true crisis”.
He added: “Britain, France, Germany and Poland alone spend around $318bn a year on defence, compared with Russia’s $190bn, and I cannot imagine those countries standing aside if a Nato member were deliberately attacked.
“For all Putin’s rhetoric and bluster, his behaviour tells us something important: he still fears what Nato can do when it is stirred into action. His strategy has always been to divide, intimidate and test the alliance without triggering its overwhelming collective strength. He should be extremely careful not to miscalculate.”
![The Ministry of Defence underlined its support for Ukraine’s actions](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/18/07/13962173b1f9365e7b8041b044c55eaaY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MTE5NzMz-2.34417666.jpg)
Former foreign secretary Sir Malcolm Rifkind warned the UK “is a nuclear weapon state, which would make a Russian missile or drone attack a much higher risk for Putin than a non-nuclear weapon target state”.
He said he believed Nato would respond, adding, “On such a high-profile issue Trump would not veto Article 5 (which does not require that we go to war with Russia, but requires the allies to decide how to respond). Even if I am wrong, the rest of Nato (Europe plus Canada) would support the UK.”
Former national security adviser Peter Ricketts said: “This was a golden opportunity handed to a Russian propagandist to try to intimidate and divide British opinion, and he took it with gusto. The Russians have regarded us as a hostile state for many years and we have to expect their sabotage/subversion will continue. But we shouldn’t be spooked by Mr Fedorov.”
A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies.”
Kyiv has stepped up operations inside Russia this year, increasingly deploying long-range missiles and drone swarms against military industries and energy facilities.
It has also targeted giant depots for Wildberries – Russia’s largest online retailer – burning billions of pounds of merchandise and bringing the war home to the Russian public more than four years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine’s strategy of long-range drone strikes is believed to be aimed at cutting Moscow’s revenue for the war and making Russian citizens feel the impact of the invasion, with the attacks contributing to mounting economic damage.
It launched three times as many of those strikes in July as it did in January, according to data from Acled, an independent conflict monitor.
Repeatedly hitting deep into Russia has forced its military to stretch air defences over a larger area.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said on Saturday that it had shot down 598 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions, as well as the Black and Azov Seas and the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea.
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has stated that Britain will continue to support Ukraine unconditionally despite Russian threats of consequences over the use of British-built drones. Russia's embassy accused London of escalating the conflict, but British officials and ministers reaffirmed their steadfast resolve to supply military equipment. While some analysts suggested Moscow might test NATO unity, former defense figures and officials emphasized that the UK is a nuclear power and that NATO allies would respond to any attack.
key_points: Andy Burnham insisted the UK will support Ukraine 100 per cent and will not be deterred by Russian threats.
Russia warned of consequences after reports that Ukrainian forces used British-manufactured drones.
Work and pensions minister Lilian Greenwood confirmed that Britain's resolve to back Ukraine remains steadfast.
Former officials debated whether Russia might miscalculate NATO's unity, noting the UK's status as a nuclear-armed state.
Ukraine has significantly increased its long-range drone strikes deep inside Russia to impact Moscow's war revenue.

title: Andy Burnham calls on wider society to help end homelessness by Christmas
author: Rowena Mason
content:
Andy Burnham has said government money alone may not be enough to get rough sleepers off the streets by Christmas, as he issued a “rallying call” for councils, charities and communities to help solve the problem.
Speaking on a visit to the north-east of England, he said he felt “very passionately” about tackling homelessness and wanted the wider society to play a part in wiping it out.
The prime minister acknowledged that not every rough sleeper might take the offer “for their own reasons”. But he said a nationwide effort to stop as much rough sleeping as possible by Christmas was the aim – replicating what happened in the Covid pandemic.
Burnham told reporters: “The government money may not fully get us there, and I’m saying to wider society, faith organisations, let’s see if we can do this together. Let’s see if Britain can do this. Give everybody an offer to come inside before Christmas. You know, that is just something we can do.
“We did it in the pandemic. We can do it again, and it’s a rallying call, really, that I’m putting out there today, with a lot of government money behind it.”
Burnham wrote in the Guardian on Tuesday that rough sleeping has become so common it now “feels like part of the scenery”, as he pledged another £100m to tackle the problem this winter.
The announcement puts tackling homelessness as a central policy for Burnham’s government, and gives voters a measure by which to judge his success.
![A row of tents outside the Midland Hotel in Manchester last year.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/23a5573cd8e3ddc77ae2197de10bcce506053f6e/0_0_8192_5464/master/8192.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham introduced schemes such as A Bed Every Night to offer emergency accommodation, but while the number of rough sleepers fell, it then began to rise again.
The prime minister said this was because “we were the only place providing that level of support, and understandably, people then travelled to Greater Manchester to access that support”.
He added: “So my point is, we can do this, but only if all areas are pulling in the same direction, and that’s what this funding is designed to achieve – to make this a nationwide initiative as we go into the Christmas period, getting everybody behind it.”
He said people being left to sleep on the streets “can often cost more to the state because people can be in and out of A&E, and in and out of hospital beds, and sometimes in contact with the police”.
As part of the national effort, Burnham said he would host a summit this autumn to “bring together leaders from across society – from business, finance, charities, health, faith communities and more – to ask what role each of them can play in ending rough sleeping”.
after newsletter promotion
![Andy Burnham stands in a grassy garden area with three women as one speaks as if she is explaining something. There are garden tools behind them and a brick wall by a large and grand-looking brick and stone building behind black iron railings.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/97a38a045f729d53f3a006d4f28f2f54ea3c352b/0_0_5304_3536/master/5304.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Burnham said on Wednesday that he would be donating 15% of the additional salary he gets as prime minister to homelessness causes.
Speaking to the Big Issue, he said he wanted to continue what he had been doing as mayor of Greater Manchester. He has already said he would donate 15% of the salary he gets for being an MP to local causes in his constituency of Makerfield.
He told the magazine: “For the best part of nine, almost 10 years, I donated 15% of my salary as mayor of Greater Manchester to tackling homelessness in Greater Manchester.
“I am making a commitment to donate the same of my prime minister’s salary. I’m donating part of my constituency MP salary to local organisations, but the extra bit that comes with being prime minister, I’m making the same commitment.
“I wouldn’t want to ask anybody to do anything that I’m not prepared to do. I want to lead from the front. This issue matters massively to me.”
The latest annual national statistics, published in February, estimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough on a single night in autumn 2025 in England. This was a new record and the fourth annual increase in a row, with 43% of those people sleeping rough in London and the south-east.
summary: Andy Burnham has issued a rallying call for councils, charities, faith organizations, and communities to help eliminate rough sleeping by Christmas. Backed by £100m in winter funding and modeled after efforts during the Covid pandemic, the initiative aims to offer indoor accommodation to every rough sleeper nationwide. Burnham also announced he will host a summit this autumn and commit 15% of his prime minister's salary to homelessness causes.
key_points: Andy Burnham stated that government funding alone may not be enough to end rough sleeping by Christmas without a nationwide community effort.
A new £100m winter funding package is being deployed to encourage all areas to pull in the same direction and offer everyone a place to come inside.
Burnham will host an autumn summit bringing together leaders from business, finance, charities, health, and faith communities.
Burnham committed to donating 15% of his additional salary as prime minister to homelessness causes.

title: Palestinian couple and teenage daughter who died in water off Shoreham named by police - follow live
author: Live Reporting Edited by Angus Thompson; Caitlin Doherty; With Writing
content:
We can now bring you photos of Hassan El-Khawas, 55, Zeina Alayn, 37, and 14-year-old Sara El-Khawas, who died after getting into difficulty in the sea in Shoreham on Tuesday.
The family are British citizens of Palestinian origin, with roots in the Rashidieh refugee camp in Lebanon, according to the Palestinian Forum in Britain.
![Hassan El-Khawas](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/8/19/8cae7670-4b78-410c-ae27-3d3372175109.jpg.webp) Image source, Al-Arab in UK
